entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and to my office, where most of the morning doing business and seeing my window-frames new painted, and then I out by coach to my Lord Bellasses, at his new house by my late Lord Treasurer’s, and there met him and Mr. Sherwin, Auditor Beale, and Creed, about my Lord’s accounts, and here my Lord shewed me his new house, which, indeed, is mighty noble, and good pictures--indeed, not one bad one in it. Thence to my tailor’s, and there did find Mercer come with Mrs. Horsfield and Gayet according to my desire, and there I took them up, it being almost twelve o’clock, or a little more, and carried them to the King’s playhouse, where the doors were not then open; but presently they did open; and we in, and find many people already come in, by private ways, into the pit, it being the first day of Sir Charles Sidly’s new play, so long expected, “The Mullberry Guarden,” of whom, being so reputed a wit, all the world do expect great matters. I having sat here awhile, and eat nothing to-day, did slip out, getting a boy to keep my place; and to the Rose Tavern, and there got half a breast of mutton, off of the spit, and dined all alone. And so to the play again, where the King and Queen, by and by, come, and all the Court; and the house infinitely full. But the play, when it come, though there was, here and there, a pretty saying, and that not very many neither, yet the whole of the play had nothing extraordinary in it, at all, neither of language nor design; insomuch that the King I did not see laugh, nor pleased the whole play from the beginning to the end, nor the company; insomuch that I have not been less pleased at a new play in my life, I think. And which made it the worse was, that there never was worse musick played--that is, worse things composed, which made me and Captain Rolt, who happened to sit near me, mad. So away thence, very little satisfied with the play, but pleased with my company. I carried them to Kensington, to the Grotto, and there we sang, to my great content, only vexed, in going in, to see a son of Sir Heneage Finch’s beating of a poor little dog to death, letting it lie in so much pain that made me mad to see it, till, by and by, the servants of the house chiding of their young master, one of them come with a thong, and killed the dog outright presently. Thence to Westminster palace, and there took boat and to Fox Hall, where we walked, and eat, and drank, and sang, and very merry. But I find Mrs. Horsfield one of the veriest citizen’s wives in the world, so full of little silly talk, and now and then a little sillily bawdy, that I believe if you had her sola a man might hazer all with her. So back by water to Westminster Palace, and there got a coach which carried us as far as the Minorys, and there some thing of the traces broke, and we forced to ‘light, and walked to Mrs. Horsfield’s house, it being a long and bad way, and dark, and having there put her in a doors, her husband being in bed, we left her and so back to our coach, where the coachman had put it in order, but could not find his whip in the dark a great while, which made us stay long. At last getting a neighbour to hold a candle out of their window Mercer found it, and so away we home at almost 12 at night, and setting them both at their homes, I home and to bed.

levels.sentence: After a morning of business and a much-anticipated play that proved a disappointment, I spent a pleasant evening singing and making merry with my companions, despite a cruel incident with a dog and a troublesome journey home.
levels.paragraph: I attended to business and visited Lord Bellasses, then took Mercer, Mrs. Horsfield, and Gayet to the premiere of Sir Charles Sidly's "The Mulberry Garden," which failed to please the King or the company. I dined alone on mutton during the play, and afterwards we sang at Kensington and made merry at Fox Hall. However, I was vexed by a young Finch beating a dog to death, and found Mrs. Horsfield to be a silly, bawdy citizen's wife. The coach ride home was plagued by a broken trace and a lost whip, and I arrived home near midnight.
levels.summary:
I rose and went to my office, where I spent most of the morning on business and oversaw the painting of my window-frames. Then I took a coach to Lord Bellasses' new house, near my late Lord Treasurer's, where I met with him, Mr. Sherwin, Auditor Beale, and Creed, to discuss my Lord's accounts.

He showed me his new house, which is mighty noble and filled with good pictures, not one bad one in it.

From there I went to my tailor's, where I found Mercer, along with Mrs. Horsfield and Gayet, as I had requested. " The house was infinitely full, and the King and Queen came with all the Court.

But the play had nothing extraordinary in it, neither language nor design, and the King did not laugh nor show pleasure the whole time. Even the music was bad, which maddened me and Captain Rolt, who sat near me.

I had slipped out during the play to the Rose Tavern for half a breast of mutton, since I had eaten nothing that day.

After the play, I carried them to Kensington to the Grotto, where we sang to my great content, though I was vexed entering to see Sir Heneage Finch's son beating a poor little dog to death; the servants eventually killed it outright to end its pain.

Then we went to Westminster Palace, took a boat to Fox Hall, and walked, ate, drank, and sang, being very merry. However, I found Mrs.

Horsfield to be one of the veriest citizen's wives in the world, full of little silly talk and occasionally a little sillily bawdy, such that if a man had her alone he might do anything with her.

We returned by water to Westminster Palace, got a coach that carried us as far as the Minorys, where one of the traces broke, forcing us to light and walk in the dark to Mrs. Horsfield's house.

After putting her inside, where her husband was already in bed, we went back to the coach, which the coachman had repaired, but he could not find his whip in the dark for a long while, until a neighbour held a candle out a window and Mercer found it.

We finally got home at almost twelve at night, and after setting Mercer and Gayet at their homes, I went to bed.
levels.outline:
- Morning business and visit to Lord Bellasses.
  - I went to my office and spent the morning on business, overseeing the painting of my window-frames.
  - I took a coach to Lord Bellasses' new house.
    - I met him, Mr. Sherwin, Auditor Beale, and Creed about his accounts.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and busy to send some things into the country, and then to the Office, where meets me Sir Richard Ford, who among other things congratulates me, as one or two did yesterday, my great purchase; and he advises me rather to forbear, if it be not done, as a thing that the world will envy me in: and what is it but my cozen Tom Pepys’s buying of Martin Abbey, in Surry! which is a mistake I am sorry for, and yet do fear that it may spread in the world to my prejudice. All the morning at the office, and at noon my clerks dined with me, and there do hear from them how all the town is full of the talk of a meteor, or some fire, that did on Saturday last fly over the City at night, which do put me in mind that, being then walking in the dark an hour or more myself in the garden, after I had done writing, I did see a light before me come from behind me, which made me turn back my head; and I did see a sudden fire or light running in the sky, as it were towards Cheapside ward, and it vanished very quick, which did make me bethink myself what holyday it was, and took it for some rocket, though it was much brighter than any rocket, and so thought no more of it, but it seems Mr. Hater and Gibson going home that night did meet with many clusters of people talking of it, and many people of the towns about the city did see it, and the world do make much discourse of it, their apprehensions being mighty full of the rest of the City to be burned, and the Papists to cut our throats. Which God prevent! Thence after dinner I by coach to the Temple, and there bought a new book of songs set to musique by one Smith of Oxford, some songs of Mr. Cowley’s, and so to Westminster, and there to walk a little in the Hall, and so to Mrs.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, to set right some little matters of my Tangier accounts, and so to the office, where busy all the morning, and then home with my people to dinner, and after dinner comes about a petition for a poor woman whose-ticket she would get paid, and so talked a little and did baiser her, and so to the office, being pleased that this morning my bookseller brings me home Marcennus’s book of musick,’ which costs me L3 2s.; but is a very fine book. So to the office and did some business, and then by coach to the New Exchange, and there by agreement at my bookseller’s shop met Mercer and Gayet, and took them by water, first to one of the Neat-houses, where walked in the garden, but nothing but a bottle of wine to be had, though pleased with seeing the garden; and so to Fox Hall, where with great pleasure we walked, and then to the upper end of the further retired walk, and there sat and sang, and brought great many gallants and fine people about us, and, upon the bench, we did by and by eat and drink what we had, and very merry: and so with much pleasure to the Old Swan, and walked with them home, and there left them, and so I home to my business at the office a little, and so to bed.

levels.sentence: After setting my Tangier accounts and office business, I bought a costly music book and spent a delightful evening with Mercer and Gayet, walking in gardens, singing, and feasting at Fox Hall before returning home to bed.
levels.paragraph: This morning I put my Tangier accounts in order and worked at the office, then dined at home. After dinner a poor woman came with a petition to get her ticket paid, and I kissed her. My bookseller brought me Marcennus's book of musick, a fine volume costing £3 2s. Later I met Mercer and Gayet at the New Exchange, took them by water to the Neat-houses and Fox Hall, where we walked, sang, and made merry among the gallants. We returned by the Old Swan, I walked them home, and then I did a little office business before bed.
levels.summary:
I rose and set right some small matters in my Tangier accounts, then went to the office and was busy all morning. I came home to dine with my people. After dinner, a poor woman presented a petition for her ticket to be paid; I talked with her a little and kissed her, then went back to the office.

, which pleased me greatly.

Later I took a coach to the New Exchange and, by agreement, met Mercer and Gayet at my bookseller's shop. We went by water first to one of the Neat-houses, where we walked in the garden—though only a bottle of wine could be had, the garden itself was a pleasure.

Then we went to Fox Hall, where we walked with great pleasure and sat in the upper end of the further retired walk. There we sang, and many gallants and fine people gathered about us. We ate and drank what we had on the bench, and were very merry.

Afterwards we went with much pleasure to the Old Swan and walked home with the women, where I left them. I returned home, did a little business at the office, and went to bed.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Betimes up, and up to my Tangier accounts, and then by water to the Council Chamber, and there received some directions from the Duke of York and the Committee of the Navy there about casting up the charge of the present summer’s fleete, that so they may come within the bounds of the sum given by the Parliament. But it is pretty to see how Prince Rupert and other mad, silly people, are for setting out but a little fleete, there being no occasion for it; and say it will be best to save the money for better uses. But Sir W. Coventry did declare that, in wisdom, it was better to do so; but that, in obedience to the Parliament, he was setting out the fifty sail talked on, though it spent all the money, and to little purpose; and that this was better than to leave it to the Parliament to make bad construction of their thrift, if any trouble should happen. Thus wary the world is grown! Thence back again presently home, and did business till noon: and then to Sir G. Carteret’s to dinner, with much good company, it being the King’s birthday, and many healths drunk: and here I did receive another letter from my Lord Sandwich, which troubles me to see how I have neglected him, in not writing, or but once, all this time of his being abroad; and I see he takes notice, but yet gently, of it, that it puts me to great trouble, and I know not how to get out of it, having no good excuse, and too late now to mend, he being coming home. Thence home, whither, by agreement, by and by comes Mercer and Gayet, and two gentlemen with them, Mr. Monteith and Pelham, the former a swaggering young handsome gentleman, the latter a sober citizen merchant. Both sing, but the latter with great skill-the other, no skill, but a good voice, and a good basse, but used to sing only tavern tunes; and so I spent all this evening till eleven at night singing with them, till I was tired of them, because of the swaggering fellow with the base, though the girl Mercer did mightily commend him before to me. This night je had agreed par’ alter at Deptford, there par’ avoir lain con the moher de Bagwell, but this company did hinder me.

levels.sentence: A day of official naval accounting and King's birthday dinner, shadowed by guilt over my long silence to Lord Sandwich, and ended with a weary evening of singing that thwarted my planned visit to Bagwell's wife.
levels.paragraph: I rose early to reckon my Tangier accounts, then attended the Council, where Sir W. Coventry argued that we must obey Parliament by fitting out fifty sail even at waste, lest thrift be misconstrued. After business and a birthday dinner at Carteret's, I was stung by a letter from Lord Sandwich gently noting my long silence. Back home, Mercer brought singers, but the swaggering Monteith tired me with tavern bass till eleven, so my planned trip to Deptford and Bagwell's wife came to nothing.
levels.summary:
Betimes I rose and set to my Tangier accounts; afterward I went by water to the Council Chamber, where the Duke of York and the Navy Committee directed me to cast up the charge of the present summer's fleet, that it might come within the bounds of the Parliament's grant.

I found it amusing that Prince Rupert and other mad, silly people argued for a small fleet, saying there was no need and we should save money for better uses. But Sir W.

Coventry declared that in wisdom it would be better to do so, yet in obedience to Parliament he was setting out the fifty sail talked on, even though it would spend all the money to little purpose; he thought this better than leaving Parliament to make a bad construction of our thrift if any trouble happened.

Thus wary is the world grown.

Thence I returned home and did business till noon, then dined at Sir G. Carteret's with much good company, it being the King's birthday, and many healths drunk.

There I received another letter from my Lord Sandwich, which troubled me to see how I have neglected him, not writing, or only once, all the time he was abroad.

He takes notice of it, but gently, and it puts me to great trouble; I know not how to get out of it, having no good excuse, and it is too late now to mend, since he is coming home.

Afterward I went home, where by agreement came Mercer and Gayet with two gentlemen, Mr. Monteith and Mr. Pelham—Monteith a swaggering, handsome young gentleman, the latter a sober citizen merchant. Both sang; Pelham had great skill, Monteith no skill but a good voice and a good bass, used only to tavern tunes.

I spent all the evening till eleven at night singing with them, and grew tired of them because of the swaggering fellow with the bass, though Mercer had mightily commended him to me before.

This night I had agreed to go to Deptford, there to lie with the wife of Bagwell, but this company hindered me.

entries.brief: A day of official naval accounting and King's birthday dinner, shadowed by guilt over my long silence to Lord Sandwich, and ended with a weary evening of singing that thwarted my planned visit to Bagwell's wife.
entries.full:
Betimes I rose and set to my Tangier accounts; afterward I went by water to the Council Chamber, where the Duke of York and the Navy Committee directed me to cast up the charge of the present summer's fleet, that it might come within the bounds of the Parliament's grant.

I found it amusing that Prince Rupert and other mad, silly people argued for a small fleet, saying there was no need and we should save money for better uses. But Sir W.

Coventry declared that in wisdom it would be better to do so, yet in obedience to Parliament he was setting out the fifty sail talked on, even though it would spend all the money to little purpose; he thought this better than leaving Parliament to make a bad construction of our thrift if any trouble happened.

Thus wary is the world grown.

Thence I returned home and did business till noon, then dined at Sir G. Carteret's with much good company, it being the King's birthday, and many healths drunk.

There I received another letter from my Lord Sandwich, which troubled me to see how I have neglected him, not writing, or only once, all the time he was abroad.

He takes notice of it, but gently, and it puts me to great trouble; I know not how to get out of it, having no good excuse, and it is too late now to mend, since he is coming home.

Afterward I went home, where by agreement came Mercer and Gayet with two gentlemen, Mr. Monteith and Mr. Pelham—Monteith a swaggering, handsome young gentleman, the latter a sober citizen merchant. Both sang; Pelham had great skill, Monteith no skill but a good voice and a good bass, used only to tavern tunes.

I spent all the evening till eleven at night singing with them, and grew tired of them because of the swaggering fellow with the bass, though Mercer had mightily commended him to me before.

This night I had agreed to go to Deptford, there to lie with the wife of Bagwell, but this company hindered me.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and put on a new summer black bombazin suit, and so to the office; and being come now to an agreement with my barber, to keep my perriwig in good order at 20s. a-year, I am like to go very spruce, more than I used to do. All the morning at the office and at noon home to dinner, and so to the King’s playhouse, and there saw “Philaster;” where it is pretty to see how I could remember almost all along, ever since I was a boy, Arethusa, the part which I was to have acted at Sir Robert Cooke’s; and it was very pleasant to me, but more to think what a ridiculous thing it would have been for me to have acted a beautiful woman. Thence to Mr. Pierces, and there saw Knepp also, and were merry; and here saw my little Lady Katherine Montagu come to town, about her eyes, which are sore, and they think the King’s evil, poor, pretty lady. Here I was freed from a fear that Knepp was angry or might take advantage to declare the essay that je did the other day, quand je was con her... Thence to the New Exchange, and there met Harris and Rolt, and one Richards, a tailor and great company-keeper, and with these over to Fox Hall, and there fell into the company of Harry Killigrew, a rogue newly come back out of France, but still in disgrace at our Court, and young Newport and others, as very rogues as any in the town, who were ready to take hold of every woman that come by them. And so to supper in an arbour: but, Lord! their mad bawdy talk did make my heart ake! And here I first understood by their talk the meaning of the company that lately were called Ballets; Harris telling how it was by a meeting of some young blades, where he was among them, and my Lady Bennet and her ladies; and their there dancing naked, and all the roguish things in the world. But, Lord! what loose cursed company was this, that I was in to-night, though full of wit; and worth a man’s being in for once, to know the nature of it, and their manner of talk, and lives. Thence set Rolt and some of at the New Exchange, and so I home, and my business being done at the office, I to bed.

levels.paragraph: This day I made myself very spruce with a new bombazin suit and a barber's agreement for my perriwig, then did my office business and dined at home before going to the King's playhouse to see Philaster. It was pleasant to find I still remembered almost all of Arethusa, the part I had once been meant to act as a boy, though I laughed at the thought of my acting a beautiful woman. Later I visited Mr. Pierces, saw Knepp and little Lady Katherine Montagu, and was freed from a fear that Knepp meant to disclose an essay I had made with her. In the evening I fell in with very loose company at Fox Hall, heard their bawdy talk, learned what the Ballets were, and came home to bed.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up and with Sir J. Minnes to Westminster, and in the Hall there I met with Harris and Rolt, and carried them to the Rhenish wine-house, where I have not been in a morning--nor any tavern, I think, these seven years and more. Here I did get the words of a song of Harris that I wanted. Here also Mr. Young and Whistler by chance met us, and drank with us. Thence home, and to prepare business against the afternoon, and did walk an hour in the garden with Sir W. Warren, who do tell me of the great difficulty he is under in the business of his accounts with the Commissioners of Parliament, and I fear some inconveniences and troubles may be occasioned thereby to me. So to dinner, and then with Sir J. Minnes to White Hall, and there attended the Lords of the Treasury and also a committee of Council with the Duke of York about the charge of this year’s fleete, and thence I to Westminster and to Mrs. Martin’s, and did hazer what je would con her, and did once toker la thigh de su landlady, and thence all alone to Fox Hall, and walked and saw young Newport, and two more rogues of the town, seize on two ladies, who walked with them an hour with their masks on; perhaps civil ladies; and there I left them, and so home, and thence to Mr. Mills’s, where I never was before, and here find, whom I indeed saw go in, and that did make me go thither, Mrs. Hallworthy and Mrs. Andrews, and here supped, and, extraordinary merry till one in the morning, Mr. Andrews coming to us: and mightily pleased with this night’s company and mirth I home to bed. Mrs. Turner, too, was with us.

levels.sentence: I mixed official business with tavern company, flirtation, and a late, merry supper at Mr. Mills's, ending the day mightily pleased.
levels.paragraph: A morning at a tavern after years, business worries with Sir W. Warren, official attendance at White Hall, a visit to Mrs. Martin, a walk at Fox Hall, and a merry late supper at Mr. Mills's with the ladies.
levels.summary:
This morning I went with Sir J. Minnes to Westminster, and in the Hall I met Harris and Rolt. I carried them to the Rhenish wine-house – the first time I have been in a tavern in the morning, I think, for over seven years – and there I got the words of a song of Harris that I had wanted. By chance Mr. Young and Mr.

Whistler met us and drank with us. Then I went home to prepare business for the afternoon, and walked an hour in the garden with Sir W. Warren, who told me of the great difficulty he is under in his accounts with the Commissioners of Parliament; I fear some inconveniences may be occasioned to me thereby.

After dinner I went with Sir J. Minnes to White Hall, where I attended the Lords of the Treasury and also a committee of Council with the Duke of York about the charge of this year’s fleet. Thence I went to Westminster to Mrs. Martin’s, and did what I would with her, and once touched the thigh of her landlady.

From there I went alone to Fox Hall, where I saw young Newport and two other town rogues seize on two ladies, who walked with them for an hour with their masks on – perhaps they were civil ladies – and I left them there.

Then I went home, and thence to Mr. Mills’s house, where I had never been before. There I found – and indeed I had seen her go in, which was what made me go thither – Mrs. Hallworthy and Mrs. Andrews. We supped and were extraordinary merry until one in the morning, Mr. Andrews coming to us, and Mrs.

Turner also being with us. I was mightily pleased with this night’s company and mirth, and so went home to bed.

entries.raw: Up, and to the office, where all the morning. At noon home to dinner, and there dined with me, besides my own people, W. Batelier and Mercer, and we very merry. After dinner, they gone, only Mercer and I to sing a while, and then parted, and I out and took a coach, and called Mercer at their back-door, and she brought with her Mrs. Knightly, a little pretty sober girl, and I carried them to Old Ford, a town by Bow, where I never was before, and there walked in the fields very pleasant, and sang: and so back again, and stopped and drank at the Gun, at Mile End, and so to the Old Exchange door, and did buy them a pound of cherries, cost me 2s., and so set them down again; and I to my little mercer’s Finch, that lives now in the Minories, where I have left my cloak, and did here baiser su moher, a belle femme, and there took my cloak which I had left there, and so by water, it being now about nine o’clock, down to Deptford, where I have not been many a day, and there it being dark I did by agreement aller a la house de Bagwell, and there after a little playing and baisando we did go up in the dark a su camera... and to my boat again, and against the tide home. Got there by twelve o’clock, taking into my boat, for company, a man that desired a passage--a certain western bargeman, with whom I had good sport, talking of the old woman of Woolwich, and telling him the whole story.

entries.brief: After a morning at the office and a merry dinner with Batelier and Mercer, I took Mercer and Mrs. Knightly to Old Ford for singing and cherries, then retrieved my cloak from Finch's, kissed his beautiful wife, and went down to Deptford to visit Mrs. Bagwell before returning home by midnight.
entries.full:
Up, and to the office, where I stayed all the morning. At noon I came home to dinner, and besides my own people, W. Batelier and Mercer dined with me, and we were very merry.

After dinner, when the others were gone, Mercer and I sang a while, and then I went out, took a coach, called Mercer at their back door, and she brought with her Mrs. Knightly, a little pretty sober girl.

I carried them to Old Ford, a town by Bow where I had never been; there we walked in the pleasant fields and sang, and on the way back we stopped and drank at the Gun at Mile End. , and set them down again.

Then I went to my little mercer Finch, who lives now in the Minories, where I had left my cloak. There I kissed his wife, a beautiful woman, and took my cloak. About nine o'clock, by water, I went down to Deptford, where I had not been in many a day.

It being dark, I went by agreement to Bagwell's house, and after a little playing and kissing we went up in the dark to her chamber. Afterward I returned to my boat and came home against the tide, getting there by twelve o'clock.

I took into my boat, for company, a western bargeman who desired a passage, and I had good sport with him, talking of the old woman of Woolwich and telling him the whole story.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and Creed and Colonell Atkins come to me about sending coals to Tangier: and upon that most of the morning. Thence Creed and I to Alderman Backewell’s about Tangier business of money, and thence I by water (calling and drinking, but not baisado, at Michell’s) to Westminster, but it being holyday did no business, only to Martin’s... and so home again by water, and busy till dinner, and then with wife, Mercer, Deb., and W. Hewer to the Duke of York’s playhouse, and there saw “The Impertinents,” a pretty good play; and so by water to Spring Garden, and there supped, and so home, not very merry, only when we come home, Mercer and I sat and sung in the garden a good while, and so to bed.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Busy all the morning at my office. At noon dined, and then I out of doors to my bookseller in Duck Lane, but su moher not at home, and it was pretty here to see a pretty woman pass by with a little wanton look, and je did sequi her round about the street from Duck Lane to Newgate Market, and then elle did turn back, and je did lose her. And so to see my Lord Crew, whom I find up; and did wait on him; but his face sore, but in hopes to do now very well again. Thence to Cooper’s, where my wife’s picture almost done, and mighty fine indeed. So over the water with my wife, and Deb., and Mercer, to Spring-Garden, and there eat and walked; and observe how rude some of the young gallants of the town are become, to go into people’s arbours where there are not men, and almost force the women; which troubled me, to see the confidence of the vice of the age: and so we away by water, with much pleasure home. This day my plate-maker comes with my four little plates of the four Yards, cost me L5, which troubles me, but yet do please me also.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and by water to White Hall, and thence to Sir W. Coventry, but he is gone out of town this morning, so thence to my Lord Arlington’s house, the first time I there since he come thither, at Goring House, a very fine, noble place; and there he received me in sight of several Lords with great respect. I did give him an account of my journey; and here, while I waited for him a little, my Lord Orrery took notice of me, and begun discourse of hangings, and of the improvement of shipping: I not thinking that he knew me, but did then discover it, with a mighty compliment of my abilities and ingenuity, which I am mighty proud of; and he do speak most excellently. Thence to Westminster Hall, and so by coach to the old Exchange, and there did several businesses, and so home to dinner, and then abroad to Duck Lane, where I saw my belle femme of the book vendor, but had no opportunity para hazer con her. So away to Cooper’s, where I spent all the afternoon with my wife and girl, seeing him-make an end of her picture, which he did Jo my great content, though not so great as, I confess, I expected, being not satisfied in the greatness of the resemblance, nor in the blue garment: but it is most certainly a most rare piece of work, as to the painting. He hath L30 for his work--and the chrystal, and case, and gold case comes to L8 3s. 4d.; and which I sent him this night, that I might be out of debt. Thence my people home, and I to Westminster Hall about a little business, and so by water home supper, and my wife to read a ridiculous book I bought today of the History of the Taylors’ Company, and all the while Deb. did comb my head, and I did toker her with my main para very great pleasure, and so to bed.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and to my office, there to set my journal for all the last week, and so by water to Westminster to the Exchequer, and thence to the Swan, and there drank and did baiser la fille there, and so to the New Exchange and paid for some things, and so to Hercules Pillars,’ and there dined all alone, while I sent my shoe to have the heel fastened at Wotton’s, and thence to White Hall to the Treasury chamber, where did a little business, and thence to the Duke of York’s playhouse and there met my wife and Deb. and Mary Mercer and Batelier, where also W. Hewer was, and saw “Hamlet,” which we have not seen this year before, or more; and mightily pleased with it; but, above all, with Betterton, the best part I believe, that ever man acted. Thence to the Fayre, and saw “Polichinelle,” and so home, and after a little supper to bed. This night lay the first night in Deb.’s chamber, which is now hung with that that hung our great chamber, and is now a very handsome room. This day Mrs. Batelier did give my wife a mighty pretty Spaniel bitch, which she values mightily, and is pretty; but as a new comer, I cannot be fond of her.

That day Mrs. Batelier gave my wife a spaniel bitch, but I cannot yet love the newcomer.

The chief pleasure of the day came when I went to the Duke of York's playhouse and met my wife, Deb, Mary Mercer, and Batelier, with W. Hewer also there.

We saw Hamlet, which we have not seen for a year or more, and I was mightily pleased with it—above all with Betterton, whom I believe to be the best part that ever man acted. From the theatre we went to the Fayre and saw Polichinelle, and so home to a little supper and to bed.

That night I lay for the first time in Deb's chamber, which has now been hung with what formerly hung our great chamber, and it makes a very handsome room. Also this day Mrs.

entries.brief: After a morning of errands and a little business, I met my wife and friends at the Duke of York's playhouse, saw Hamlet with Betterton's incomparable acting, and came home to sleep for the first time in Deb's newly hung chamber.
entries.full:
This morning I rose and went to my office, where I settled my journal for the past week, then took a boat to Westminster and the Exchequer. From there I went to the Swan, where I drank and kissed the girl, and then to the New Exchange to pay for some things.

I dined alone at Hercules Pillars, and in the meantime sent my shoe to Wotton's to have the heel fastened. Afterwards I went to White Hall and spent a little time on business at the Treasury chamber.

The chief pleasure of the day came when I went to the Duke of York's playhouse and met my wife, Deb, Mary Mercer, and Batelier, with W. Hewer also there.

We saw Hamlet, which we have not seen for a year or more, and I was mightily pleased with it—above all with Betterton, whom I believe to be the best part that ever man acted. From the theatre we went to the Fayre and saw Polichinelle, and so home to a little supper and to bed.

That night I lay for the first time in Deb's chamber, which has now been hung with what formerly hung our great chamber, and it makes a very handsome room. Also this day Mrs.

Batelier gave my wife a mighty pretty spaniel bitch, which my wife values greatly; it is pretty enough, but because it is a newcomer I cannot yet be fond of her.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up and all the morning at the office busy, and after dinner to the office again busy till about four, and then I abroad (my wife being gone to Hales’s about drawing her hand new in her picture) and I to see Betty Michell, which I did, but su mari was dentro, and no pleasure. So to the Fair, and there saw several sights; among others, the mare that tells money, and many things to admiration; and, among others, come to me, when she was bid to go to him of the company that most loved a pretty wench in a corner. And this did cost me 12d. to the horse, which I had flung him before, and did give me occasion to baiser a mighty belle fille that was in the house that was exceeding plain, but fort belle. At night going home I went to my bookseller’s in Duck Lane, and find her weeping in the shop, so as ego could not have any discourse con her nor ask the reason, so departed and took coach home, and taking coach was set on by a wench that was naught, and would have gone along with me to her lodging in Shoe Lane, but ego did donner her a shilling... and left her, and home, where after supper, W. Batelier with us, we to bed. This day Mrs. Martin come to see us, and dined with us.

entries.raw: Up betimes, and Knepp’s maid comes to me, to tell me that the women’s day at the playhouse is to-day, and that therefore I must be there, to encrease their profit. I did give the pretty maid Betty that comes to me half-a-crown for coming, and had a baiser or two-elle being mighty jolie. And so I about my business. By water to St. James’s, and there had good opportunity of speaking with the Duke of York, who desires me again, talking on that matter, to prepare something for him to do for the better managing of our Office, telling me that, my Lord Keeper and he talking about it yesterday, my Lord Keeper did advise him to do so, it being better to come from him than otherwise, which I have promised to do. Thence to my Lord Burlington’s houses the first time I ever was there, it being the house built by Sir John Denham, next to Clarendon House; and here I visited my Lord Hinchingbroke and his lady; Mr. Sidney Montagu being come last night to town unexpectedly from Mount’s Bay, where he left my Lord well, eight days since, so as we may now hourly expect to hear of his arrival at Portsmouth. Sidney is mighty grown; and I am glad I am here to see him at his first coming, though it cost me dear, for here I come to be necessitated to supply them with L500 for my Lord. levels.sentence: A day of pressing duties—to the playhouse women, the Duke of York, and my Lord's family—was sweetened by a pretty maid's kisses but shadowed by Sidney Montagu's arrival with a demand for money.
levels.paragraph: I rose early to a day crowded with claims on me: Knepp's maid reminded me of the women's day at the playhouse; the Duke of York asked me to draft a plan for better managing our Office; and at Lord Burlington's house I found Sidney Montagu newly come from Mount's Bay, with news that Lord Sandwich needed money and expected me to supply L500. I paid the pretty messenger with half-a-crown and a kiss or two, promised the Duke what he asked, and felt my duty to my Lord more keenly because I had written to him so seldom during the voyage. Sir W. Godolphin arrived before I could think further.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and to the office, and before the office did speak with my Lord Brouncker, and there did get his ready assent to T. Hater’s having of Mr. Turner’s place, and so Sir J. Minnes’s also: but when we come to sit down at the Board, comes to us Mr. Wren this day to town, and tells me that James Southern do petition the Duke of York for the Storekeeper’s place of Deptford, which did trouble me much, and also the Board, though, upon discourse, after he was gone, we did resolve to move hard for our Clerks, and that places of preferment may go according to seniority and merit. So, the Board up, I home with my people to dinner, and so to the office again, and there, after doing some business, I with Mr. Turner to the Duke of Albemarle’s at night; and there did speak to him about his appearing to Mr. Wren a friend to Mr. Turner, which he did take kindly from me; and so away thence, well pleased with what we had now done, and so I with him home, stopping at my Lord Brouncker’s, and getting his hand to a letter I wrote to the Duke of York for T.

Minnes's, but at the Board Mr. Wren told me that James Southern was petitioning the Duke of York for the Storekeeper's place at Deptford, which troubled me and the Board. After Wren left, we agreed to press hard for our clerks and for preferment by seniority and merit. That night, with Mr. Turner, I visited the Duke of Albemarle and asked him to befriend Turner before Wren; he took it kindly. I came away well pleased, stopped at Lord Brouncker's to get his signature on my letter to the Duke of York for T. Hater, and felt hopeful.

This morning, before the Board sat, I spoke with Lord Brouncker and secured his ready assent for T. Hater to have Mr. Turner's place, as well as Sir J. Minnes's place. But once we were at the Board, Mr.

Wren came to town and told me that James Southern was petitioning the Duke of York for the Storekeeper's place of Deptford. This troubled me and the whole Board.

After Wren left, we reasoned together and resolved to move hard on behalf of our clerks, insisting that places of preferment should go according to seniority and merit.

After the Board rose, I went home with my people to dinner, then returned to the office and did some business. In the evening I went with Mr. Turner to the Duke of Albemarle's house, where I spoke to the Duke about appearing to Mr. Wren as a friend to Mr. Turner; he took my request kindly.

We came away well pleased with what we had done, and on the way home I stopped at Lord Brouncker's to get his hand to a letter I had written to the Duke of York for T. Hater. I felt hopeful that our efforts would keep the places in the hands of our own clerks.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Lay long in bed talking with my wife, she being unwilling to have me go abroad, saying and declaring herself jealous of my going out for fear of my going to Deb., which I do deny, for which God forgive me, for I was no sooner out about noon but I did go by coach directly to Somerset House, and there enquired among the porters there for Dr. Allbun, and the first I spoke with told me he knew him, and that he was newly gone into Lincoln’s Inn Fields, but whither he could not tell me, but that one of his fellows not then in the way did carry a chest of drawers thither with him, and that when he comes he would ask him. This put me into some hopes, and I to White Hall, and thence to Mr. Povy’s, but he at dinner, and therefore I away and walked up and down the Strand between the two turnstiles, hoping to see her out of a window, and then employed a porter, one Osberton, to find out this Doctor’s lodgings thereabouts, who by appointment comes to me to Hercules pillars, where I dined alone, but tells me that he cannot find out any such, but will enquire further. Thence back to White Hall to the Treasury a while, and thence to the Strand, and towards night did meet with the porter that carried the chest of drawers with this Doctor, but he would not tell me where he lived, being his good master, he told me, but if I would have a message to him he would deliver it. At last I told him my business was not with him, but a little gentlewoman, one Mrs. Willet, that is with him, and sent him to see how she did from her friend in London, and no other token. He goes while I walk in Somerset House, walk there in the Court; at last he comes back and tells me she is well, and that I may see her if I will, but no more. So I could not be commanded by my reason, but I must go this very night, and so by coach, it being now dark, I to her, close by my tailor’s, and she come into the coach to me, and je did baiser her.... I did nevertheless give her the best council I could, to have a care of her honour, and to fear God, and suffer no man para avoir to do con her as je have done, which she promised. Je did give her 20s. and directions para laisser sealed in paper at any time the name of the place of her being at Herringman’s, my bookseller in the ‘Change, by which I might go para her, and so bid her good night with much content to my mind, and resolution to look after her no more till I heard from her. And so home, and there told my wife a fair tale, God knows, how I spent the whole day, with which the poor wretch was satisfied, or at least seemed so, and so to supper and to bed, she having been mighty busy all day in getting of her house in order against to-morrow to hang up our new hangings and furnishing our best chamber.

levels.sentence: Despite my wife's jealousy, I spent the day tracking down Deb Willet, kissed her in a coach, gave her money and advice, and returned to tell my wife a fair tale.
levels.paragraph: I lay long in bed while my wife told me she was jealous that I meant to visit Deb; I denied it, and God forgive me, I was no sooner out than I went straight to Somerset House to find her. After much searching and several messengers, I found her that night, took her into a coach, kissed her, and told her to guard her honour. I gave her twenty shillings and a way to write to me, resolved to see her no more until she did. Then I went home and told my wife a fair tale, which she seemed content with, and we ended the day preparing our best chamber for new hangings.
levels.summary:
I began the day lying long in bed with my wife, who was unwilling I should go out and plainly declared herself jealous, fearing I meant to visit Deb. I denied it, God forgive me, for no sooner was I out about noon than I took a coach directly to Somerset House.

There I asked the porters for Dr Allbun, and the first I spoke with knew him and said he was newly gone into Lincoln's Inn Fields, though he could not tell me where; one of his fellows had carried a chest of drawers thither with him, and the porter promised to ask. This put me into hopes.

From there I went to White Hall and then to Mr Povy's, but he was at dinner, so I walked up and down the Strand between the two turnstiles, hoping to see her out of a window.

I employed a porter, one Osberton, to find out the Doctor's lodgings thereabouts; he met me at the Hercules Pillars, where I dined alone, but told me he could not find any such and would enquire further.

I went back to White Hall to the Treasury a while, and then into the Strand again, and towards night I met the very porter who had carried the chest of drawers with this Doctor. He would not tell me where the Doctor lived, because he was his good master, but said if I had a message he would deliver it.

I told him my business was not with the Doctor but with a little gentlewoman, one Mrs. Willet, who was with him, and sent him to see how she did from her friend in London, and no other token.

While he went I walked in the Court at Somerset House. At last he came back and told me she was well, and that I might see her if I would, but no more. I could not be commanded by my reason, but I must go that very night.

So by coach, it being now dark, I went to her, close by my tailor's, and she came into the coach to me, and I did kiss her. I gave her the best counsel I could, to have a care of her honour, and to fear God, and suffer no man to have to do with her as I had done, which she promised. I gave her 20s.

and directions to leave sealed in paper at any time the name of the place of her being at Herringman's, my bookseller in the 'Change, so that I might go to her; then I bid her good night with much content to my mind, and a resolution to look after her no more till I heard from her.

And so home, where I told my wife a fair tale, God knows, of how I had spent the whole day, and the poor wretch was satisfied, or at least seemed so. Then to supper and to bed, she having been mighty busy all day in getting the house in order against to-morrow, to hang up our new hangings and furnish our best chamber.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and at the Office all the morning, with my heart full of joy to think in what a safe condition all my matters now stand between my wife and Deb, and me, and at noon running up stairs to see the upholsters, who are at work upon hanging my best room, and setting up my new bed, I find my wife sitting sad in the dining room; which enquiring into the reason of, she begun to call me all the false, rotten-hearted rogues in the world, letting me understand that I was with Deb. yesterday, which, thinking it impossible for her ever to understand, I did a while deny, but at last did, for the ease of my mind and hers, and for ever to discharge my heart of this wicked business, I did confess all, and above stairs in our bed chamber there I did endure the sorrow of her threats and vows and curses all the afternoon, and, what was worse, she swore by all that was good that she would slit the nose of this girle, and be gone herself this very night from me, and did there demand 3 or L400 of me to buy my peace, that she might be gone without making any noise, or else protested that she would make all the world know of it. So with most perfect confusion of face and heart, and sorrow and shame, in the greatest agony in the world I did pass this afternoon, fearing that it will never have an end; but at last I did call for W. Hewer, who I was forced to make privy now to all, and the poor fellow did cry like a child, obtained what I could not, that she would be pacified upon condition that I would give it under my hand never to see or speak with Deb, while I live, as I did before with Pierce and Knepp, and which I did also, God knows, promise for Deb. too, but I have the confidence to deny it to the perjury of myself.

levels.sentence: Though I began the day rejoicing that all matters were safe between my wife, Deb, and me, I was soon discovered, forced to confess my renewed pursuit of Deb, and spent the afternoon enduring my wife's curses and threats before purchasing my peace with a written promise I intend to deny.
levels.paragraph: I started the day at the Office with my heart full of joy, thinking how safely matters stood between my wife, Deb, and me, but when I ran upstairs to see the upholsterers hanging my best room and setting up my new bed, I found my wife sitting sad in the dining room. She taxed me with being with Deb yesterday, and though I denied it for a while, I finally confessed all for the ease of my mind and hers. Upstairs in our bedchamber I then endured the sorrow of her threats, vows, and curses all afternoon, as she swore to slit the girl's nose and demanded three or four hundred pounds to leave me quietly. At last I called W. Hewer, who wept like a child and persuaded her to accept a written promise that I would never see or speak with Deb again.
levels.summary:
I went to the Office all morning with my heart full of joy, congratulating myself that all my matters now stood safe between my wife, Deb, and me. At noon I ran upstairs to see the upholsterers, who were at work hanging my best room and setting up my new bed, and there I found my wife sitting sad in the dining room.

She soon began to call me every false, rotten-hearted rogue in the world, letting me know that she understood I had been with Deb yesterday.

Thinking it impossible that she could ever have known, I denied it for a while, but at last, for the ease of my mind and hers and to discharge my heart of this wicked business, I confessed all.

Upstairs in our bedchamber I endured the sorrow of her threats, vows, and curses all the afternoon.

She swore by all that was good that she would slit the nose of this girl and be gone herself that very night from me, and she demanded three or four hundred pounds to buy my peace, so that she might leave without making any noise; otherwise she protested she would make all the world know of it.

I passed the afternoon in the most perfect confusion of face and heart, in sorrow and shame, in the greatest agony in the world, fearing that it would never have an end.

At last I called for W. Hewer, who I was forced to make privy now to all; the poor fellow cried like a child and obtained what I could not, for he persuaded her to be pacified upon condition that I would give it under my hand never to see or speak with Deb while I live, as I did before with Pierce and Knepp.

I did so, and I also promised, God knows, for Deb too, but I have the confidence to deny it, to the perjury of myself.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and walked abroad in the garden, and find that Mrs. Tooker has not any of her daughters here as I expected and so walked to the yard, leaving Middleton at the pay, and there I only walked up and down the yard, and then to the Hill-House, and there did give order for the coach to be made ready; and got Mr. Gibson, whom I carried with me, to go with me and Mr. Coney, the surgeon, towards Maydston which I had a mighty mind to see, and took occasion, in my way, at St. Margett’s, to pretend to call to see Captain Allen to see whether Mrs. Jowles, his daughter, was there; and there his wife come to the door, he being at London, and through a window, I spied Jowles, but took no notice of he but made excuse till night, and then promised to come and see Mrs. Allen again, and so away, it being a mighty cold and windy, but clear day; and had the pleasure of seeing the Medway running, winding up and down mightily, and a very fine country; and I went a little out of the way to have visited Sir John Bankes, but he at London; but here I had a sight of his seat and house, the outside, which is an old abbey just like Hinchingbroke, and as good at least, and mighty finely placed by the river; and he keeps the grounds about it, and walls and the house, very handsome: I was mightily pleased with the sight of it. Thence to Maydstone, which I had a mighty mind to see, having never been there; and walked all up and down the town, and up to the top of the steeple, and had a noble view, and then down again: and in the town did see an old man beating of flax, and did step into the barn and give him money, and saw that piece of husbandry which I never saw, and it is very pretty: in the street also I did buy and send to our inne, the Bell, a dish of fresh fish. And so, having walked all round the town, and found it very pretty, as most towns I ever saw, though not very big, and people of good fashion in it, we to our inne to dinner, and had a good dinner; and after dinner a barber come to me, and there trimmed me, that I might be clean against night, to go to Mrs. Allen. And so, staying till about four o’clock, we set out, I alone in the coach going and coming; and in our way back, I ‘light out of the way to see a Saxon monument, as they say, of a King, which is three stones standing upright, and a great round one lying on them, of great bigness, although not so big as those on Salisbury Plain; but certainly it is a thing of great antiquity, and I mightily glad to see it; it is near to Aylesford, where Sir John Bankes lives. So homeward, and stopped again at Captain Allen’s, and there ‘light, and sent the coach and Gibson home, and I and Coney staid; and there comes to us Mrs. Jowles, who is a very fine, proper lady, as most I know, and well dressed. Here was also a gentleman, one Major Manly, and his wife, neighbours; and here we staid, and drank, and talked, and set Coney and him to play while Mrs. Jowles and I to talk, and there had all our old stories up, and there I had the liberty to salute her often, and pull off her glove, where her hand mighty moist, and she mighty free in kindness to me, and je do not at all doubt that I might have had that that I would have desired de elle had I had time to have carried her to Cobham, as she, upon my proposing it, was very willing to go, for elle is a whore, that is certain, but a very brave and comely one. Here was a pretty cozen of hers come in to supper also, of a great fortune, daughter-in-law to this Manly, mighty pretty, but had now such a cold, she could not speak. Here mightily pleased with Mrs. Jowles, and did get her to the street door, and there to her su breasts, and baiser her without any force, and credo that I might have had all else, but it was not time nor place. Here staid till almost twelve at night, and then with a lanthorn from thence walked over the fields, as dark as pitch, and mighty cold, and snow, to Chatham, and Mr. Coney with great kindness to me: and there all in bed before I come home, and so I presently to bed.

levels.sentence: I took a cold, windy day-trip to Maidstone, pleased by the countryside and old sights, then spent a late, flirtatious evening at Captain Allen's with the willing Mrs. Jowles before walking home through snow.
levels.paragraph: I set out with Gibson and Coney for Maidstone, stopping on the way to spy Mrs. Jowles through a window at Captain Allen's without letting on. I delighted in the Medway valley, Sir John Bankes's abbey-house, and the pretty town of Maidstone, where I watched flax-beating and bought fish for dinner. On the way back I viewed an ancient Saxon monument, then returned to Captain Allen's, where Mrs. Jowles allowed me great liberties. We stayed near midnight, and I walked through snow and darkness back to Chatham with Coney.
levels.summary:
Waking, I walked in the garden and found that Mrs Tooker had not brought any of her daughters as I had expected. I went to the yard, leaving Middleton at the pay, and after walking up and down I gave orders at the Hill-House for the coach to be made ready.

I took Mr Gibson with me, and Mr Coney the surgeon, and set out for Maidstone, which I had a mighty mind to see.

On the way, at St Margett's, I pretended to call on Captain Allen to see whether his daughter Mrs Jowles was there. His wife came to the door—he was in London—and I spied Jowles through a window but took no notice, excusing myself until night and promising to come again.

It was a mighty cold and windy but clear day, and I had the pleasure of seeing the Medway winding through a very fine country.

I went a little out of my way to visit Sir John Bankes, but he was in London; still I had a sight of his house, an old abbey just like Hinchingbroke and as good, finely placed by the river with handsome grounds and walls.

At Maidstone I walked all about the town and up to the top of the steeple for a noble view. I saw an old man beating flax, stepped into the barn to give him money, and found that piece of husbandry very pretty.

I bought a dish of fresh fish and sent it to our inn, the Bell, and after a good dinner a barber came and trimmed me so I should be clean to visit Mrs Allen at night.

Staying until about four, I set out alone in the coach, and on the way back stopped to see a Saxon monument near Aylesford—three upright stones with a great round one lying across them, a thing of great antiquity.

I stopped again at Captain Allen's, sent the coach and Gibson home, and stayed with Coney. Mrs Jowles came in, a very fine, proper, well-dressed lady, and there was also Major Manly and his wife, and later a pretty cozen of hers, daughter-in-law to Manly, who had such a cold she could not speak.

I set Coney and the Major to play while Mrs Jowles and I talked over all our old stories; I had the liberty to salute her often and pull off her glove, and found her mighty free and kind.

I do not doubt I might have had what I desired had there been time to carry her to Cobham, for she was very willing; she is certainly a whore, but a brave and comely one.

I got her to the street door and there kissed and touched her breasts without any force, and believe I might have had all else had it been time and place.

We stayed till almost twelve, and then with a lantern I walked with Coney over the fields,—dark as pitch, mighty cold and snowy,—to Chatham. Everyone was already in bed when I got home, and I presently went to bed.

prose.brief: I took a cold, windy day-trip to Maidstone, pleased by the countryside and old sights, then spent a late, flirtatious evening at Captain Allen's with the willing Mrs. Jowles before walking home through snow.
prose.full:
Waking, I walked in the garden and found that Mrs Tooker had not brought any of her daughters as I had expected. I went to the yard, leaving Middleton at the pay, and after walking up and down I gave orders at the Hill-House for the coach to be made ready.

I took Mr Gibson with me, and Mr Coney the surgeon, and set out for Maidstone, which I had a mighty mind to see.

On the way, at St Margett's, I pretended to call on Captain Allen to see whether his daughter Mrs Jowles was there. His wife came to the door—he was in London—and I spied Jowles through a window but took no notice, excusing myself until night and promising to come again.

It was a mighty cold and windy but clear day, and I had the pleasure of seeing the Medway winding through a very fine country.

I went a little out of my way to visit Sir John Bankes, but he was in London; still I had a sight of his house, an old abbey just like Hinchingbroke and as good, finely placed by the river with handsome grounds and walls.

At Maidstone I walked all about the town and up to the top of the steeple for a noble view. I saw an old man beating flax, stepped into the barn to give him money, and found that piece of husbandry very pretty.

I bought a dish of fresh fish and sent it to our inn, the Bell, and after a good dinner a barber came and trimmed me so I should be clean to visit Mrs Allen at night.

Staying until about four, I set out alone in the coach, and on the way back stopped to see a Saxon monument near Aylesford—three upright stones with a great round one lying across them, a thing of great antiquity.

I stopped again at Captain Allen's, sent the coach and Gibson home, and stayed with Coney. Mrs Jowles came in, a very fine, proper, well-dressed lady, and there was also Major Manly and his wife, and later a pretty cozen of hers, daughter-in-law to Manly, who had such a cold she could not speak.

I set Coney and the Major to play while Mrs Jowles and I talked over all our old stories; I had the liberty to salute her often and pull off her glove, and found her mighty free and kind.

I do not doubt I might have had what I desired had there been time to carry her to Cobham, for she was very willing; she is certainly a whore, but a brave and comely one.

I got her to the street door and there kissed and touched her breasts without any force, and believe I might have had all else had it been time and place.

We stayed till almost twelve, and then with a lantern I walked with Coney over the fields,—dark as pitch, mighty cold and snowy,—to Chatham. Everyone was already in bed when I got home, and I presently went to bed.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and to the office, and thence before the office sat to the Excise Office with W. Hewer, but found some occasion to go another way to the Temple upon business, and I by Deb.’s direction did know whither in Jewen Street to direct my hackney coachman, while I staid in the coach in Aldgate Street, to go thither just to enquire whether Mrs. Hunt, her aunt, was in town, who brought me word she was not; thought this was as much as I could do at once, and therefore went away troubled through that I could do no more but to the office I must go and did, and there all the morning, but coming thither I find Bagwell’s wife, who did give me a little note into my hand, wherein I find her para invite me para meet her in Moorfields this noon, where I might speak with her, and so after the office was up, my wife being gone before by invitation to my cozen Turner’s to dine, I to the place, and there, after walking up and down by the windmills, I did find her and talk with her, but it being holiday and the place full of people, we parted, leaving further discourse and doing to another time. Thence I away, and through Jewen Street, my mind, God knows, running that way, but stopped not, but going down Holborne hill, by the Conduit, I did see Deb. on foot going up the hill. I saw her, and she me, but she made no stop, but seemed unwilling to speak to me; so I away on, but then stopped and ‘light, and after her and overtook her at the end of Hosier lane in Smithfield, and without standing in the street desired her to follow me, and I led her into a little blind alehouse within the walls, and there she and I alone fell to talk and baiser la and toker su mammailles, but she mighty coy, and I hope modest.... I did give her in a paper 20s., and we did agree para meet again in the Hall at Westminster on Monday next; and so giving me great hopes by her carriage that she continues modest and honest, we did there part, she going home and I to Mrs. Turner’s, but when I come back to the place where I left my coach it was gone, I having staid too long, which did trouble me to abuse the poor fellow, so that taking another coach I did direct him to find out the fellow and send him to me. At my cozen Turner’s I find they are gone all to dinner to Povy’s, and thither I, and there they were all, and W. Batelier and his sister, and had dined; but I had good things brought me, and then all up and down the house, and mightily pleased to see the fine rooms: but, the truth is, there are so many bad pictures, that to me make the good ones lose much of the pleasure in seeing them. The. and Betty Turner in new flowered tabby gowns, and so we were pretty merry, only my fear upon me for what I had newly done, do keep my content in. So, about five or six o’clock, away, and I took my wife and the two Bateliers, and carried them homeward, and W. Batelier ‘lighting, I carried the women round by Islington, and so down Bishopsgate Street home, and there to talk and sup, and then to bed.

levels.sentence: I stole meetings with Bagwell’s wife and Deb today, and though each encounter gave me pleasure, guilt followed me even into the evening’s company.
levels.paragraph: I went out on business in the morning, but my true errands were secret ones: first to enquire after Deb’s aunt in Jewen Street, and then to keep a noon appointment with Bagwell’s wife in Moorfields, where the holiday crowd let us do no more than talk. Later I saw Deb on Holborne Hill, followed her into a blind alehouse, and took liberties with her, though she stayed coy and modest; I gave her twenty shillings and agreed to meet her again at Westminster. My coach had gone when I returned, and at Povy’s, among friends, I tried to be merry but could not shake my fear of what I had done. At last I carried my wife home by Islington, and we supped quietly.
levels.summary:

By Deb’s direction I knew where in Jewen Street to send my hackney coachman while I waited in the coach in Aldgate Street, so I sent him to enquire whether Mrs.

Hunt, her aunt, was in town; the answer was that she was not. This was all I could do at that moment, and I went away troubled because I could do no more.

Coming to the office, I found Bagwell’s wife, who slipped a note into my hand inviting me to meet her in Moorfields at noon.

They were all there—W. Batelier and his sister—and had already dined, but good things were brought me. I was mightily pleased with the fine rooms, though in truth there are so many bad pictures that they lessen the pleasure of the good ones. The.

and Betty Turner were in new flowered tabby gowns, and we were pretty merry, only my fear of what I had newly done kept my content from being full.

About five or six o’clock I took my wife and the two Bateliers homeward; W. Batelier alighted, and I carried the women round by Islington and so down Bishopsgate Street home. We talked and supped, and then to bed.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Troubled, about three in the morning, with my wife’s calling her maid up, and rising herself, to go with her coach abroad, to gather May-dew, which she did, and I troubled for it, for fear of any hurt, going abroad so betimes, happening to her; but I to sleep again, and she come home about six, and to bed again all well, and I up and with Mr. Gibson by coach to St. James’s, and thence to White Hall, where the Duke of York met the Office, and there discoursed of several things, particularly the Instructions of Commanders of ships. But here happened by chance a discourse of the Council of Trade, against which the Duke of York is mightily displeased, and particularly Mr. Child, against whom he speaking hardly, Captain Cox did second the Duke of York, by saying that he was talked of for an unfayre dealer with masters of ships, about freight: to which Sir T. Littleton very hotly and foolishly replied presently, that he never heard any honest man speak ill of Child; to which the Duke of York did make a smart reply, and was angry; so as I was sorry to hear it come so far, and that I, by seeming to assent to Cox, might be observed too much by Littleton, though I said nothing aloud, for this must breed great heart-burnings. After this meeting done, the Duke of York took the Treasurers into his closet to chide them, as Mr. Wren tells me; for that my Lord Keeper did last night at the Council say, when nobody was ready to say any thing against the constitution of the Navy, that he did believe the Treasurers of the Navy had something to say, which was very foul on their part, to be parties against us. They being gone, Mr. Wren took boat, thinking to dine with my Lord of Canterbury; but, when we come to Lambeth, the gate was shut, which is strictly done at twelve o’clock, and nobody comes in afterwards: so we lost our labour, and therefore back to White Hall, and thence walked my boy Jacke with me, to my Lord Crew, whom I have not seen since he was sick, which is eight months ago, I think and there dined with him: he is mightily broke. A stranger a country gentleman, was with him: and he pleased with my discourse accidentally about the decay of gentlemen’s families in the country, telling us that the old rule was, that a family might remain fifty miles from London one hundred years, one hundred miles from London two hundred years, and so farther, or nearer London more or less years. He also told us that he hath heard his father say, that in his time it was so rare for a country gentleman to come to London, that, when he did come, he used to make his will before he set out. Thence: to St.

entries.brief: I was troubled by my wife's early May-dew outing, and then at White Hall I witnessed a sharp quarrel between the Duke of York and Sir T. Littleton over Mr Child, followed by the Duke chiding the Treasurers, before I dined with the much-broken Lord Crew and heard his old rule about country families and London.
entries.full:
About three in the morning I was troubled to find my wife calling her maid up and rising herself to go abroad in her coach to gather May-dew. I feared some hurt might happen to her by going out so betimes, but she came home about six and went to bed again all well.

I myself then got up, and with Mr Gibson took a coach to St. James's, and thence to White Hall.

At White Hall the Duke of York met the Office, and we discoursed of several things, particularly the Instructions of Commanders of ships. There happened by chance a discourse of the Council of Trade, against which the Duke is mightily displeased, and particularly against Mr Child.

Captain Cox seconded the Duke by saying that Child was talked of as an unfair dealer with masters of ships about freight. To this Sir T. Littleton very hotly and foolishly replied that he never heard any honest man speak ill of Child.

The Duke made a smart reply and was angry; I was sorry to hear it come so far, and feared that by seeming to assent to Cox I might be observed too much by Littleton, though I said nothing aloud. I felt this must breed great heartburnings.

After the meeting, the Duke took the Treasurers into his closet to chide them, as Mr Wren told me; for my Lord Keeper did last night at the Council say, when nobody was ready to say anything against the constitution of the Navy, that he did believe the Treasurers of the Navy had something to say.

This was very foul on their part, to be parties against us.

Then Mr Wren took boat, thinking to dine with my Lord of Canterbury; but when we came to Lambeth, the gate was shut, which is strictly done at twelve o'clock, and nobody comes in afterwards. So we lost our labour and returned to White Hall.

Thence I walked with my boy Jacke to my Lord Crew, whom I have not seen since he was sick, which is eight months ago, and I dined with him. He is mightily broke. A stranger, a country gentleman, was with him; and he was pleased with my discourse, accidentally, about the decay of gentlemen's families in the country.

He told us that the old rule was that a family might remain fifty miles from London one hundred years, one hundred miles from London two hundred years, and so farther, or nearer London, more or less years.

He also told us he had heard his father say that in his time it was so rare for a country gentleman to come to London that, when he did come, he used to make his will before he set out.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and to Westminster Hall, where the term is, and this the first day of my being there, and here by chance met Roger Pepys, come to town the last night: I was glad to see him. After some talk with him and others, and among others Sir Charles Harbord and Sidney Montagu, the latter of whom is to set out to-morrow towards Flanders and Italy, I invited them to dine with me to-morrow, and so to Mrs. Martin’s lodging, who come to town last night, and there je did hazer her, she having been a month, I think, at Portsmouth with her husband, newly come home from the Streights. But, Lord! how silly the woman talks of her great entertainment there, and how all the gentry come to visit her, and that she believes her husband is worth L6 or L700, which nevertheless I am glad of, but I doubt they will spend it a fast. Thence home, and after dinner my wife and I to the Duke of York’s playhouse, and there, in the side balcony, over against the musick, did hear, but not see, a new play, the first day acted, “The Roman Virgin,” an old play, and but ordinary, I thought; but the trouble of my eyes with the light of the candles did almost kill me. Thence to my Lord Sandwich’s, and there had a promise from Sidney to come and dine with me to-morrow; and so my wife and I home in our coach, and there find my brother John, as I looked for, come to town from Ellington, where, among other things, he tell me the first news that my is with child, and fat gone, which I know not whether it did more trouble or please me, having no great care for my friends to have children; though I love other people’s. So, glad to see him, we to supper, and so to bed.

levels.paragraph: We went to Westminster Hall, where I met old acquaintances and made arrangements for tomorrow. Afterwards, I visited Mrs. Martin and was intimate with her, despite her foolish talk about her husband's fortune. Later, my wife and I tried to see a new play, but my eyes troubled me in the candlelight, and we left. At home, I found my brother John, who told me my sister is pregnant, which left me with mixed feelings.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up very betimes, and so continued all the morning with W. Hewer, upon examining and stating my accounts, in order to the fitting myself to go abroad beyond sea, which the ill condition of my eyes, and my neglect for a year or two, hath kept me behindhand in, and so as to render it very difficult now, and troublesome to my mind to do it; but I this day made a satisfactory entrance therein. Dined at home, and in the afternoon by water to White Hall, calling by the way at Michell’s, where I have not been many a day till just the other day, and now I met her mother there and knew her husband to be out of town. And here je did baiser elle, but had not opportunity para hazer some with her as I would have offered if je had had it. And thence had another meeting with the Duke of York, at White Hall, on yesterday’s work, and made a good advance: and so, being called by my wife, we to the Park, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman, a friend of hers, being with us. Thence to “The World’s End,” a drinking-house by the Park; and there merry, and so home late.

levels.sentence: I spent the morning finally making a satisfactory start on my neglected accounts in preparation for going abroad, then kissed Mrs. Michell in her mother's presence, advanced my business with the Duke of York, and finished the night merrily with my wife, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman at The World's End.
levels.paragraph: This day I made a satisfactory beginning at settling my long-neglected accounts, though my weak eyes had made the task troublesome. After dinner I went to Whitehall, stopping at Michell's, where I kissed her but found no opportunity to go further. I then met again with the Duke of York and advanced yesterday's business, before joining my wife, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman in the Park and at The World's End drinking-house, where we were merry until late.
levels.summary:
I rose very early and spent the whole morning with W. Hewer examining and stating my accounts, in order to fit myself to go abroad beyond sea.

The ill condition of my eyes, and my neglect for a year or two, had left me behindhand, making the work difficult and troublesome to my mind; but this day I made a satisfactory entrance therein, and so dined at home.

In the afternoon I took water to Whitehall, calling by the way at Michell's, where I had not been for many a day until the other day.

I met her mother there, and knew her husband to be out of town; and here I did kiss her, but had not the opportunity to do something more with her as I would have offered if I had had it. Then I had another meeting with the Duke of York at Whitehall, on yesterday's work, and made a good advance.

Being called by my wife, we went to the Park, Mary Batelier and a Dutch gentleman, a friend of hers, being with us. Thence to The World's End, a drinking-house by the Park, where we were merry, and so home late.

periods.label: Week of Jan 18

levels.sentence: Mr. Downing told me he had made me a Clerk of the Council, but I feared his favour was only to save his own salary, and the rest of the day was spent in errands, a feast, and news that the other clerks were turned out.
levels.paragraph: This morning Mr. Downing surprised me by saying he had got me made one of the Clerks of the Council; I thanked him, but not heartily, for I suspected he only wanted to ease himself of the salary he pays me. After a morning draft with Sheply and Pierce, I went to Whitehall and got Sir Ant. Cooper's leave to keep our lodgings, so Sheply can go to the country. Later I was kept waiting at Downing's, where I read the Dutch Ambassador's answer contradicting my Lord's reasons for coming home. I dined on turkey with Mrs. Jem, then went to the French Ordinary where Downing feasted several Parliament men, and he gave me a note to invite more members to dinner tomorrow. At Whitehall I heard from the clerks that they are all turned out except the two Leighs, though my name was mentioned last night.
levels.summary:
I was sent for to Mr. Downing's bedside this morning, and he told me he had done me a kindness by getting me made one of the Clerks of the Council.

I was quite stumbled and did not know whether to thank him; I did at last, but not heartily, for I feared that he had done it only to ease himself of the salary he gives me. Mr. Sheply was waiting below, and we went with Mr. Pierce to the Harp and Ball for our morning draft, and then to Whitehall. There I met Sir Ant.

Cooper, gave him my Lord's answer, and he gave us leave to keep the lodgings still, so we resolved that Mr. Sheply could now go into the country, and would do so to-morrow.

By Mr. Downing's order I went back and stayed till noon expecting someone to come and read writings, but he never came; so I sat alone reading the Dutch Ambassador's answer to our State, which labour to contradict my Lord's arguments for coming home. Then I went to my office, and with Mr.

Sheply and Moore dined upon a turkey with Mrs. Jem. After that Mr. Moore and I went to the French Ordinary, where Mr. Downing this day feasted Sir Arth. Haselrigge and a great many more of the Parliament; he stayed to put him in mind of me. He gave me a note to go and invite some other members to dinner to-morrow.

I went to White Hall and stayed at Marsh's with Simons, Luellin, and all the rest of the Clerks of the Council, who I hear are all turned out, only the two Leighs. They all tell me that my name was mentioned last night, but that nothing was done in it.

I then left some of my notes at the lodgings of the members and went home to bed. All day I have been uneasy about Downing's true intent, and the news of the clerks being turned out makes me fear for my own place.
