periods.label: Week of Aug 8

levels.sentence: After ordering a velvet coat, hearing Sir Samuel Morland’s secret service story, dining at the Tower, settling accounts, and going to White Hall, I came home and made sport with the girl and boy combing my head.
levels.paragraph: I went first to the Privy Seal, then to my Lord’s to agree with Mr. Pim on a velvet coat. Back at the Privy Seal, Sir Samuel Morland told me at length how he had served the King under the Protector and what he had sacrificed. I dined at the Tower with my father, Mr. Fairbrother, and Cooke, and received a firkin of butter from Captain Cuttance. I settled my brother’s allowance and my Master of Arts fee before going to White Hall with my wife, then came home and made sport having the servants comb my head.
levels.summary:
At the Privy Seal I attended to business, then went to my Lord’s, where the tailor Mr. Pim and I agreed that he should make me a velvet coat. Returning to the Privy Seal, I found Sir Samuel Morland with a Baronet’s grant that the King had given him to make money of.

He stayed with me a great while and told me the whole manner of his serving the King during the Protectorate: how Thurloe’s bad usage first drove him to it, how he discovered Sir R. Willis, and how he had sunk his fortune for the King.

Now the King has given him a pension of L500 a year out of the Post Office for life and the benefit of two Baronets; this makes me begin to think he is not so much a fool as I once took him to be.

I went home by water to the Tower, where my father, Mr. Fairbrother, and Cooke dined with me. After dinner young Captain Cuttance of the Speedwell came in, sent up for the gratuity given to the seamen who brought the King over, and he brought my wife a firkin of butter, which was very welcome.

My father then took his leave, after I had given him 40s. for the last half year’s allowance for my brother John at Cambridge. I also settled with Mr. Fairbrother for my Master of Arts degree, which cost me about L9 16s.

In the afternoon I went to White Hall with my wife by water, and busied myself at the Privy Seal and elsewhere. At night we came home by water, and I made good sport in the kitchen by having the girl and the boy comb my head before I went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Sep 4

levels.sentence: I saw my mother and Pall off to Brampton, dined merrily at my uncle Fenner's, was troubled by my wife's secret appointment with a French footman, and then heard that my aunt Kite is dying and wants me to take charge.
levels.paragraph: I went to the Privy Seal on business, then met my mother, wife, and Pall and put them into the waggon for Brampton, Pall crying bitterly. Afterwards I drank with my wife, Aunt Bell, and Charles Pepys, and dined at Uncle Fenner's, though my mind was troubled when a French footman privately spoke to my wife and she promised to go somewhere tomorrow. After dinner came news that Aunt Kite, the butcher's widow, is near death and has sent for my uncle and me to take charge of her affairs and her daughter.
levels.summary:
This morning I went to the Privy Seal on business, and on the way took leave of my mother, who is setting out for Brampton today. , and advised her how to behave toward my father and mother. Because it was late, I took them all to Beard's, put them into the waggon, and saw them depart; Pall cried exceedingly.

Then I went in with my wife, Aunt Bell, and Charles Pepys, whom we met there, and after drinking we went to my uncle Fenner's for dinner.

On the way, a French footman with feathers came looking for my wife and spoke to her privately; I could not learn what they said, only that my wife promised to go to some place tomorrow morning, which troubles my mind, for I do not know where it is.

At my uncle's, both his sons and daughters were present, and we were merry and dined.

After dinner, news came that my aunt Kite, the butcher's widow in London, is sick and ready to die. She has sent for my uncle and me to come take charge of things and be entrusted with the care of her daughter.

periods.label: Week of May 28

levels.sentence: After making up my journal and settling some business, I dined with my father, had Sarah clean my hair and wash my feet, cut off my beard in a sudden fit, and reflected on the month's news—the Queen's arrival, peace with Argier, and the discontent over the Act for Uniformity.
levels.paragraph: I started the day catching up on my journal and ended it with a cleaner head and a shaved chin, after a round of errands, a debt dunned by Anthony Joyce, and dinner with my father. Between White Hall and the office I heard the latest court news—the Queen is at Hampton Court and has pleased the King, which I fear will vex Madam Castlemaine. I cut off my beard in a sudden fit, had Sarah comb my head and wash my feet, and took stock of my estate, which I find worth about £530 clear. The month closes with fair weather, peace with Argier, and much public discontent over the Act for Uniformity.
levels.summary:
This morning I lay long in bed, then rose to bring my journal up to date for the past few days. Anthony Joyce came and dunned me for the tallow I had ordered from him lately; it vexes me to owe him, but I promised to pay him next. Afterwards I went to White Hall, hearing that Sir G.

Carteret was in town, but I could not find him, and so returned to Tom's, from whence I took my father to my house. He dined with me, and we discoursed about our businesses with uncle Thomas and T. Trice.

After he departed, I went to the office, where we met; then walked to my Brother's, the Wardrobe, and other places on business, and so home.

At home I had Sarah comb my head clean; it was so foul with powdering and other troubles that I am resolved to try keeping my head dry without powder.

In a sudden fit I also cut off all my beard, which I had been raising for a great while, so that I may use my pumice-stone on my whole face, as I already do my chin, saving time in a genteel way. Sarah then washed my feet in a bath of herbs, and I went to bed.

The month ends with very fair weather; my health is pretty well, though wind still torments me extremely from time to time.

As for news: the Queen was brought a few days since to Hampton Court, and everyone says she is a fine, handsome, discreet lady, and the King is pleased enough with her, which I fear will put Madam Castlemaine's nose out of joint. The Court is wholly at Hampton now.

Peace with Argier has lately been made, which is good news. My father is lately come to town to see us, and though it has cost and will cost more money, I am pleased with the alterations on my house at Brampton. My Lord Sandwich has lately come with the Queen from sea, very well and in good repute.

Upon auditing my estate I find myself worth about £530 clear.

The Act for Uniformity is lately printed, which it is thought will make mad work among the Presbyterian ministers; people of all sides are very discontented, some thinking themselves used contrary to promise too hardly, and others that they are not rewarded as much as they expected by the King. God keep us all.

I have by a late oath obliged myself from wine and plays, of which I find good effect.

periods.label: Week of Dec 31

levels.phrase: A year of mirth and content
levels.sentence: On the last day of 1662 I danced at the King's ball, reviewed my year with gratitude for my health, purse, and growing esteem, and resolved to renew my oaths of orderliness despite small household troubles and the heavy unsettled business with my uncle Thomas.
levels.paragraph: This last day of 1662 I spent in mirth — a merry dinner, a Tangier business errand, and a glorious ball at White Hall where I saw the King and Queen dance. I returned weary but content, and reviewed my year with gratitude: my purse near £650, my home convenient, my health good, and my industry at the office winning me notice. Yet small cares lingered: a proud maid to part with, a boy I must turn away, and my uncle Thomas's business hanging over me.
levels.summary:
I lay pretty long in bed, then went to Westminster Hall and the Swan, where Mr. W. Bowyer told me about his fair cousin Butler and Colonel Dillon being quite broke off, because he had opened letters from Ireland complaining of his knavery and forging others to the contrary.

After a barber's, I took my wife to dinner at Mrs. Pierce's by invitation. Dr. Clerke, his wife and sister, and Mr. Knight, the King's chief surgeon, with his wife, were there. We were pretty merry, the two men being excellent company, though I confess I was wedded from my opinion of Mrs.

Pierce's beauty when I saw her naked neck, she being undrest when we came in, and of Mrs. Clerke's genius, which I so much admired, finding her so conceited and fantastical in her dress and carriage this day, though the truth is, witty enough.

After dinner with much ado the doctor and I got away to follow our business for a while, he to his patients and I to the Tangier Committee, where the Duke of York was, and we stayed at it a good while. Then in order to despatch the boats and provisions for Tangier away, Mr. Povy, in his coach, carried Mr.

Gauden and me into London to Mr. Bland's, the merchant, where we stayed discoursing upon the reason of the delay of the going away of these things a great while. Then we ate a dish of anchovies and drank wine and cider, very merry; but above all things I was pleased to hear Mrs.

Bland talk like a merchant in her husband's business very well, and it seems she understands it and performs a great deal.

Thence merry back, Mr. Povy and I to White Hall, he carrying me thither on purpose to bring me into the ball this night before the King. All the way he talked very ingeniously, and I find him a fine gentleman, one that loves to live nobly and neatly, as I perceive by his discourse of his house, pictures, and horses.

He brought me first to the Duke's chamber, where I saw the Duke and Duchess at supper, and thence into the room where the ball was to be, crammed with fine ladies, the greatest of the Court.

By and by came the King and Queen, the Duke and Duchess, and all the great ones: and after seating themselves, the King took out the Duchess of York; the Duke, the Duchess of Buckingham; the Duke of Monmouth, my Lady Castlemaine; and so other lords other ladies: and they danced the Bransle.

After that, the King led a lady a single Coranto, and then the rest of the lords, one after another, other ladies; very noble it was, and great pleasure to see. Then to country dances, the King leading the first, which he called for, which was, says he, "Cuckolds all awry," the old dance of England.

Of the ladies that danced, the Duke of Monmouth's mistress, my Lady Castlemaine, and a daughter of Sir Harry de Vicke's were the best. The manner was, when the King dances, all the ladies in the room, and the Queen herself, stand up: and indeed he dances rarely, and much better than the Duke of York.

Having stayed here as long as I thought fit, to my infinite content, I went out, leaving them dancing, and to Mrs.

Pierce's, where I found the company had stayed very long for my coming, but all gone but my wife, and so I took her home by coach and so to my Lord's again, where after some supper to bed, very weary and in a little pain from riding a little uneasily to-night in the coach.

Thus ends this year with great mirth to me and my wife. Our condition is thus: we are at present spending a night or two at my Lord's lodgings at White Hall. Our home at the Navy-office is finished and made very convenient.

My purse is worth about £650, besides my goods of all sorts, which yet might have been more but for my late layings out upon my house and public assessment, and yet would not have been so much if I had not lived a very orderly life all this year by virtue of the oaths that God put into my heart to take against wine, plays, and other expenses, which I am now going to renew, I under God owing my present content thereunto.

My family is myself and wife; William, my clerk; Jane, my wife's upper maid, but growing proud and negligent upon it, we must part, which troubles me; Susan, our cook-maid, a pretty willing wench but no good cook; and Wayneman, my boy, who I am now turning away for his naughty tricks.

We have had from the beginning our healths to this day very well, blessed be God! Our late maid Sarah going from us, though put away by us, to live with Sir W. Pen does trouble me, though I love the wench, so that we do make ourselves a little strange to him and his family for it, and resolve to do so.

The same we are for other reasons to my Lady Batten and hers. I have lately had it in my thoughts, and can hardly bring myself off of it, since Mrs.

Gosnell cannot be with us, to find out another woman for my wife that can sing or dance, and yet finding it hard to save anything at the year's end as I now live, I think I shall not be such a fool till I am more warm in my purse, besides my oath of entering into no such expenses till I am worth £1000.

By my last year's diligence in my office, blessed be God, I am come to a good degree of knowledge therein, and am acknowledged so by all the world, even the Duke himself, to whom I have a good access, and by that, and my being Commissioner with him for Tangier, he takes much notice of me; and I doubt not but, by the continuance of the same endeavours, I shall in a little time come to be a man much taken notice of in the world, specially being come to so great an esteem with Mr.

Coventry.

The only weight that lies heavy upon my mind is the ending the business with my uncle Thomas about my dead uncle's estate, which is very ill on our side, and I fear when all is done I must be forced to maintain my father myself, or spare a good deal towards it out of my own purse, which will be a very great pull back to me in my fortune.

But I must be contented and bring it to an issue one way or other.

Public matters stand thus: the King is bringing, as is said, his family, and Navy, and all other his charges, to a less expense; in the mean time himself following his pleasures more than with good advice he would do, at least to be seen to all the world to do so.

His dalliance with my Lady Castlemaine being public, every day, to his great reproach; and his favouring of none at Court so much as those that are the confidants of his pleasure, as Sir H.

Bennet and Sir Charles Barkeley; which, good God, put it into his heart to mend before he makes himself too much contemned by his people for it!

The Duke of Monmouth is in so great splendour at Court, and so dandled by the King, that some doubt, if the King should have no child by the Queen, which there is yet no appearance of, whether he would not be acknowledged for a lawful son; and that there will be a difference follow upon it between the Duke of York and him; which God prevent!

My Lord Chancellor is threatened by people to be questioned the next sitting of the Parliament by some spirits that do not love to see him so great; but certainly he is a good servant to the King. The Queen-Mother is said to keep too great a Court now; and her being married to my Lord St.

Albans is commonly talked of; and that they had a daughter between them in France, how true, God knows.

The Bishops are high, and go on without any diffidence in pressing uniformity; and the Presbyters seem silent in it, and either conform or lay down, though without doubt they expect a turn, and would be glad these endeavours of the other Fanatiques would take effect; there having been a plot lately found, for which four have been publicly tried at the Old Bailey and hanged.

My Lord Sandwich is still in good esteem, and now keeping his Christmas in the country; and I in good esteem, I think, as any man can be, with him. Mr. Moore is very sickly, and I doubt will hardly get over his late fit of sickness that still hangs on him.

In fine, for the good condition of myself, wife, family, and estate, in the great degree that it is, and for the public state of the nation so quiet as it is, the Lord God be praised!

By my last year's diligence in my office, blessed be God, I am come to a good degree of knowledge therein, and am acknowledged so by all the world, even the Duke himself, to whom I have a good access, and by that, and my being Commissioner with him for Tangier, he takes much notice of me; and I doubt not but, by the continuance of the same endeavours, I shall in a little time come to be a man much taken notice of in the world, specially being come to so great an esteem with Mr.

Coventry.

The only weight that lies heavy upon my mind is the ending the business with my uncle Thomas about my dead uncle's estate, which is very ill on our side, and I fear when all is done I must be forced to maintain my father myself, or spare a good deal towards it out of my own purse, which will be a very great pull back to me in my fortune.

But I must be contented and bring it to an issue one way or other.

Public matters stand thus: the King is bringing, as is said, his family, and Navy, and all other his charges, to a less expense; in the mean time himself following his pleasures more than with good advice he would do, at least to be seen to all the world to do so.

His dalliance with my Lady Castlemaine being public, every day, to his great reproach; and his favouring of none at Court so much as those that are the confidants of his pleasure, as Sir H.

Bennet and Sir Charles Barkeley; which, good God, put it into his heart to mend before he makes himself too much contemned by his people for it!

The Duke of Monmouth is in so great splendour at Court, and so dandled by the King, that some doubt, if the King should have no child by the Queen, which there is yet no appearance of, whether he would not be acknowledged for a lawful son; and that there will be a difference follow upon it between the Duke of York and him; which God prevent!

My Lord Chancellor is threatened by people to be questioned the next sitting of the Parliament by some spirits that do not love to see him so great; but certainly he is a good servant to the King. The Queen-Mother is said to keep too great a Court now; and her being married to my Lord St.

Albans is commonly talked of; and that they had a daughter between them in France, how true, God knows.

The Bishops are high, and go on without any diffidence in pressing uniformity; and the Presbyters seem silent in it, and either conform or lay down, though without doubt they expect a turn, and would be glad these endeavours of the other Fanatiques would take effect; there having been a plot lately found, for which four have been publicly tried at the Old Bailey and hanged.

My Lord Sandwich is still in good esteem, and now keeping his Christmas in the country; and I in good esteem, I think, as any man can be, with him. Mr. Moore is very sickly, and I doubt will hardly get over his late fit of sickness that still hangs on him.

In fine, for the good condition of myself, wife, family, and estate, in the great degree that it is, and for the public state of the nation so quiet as it is, the Lord God be praised!

  - Ballroom crammed with Court ladies; King, Queen and great ones arrive

    - Best lady dancers: Monmouth's mistress, Lady Castlemaine, daughter of Sir Harry de Vicke

periods.phrase: A year of mirth and content
periods.sentence: On the last day of 1662 I danced at the King's ball, reviewed my year with gratitude for my health, purse, and growing esteem, and resolved to renew my oaths of orderliness despite small household troubles and the heavy unsettled business with my uncle Thomas.
periods.paragraph: This last day of 1662 I spent in mirth — a merry dinner, a Tangier business errand, and a glorious ball at White Hall where I saw the King and Queen dance. I returned weary but content, and reviewed my year with gratitude: my purse near £650, my home convenient, my health good, and my industry at the office winning me notice. Yet small cares lingered: a proud maid to part with, a boy I must turn away, and my uncle Thomas's business hanging over me.

periods.label: Week of Jul 15

levels.sentence: After a lazy morning at the office and errands about town, I waited at Westminster for Mrs. Lane's bands, toyed with the pretty daughter at Mrs. Howlett's shop, then ate a chicken with Mrs. Lane at the Crown and took such liberties with her that I came away ashamed, sweating, and resolved to sin no more.
levels.paragraph: Up and to my office, where Sir J. Minnes and I did but little business; then, after a bite at home, I went to my bookseller's, bespoke a pocket ruler of Thomson the instrument maker, and passed by the Temple and Wardrobe to Westminster Hall. There Mrs. Lane was fetching my bands from the starchers, and in her absence I flirted with Mrs. Howlett's daughter, who will be a handsome wench, buying gloves for the sake of talk. When Mrs. Lane returned, her bands not yet done, we met at the Crown in Palace Yard, ate a chicken, drank, and were merry, and I towzed her at will; yet the last act shames me, and I resolve never to do more so. I stayed late till the bands were done, then by water to the Temple and walked home all in a sweat, fearful of a cold, and so to bed.
levels.summary:
This morning I was up and at my office, but Sir J. Minnes and I dispatched only a little business.

After eating a bit of victuals at home, I went abroad on several errands: to my bookseller's, and then to Thomson the instrument maker's to bespeak a ruler for my pocket for measuring timber, which I believe he will make to my mind.

From there I went to the Temple, the Wardrobe, and lastly to Westminster Hall, where I expected bands that Mrs. Lane was making for me.

While Mrs. Lane went to the starchers for the bands, I stayed at Mrs. Howlett's shop, where only her daughter—she whom I call my wife—was present, her parents being abroad.

I bought a pair of gloves merely to talk with her, and found her a pretty-spoken girl who will prove a mighty handsome wench; I could love her very well. Presently Mrs.

Lane came back, and because my bands were not done, she and I posted to the Crown in the Palace Yard, where we ate a chicken I sent for, drank, and were mighty merry. I had my full liberty of towzing her and doing what I would, but the last thing of all I am heartily ashamed of, and I do resolve never to do more so.

It was strange to see how her mind ran upon a husband. She showed me her hands to have her fortune told, and every question ended with whom and when she should marry.

I pleased her by saying, as I know she would have me, the same things that all the artists in town had told her: she should live long, be rich, have a good husband, but few children, and suffer a great fit of sickness, with twenty other things.

I stayed late until my bands were finished, then took a boat to the Temple and walked home, all in a sweat from tumbling her and walking. After a little supper I went to bed, fearful of having taken cold.

periods.label: Week of Jul 22

levels.sentence: A morning ride in search of my lost dog turned into unexpected musical delight, and after hastening home I crowded in with the Speaker to hear him offer Parliament's work for the King's royal consent.
levels.paragraph: Riding out to the Wells to look for my dog, I found none of him but plenty of gallant company in the warm weather. A group of citizens singing under a tree in four or five parts pleased me more than almost any music I have known, given the time and place. After drinking three cups with them and watching horsemen make matches, I breakfasted at Yowell on hashed remains of last night's supper. Then I rode hard home, noted Mr. Gauden's fine house without calling, and went by water to Westminster, where I crowded in behind the Speaker to hear him address the King in the Lords' House.
levels.summary:
I rose about seven and, after a little study, resolved to ride to the Wells to look for our dog, but we could hear nothing of him. The day being much warmer than yesterday, there was great store of gallant company, which pleased me more than the day before.

At a distance, under a tree on the common, a company got together that sang; I took them for the Waytes, but riding up I found them only voices — some citizens met by chance, singing in four or five parts excellently.

I have not been more pleased with a snapp of musique, considering the circumstances of the time and place, in all my life.

We drank three cups each, then rode up to the horsemen upon the hill, where they were making matches to run, and so went away to Yowell, where we found our breakfast, the remains of our supper last night hashed.

After the smith had set on two new shoes to Creed's horse, we mounted and, with little discourse, I being intent upon getting home in time, rode hard home. I observed Mr.

Gauden's house, which stands very finely with a graceful view to the highway, but did not call there, it being too late for me to stay and wanting their dog too. We set up our horses at Fox Hall, and I went by water, observing the King's barge attending his going to the House this day, arriving home about one o'clock.

I got myself ready, shifted, and went by water to Westminster, where I came most luckily to the Lords' House as the House of Commons were going into the Lord's House.

I crowded in along with the Speaker and got to stand close behind him, where he made his speech to the King, who sat with his crown on and robes, and all the Lords in their robes, a fine sight. He told his Majesty what they had done this Parliament and now offered for his royall consent.

periods.label: Week of Sep 2

levels.sentence: A busy day spent on errands, visits, and the strange delights of Bartholomew Fayre, from L'Estrange's first newsbooks to a German clockwork sea.
levels.paragraph: I rose early, practiced my viall, and then went by water to Westminster, where I bought the first of L'Estrange's newsbooks. I spoke with Mrs. Lane, visited Mrs. Harper, and found a maid for my wife, then dined at Mr. Povy's and admired his new cellars. Afterwards I took my wife to Bartholomew Fayre, where we saw dancing monkeys and other oddities, and wound up with a clockwork show of the sea. I read a proclamation for apprehending Lord Bristoll, then supped and went to bed.
levels.summary:
I was up betimes and spent an hour at my viall before going by water to White Hall and Westminster Hall, where I bought the first newsbooks of L'Estrange's writing, he beginning this week and making, methinks, but a simple beginning. I then spoke to Mrs.

Lane, who seems desirous to have me come see her and have her company as I had a little while ago; but I thought that if she were very modest, considering how I tumbled her and tossed her, she should not be so forward. Thence I went to Mrs. Harper's, sent for Creed, and there Mrs.

Harper sent for a maid to come live with my wife. I liked the maid's looks well enough, believing she might do well, she looking very modestly and speaking so too, and I directed her to speak with my wife.

Creed and I went to Mr. Povy's, but he was not at home, so we walked in Lincoln's Inn walks, which they are making very fine, and about one o'clock went back to Povy's.

He came in, and we sat down to dinner with his lady, whom I never saw before — a handsome old woman that brought him money and makes him do as he does.

We had plenty of meat and drink, though I drank no wine, being mightily urged to it, and I observed the exact manner of his household as I never saw in my life anywhere, he being the most full and satisfied man in the world with anything.

After dinner I saw his new cellars, so fine with noble arches and contrivances for barrels and bottles, and in the next room such a grotto and fountain as will be as pleasant as anything in the world in summer.

Yet he prides himself too much and expects all admiration, though everything does highly deserve it, which is a little troublesome.

Creed and I departed, and by his importunity went by coach to Bartholomew Fayre, though I had no mind to go without my wife; so I rode through the fair without lighting and went home, leaving him there.

I made my wife get herself presently ready and carried her by coach to the fair, where I showed her the monkeys dancing on ropes, which was strange but such dirty sport that I was not pleased with it. There was also a horse with hoofs like ram's horns, a goose with four feet, and a cock with three.

We went to another place and saw German clockworks, the Salutation of the Virgin Mary, and several scriptural stories; but above all there was represented the sea, with Neptune, Venus, mermaids, and a figure on a dolphin, the sea rocking so well done that, had it been in a gaudy manner and place and at a little distance, it had been admirable.

I then went home by coach with my wife, spent awhile at the office, and so to supper and to bed. This day I read a proclamation for calling in and commanding everybody to apprehend my Lord Bristoll.

periods.label: Week of Sep 23

levels.sentence: After a sobering morning with Sir Philip Warwick about the Navy accounts, I spent the afternoon misbehaving with Mrs. Lane, yet ended the night ashamed before my hardworking wife and resolved to amend.
levels.paragraph: This morning I saw my brother John off to my father's and then went to Sir Philip Warwick, who convinced me the King can owe the Navy no more than £5,000—so Sir G. Carteret must owe the King, even with the Navy debt paid. I left doubting whether I had spoken with enough gravity, though I blamed both my self-distrust and his haste. The office did little without Mr. Coventry, and we seemed a pack of coxcombs. In the afternoon I slipped away to Westminster, found Mrs. Lane, and took her to Lambeth, where I went as far as she would let me—thank God not the main thing—and then came home to find my dear wife hard at work, which grieved me to the heart.
levels.summary:
After taking leave of my brother John as he set out to my father's, I went by water to Sir Philip Warwick. He convinced me that the King cannot be in debt to the Navy more than £5,000 at this time, which made it appear that Sir G. Carteret owes the King money even though the whole Navy debt is paid.

I parted from him feeling doubtful that I had spoken with the gravity and weight such a business required, though I hoped it was only my own self-distrust and the haste he was in, with great personages waiting outside.

At the office we sat doing little now that Mr. Coventry is absent, and I vexed myself to see what coxcombs we are without him to undertake such business. In the afternoon, having told my wife I was going to Deptford, I went by water to Westminster Hall instead, found Mrs.

Lane, and carried her over to Lambeth, where we had lately been. There I did what I would with her except the main thing, which she would not consent to—for which God be praised—and I trust in the Lord I shall never do so again while I live.

When I was tired of her company I landed her at Whitehall and went home to my office, writing letters until almost twelve at night.

Then I came home to supper and bed, and there found my poor wife hard at work, which grieved my heart to see that I should abuse so good a wretch. I know it is just with God to make her bad with me for my wronging her, but I do resolve never to do the like again.

periods.paragraph: This morning I saw my brother John off to my father's and then went to Sir Philip Warwick, who convinced me the King can owe the Navy no more than £5,000—so Sir G. Carteret must owe the King, even with the Navy debt paid. I left doubting whether I had spoken with enough gravity, though I blamed both my self-distrust and his haste. The office did little without Mr. Coventry, and we seemed a pack of coxcombs. In the afternoon I slipped away to Westminster, found Mrs. Lane, and took her to Lambeth, where I went as far as she would let me—thank God not the main thing—and then came home to find my dear wife hard at work, which grieved me to the heart.

periods.label: Week of Nov 4

levels.sentence: I opposed Sir W. Pen at the office, chased Howlett's daughter in Westminster Hall, flirted with a lodger at Unthank's, consulted Dr. Turner about freight, and caught a cold, while Captain Taylor gave me a plate for his ship's demorage.
levels.paragraph: This morning at the office I crossed Sir W. Pen over a mulct on the purser of the James, which made him storm out like an asse. In the afternoon I ran errands by coach, tried to overtake Howlett's daughter in Westminster Hall, and chatted with a pretty lodger at Unthank's. I then consulted Dr. Turner at Doctors' Commons about freight from East India ships. That night I came home with a scurvy cold, having earlier received a piece of plate from Captain Taylor for the demorage of his ship William.
levels.summary:
I rose and went to the office, where we sat all morning. There Sir W. Pen and I had words: I opposed him when he would have excused a mulct imposed on the purser of the James for being absent from duty, which he claimed was by his business and order.

He was mighty angry and went out of the office like an asse discontented. I was not sorry at all, for I would not have him think that I dare not oppose him where I see reason and cause.

After dinner I took a coach abroad on several businesses, among them to Westminster Hall, where I saw Howlett's daughter going out at the other end. I followed her, intending to offer talk and dally a little, but I could not overtake her. Then I called at Unthank's for something of my wife's not done.

A pretty little gentlewoman, a lodger there, came out to tell me it was not yet done; though this vexed me, I took the opportunity to take her by the hand with the boot, and so found matter to talk a little longer to her.

I was ready to laugh at myself to see how my anger would not operate, my disappointment coming to me by such a messenger.

Thence I went to Doctors' Commons and consulted Dr. Turner about differences we have with the officers of the East India ships concerning goods brought by them without paying freight, which we demand of them.

So home to my office, where I wrote letters late, then to supper and to bed, having got a scurvy cold by lying cold in my head the last night.

This day Captain Taylor brought me a piece of plate, a little small state dish, expecting that I should get him some allowance for demorage of his ship William, kept long at Tangier, which I shall and may justly do.

periods.label: Week of Dec 30

levels.sentence: I kept our Christmas all alone with my wife, witnessed Warren's open defiance of Batten at the office, and looked forward to the end of my vows on the morrow.
levels.paragraph: At the office, Sir W. Warren openly defied Sir W. Batten over a contract, and I could see Pen secretly relished it. My head ached from the press of business, but I dined at home with my wife on turkey and mince pie, keeping Christmas in a quiet, solitary state. Tomorrow my vows against plays and wine expire, and I already resolve to make new ones, finding so much good in them.
levels.summary:
This morning I went to the office and sat through the entire session. Among other matters, Sir W. Warren came about a contract and took the opportunity, with Sir W. Batten absent, to openly defy him, complaining that Batten opposed everything he offered. Sir W.

Pen rebuked Warren for it, but I knew Pen was secretly pleased to hear such talk. After that, we returned to business without further incident.

At noon, I went to the Exchange for a while, then came home to dinner. My head ached terribly from being overloaded with business. My wife and I dined alone on a fine turkey and a mince pie, in a kind of state, though we are poor wretches.

We have kept this Christmas almost entirely by ourselves, not straying out once. Tomorrow my vows against plays and wine come to an end, but I hope to make new ones soon, for I find so much good and God's blessing in keeping them.

periods.label: Week of May 11

levels.sentence: After two hours of roaring stone-like agony, I was delivered by chance when tumbling onto my knees, and the pain ebbed enough for me to sleep.
levels.paragraph: I rose full of pain from yesterday's cold, went to the office, and came home to dinner in extraordinary misery. After dinner the pain forced me to bed, swelling into a fit as great as ever I had with the stone, in belly and back. A glyster brought little relief, and for two hours I lay crying and roaring in anguish. At last, by chance, I got upon my knees amid my tumblings, and the pain began to lessen; within an hour I was in little pain and slept well all night.
levels.summary:
Up this morning full of pain, which I believe came from the cold I got yesterday. I went to the office and sat through the session, then came home to dinner in extraordinary discomfort. After dinner the pain worsened until I was forced to take to my bed.

For an hour or two it rose to as great a torment as ever I remember in any fit of the stone, striking both the lower part of my belly and my back.

At first I could break no wind. I took a glyster, but it brought away only a little and my height of pain followed it. For two hours I lay in the most extraordinary anguish, crying and roaring, not knowing what to do.

Then by chance, among my tumbling and turning, I got upon my knees in bed, and my pain began to lessen little by little. Within an hour I was in very little pain, though still I could not break wind nor make water.

Even so, I continued in that state and slept well all night. It is strange how the pain came and went so suddenly, and I must note that getting on my knees seemed to be the turning point.

periods.label: Week of Oct 19

levels.sentence: I spent the morning at the office, dined with Uncle Thomas, caressed Bagwell's wife in return for promises to help her husband, heard troubling news about Tangier from Mr. Cholmely, bought two silver tumblers, and finished late at the office.
levels.paragraph: Up early and to the office, where I worked all morning. At noon, Uncle Thomas came to dine and received money from me. Later, in my office, I caressed Bagwell's wife, finding her increasingly receptive to my good words and promises to get her husband a place, which I intend to do. I then visited Lord Sandwich and walked with Mr. Cholmely, who told me that Tangier is in a bad condition under Fitzgerald, a man of no honour or honesty, who offends everyone and does nothing well. On my way home, I bought two silver tumblers, returned to work late at the office, then went home to supper and bed.
levels.summary:
I began the day at the office, attending to business all morning. At noon, my uncle Thomas came to dine with me, and I gave him some money, as was our custom. After that, I returned to my office and called in Bagwell's wife, where I caressed her.

She grows more amenable each day, and I made her good words and promises to get her husband a place—a promise I fully intend to keep, as I have my own designs.

Later, I went to Lord Sandwich's lodgings, and then walked with Mr. Cholmely to Fleet Street. On the way, he told me that Tangier is likely in a bad condition under this same Fitzgerald, a man of no honour, presence, or little honesty.

Fitzgerald seeks to raise the Irish and suppress the English interest there, offends everybody, and does nothing well, which I am sorry to hear. I returned home by way of buying two silver tumblers, then spent the rest of the evening busy at my office, and finally went home to supper and to bed.

periods.label: Week of Dec 14

levels.sentence: I walked to Deptford, dined with the poor Bagwells, and then forced my attentions on Bagwell's wife, though I found little contentment in my conquest before returning home to friends and a long evening at the office.
levels.paragraph: This morning I walked to Deptford, and after some business at the yard, I went unseen to Bagwell's house, where the poor folk kindly gave me dinner. Once I sent Bagwell abroad, I pressed myself on his wife, and though I had my way against her resistance, it was not to my full contentment. I returned home and dined with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, then spent the rest of the day and much of the night at the office.
levels.summary:
This morning I walked to Deptford, and after doing something at the yard, I walked without being observed to Bagwell's house. There I was very kindly treated, and the poor people got a dinner for me in their fashion, of which I ate very well.

After dinner I found occasion to send Bagwell abroad, and then I was alone with his wife; I attempted what I wanted, and against her force I did it, yet not to my contentment. By and by he came back, and I took leave and walked home.

Back home I dined with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, who had come to see me. After dinner I left them and went to the office, where we sat all the afternoon, and I stayed late. Then I went to supper and came back to the office again very late, after which I finally went home to bed.

periods.label: Week of Dec 28

levels.sentence: On a freezing morning I went to White Hall with Sir W. Pen, did my usual business with the Duke, then moved from Jane at the barber's to Herbert's young kinswoman at the Swan and Mrs. Martin in Bow Streete, before making mirth at Lord Brunker's French dinner, ordering Hooke's Microscope, and ending with a fruitless late visit to Sir Ph. Warwicke's.
levels.paragraph: On this frosty morning I went to White Hall with Sir W. Pen, did my business with the Duke, and paid what was owing at the basins. The rest of the day ran through my usual pleasures: a private word and promised Sunday meeting with Jane at the barber's, wanton sport at the Swan with Herbert's young kinswoman, and a paid, unsatisfying encounter with Mrs. Martin at her new Bow Streete lodgings. At Lord Brunker's I made mirth with a sailors' ballad, ate the best French dinner I had seen in many days, and then ordered Hooke's new Microscope at the bookseller's. The evening closed with office business and a fruitless late visit to Sir Ph. Warwicke's, where company kept me from speaking with him.
levels.summary:
After rising, I found the morning fine and hard with frost, so I walked a good way toward White Hall until Sir W. Pen's coach overtook me, and I rode thither with him. There we did our usual business with the Duke, and then I was forced to pay a great deal of money in basins at White Hall.

From there I went to my barber Gervas and found a little opportunity to speak with my Jane alone. I gave her something, and she of herself told me where I might come to her on Sunday next; I will not fail. Her modest, harmless way of bringing it out was very pretty.

Afterwards at the Swan I sported a good while with Herbert's young kinswoman, the old people being abroad, and no harm done. Then at the Hall I agreed with Mrs. Martin and went to her new lodgings in Bow Streete—pitiful poor things, though she thinks them pretty and they are good enough for her condition.

I did ce que je voudrais avec her most freely, but it cost me 2s. in wine and cake, and I went away sick of her impudence.

By coach I came to my Lord Brunker's in the Piazza, Covent Garden, where I occasioned much mirth with a ballad I brought, made from the seamen at sea to their ladies in town; I said Sir W. Pen, Sir G. Ascue, and Sir J. Lawson made them.

Here was a most noble French dinner and banquet, the best I have seen in many a day, and good discourse. Thence to my bookseller's, and at his binder's I saw Hooke's book of the Microscope, so pretty that I presently bespoke it.

I went home to the office, where we met to do something, and then, though very late, by coach to Sir Ph. Warwicke's; but he had company with him, so I could not speak with him.

  - Went by coach to the Piazza in Covent Garden
  - Brought a ballad made from seamen at sea to their ladies in town, and said Sir W. Pen, Sir G. Ascue, and Sir J. Lawson made them
  - Occasioned much mirth; enjoyed a most noble French dinner and banquet with good discourse
- Bookseller and late evening
  - At the bookseller's binder's saw Hooke's book of the Microscope, so pretty that I bespoke it
  - Went home to the office, where we met to do something
  - Took a coach very late to Sir Ph. Warwicke's, but he had company and I could not speak with him
periods.sentence: On a freezing morning I went to White Hall with Sir W. Pen, did my usual business with the Duke, then moved from Jane at the barber's to Herbert's young kinswoman at the Swan and Mrs. Martin in Bow Streete, before making mirth at Lord Brunker's French dinner, ordering Hooke's Microscope, and ending with a fruitless late visit to Sir Ph. Warwicke's.
periods.paragraph: On this frosty morning I went to White Hall with Sir W. Pen, did my business with the Duke, and paid what was owing at the basins. The rest of the day ran through my usual pleasures: a private word and promised Sunday meeting with Jane at the barber's, wanton sport at the Swan with Herbert's young kinswoman, and a paid, unsatisfying encounter with Mrs. Martin at her new Bow Streete lodgings. At Lord Brunker's I made mirth with a sailors' ballad, ate the best French dinner I had seen in many days, and then ordered Hooke's new Microscope at the bookseller's. The evening closed with office business and a fruitless late visit to Sir Ph. Warwicke's, where company kept me from speaking with him.

periods.label: Week of Jan 18

levels.sentence: I schemed over Jane's marriage to a fiddler, kissed a serving girl at the Swan, proudly bought Hooke's microscopy book, learned a hare's foot cure from Mr. Batten, and came home to news of Doll's departure.
levels.paragraph: I rose and went to Westminster, spoke with Sir Ph. Warwicke, and then to Jervas where I found them planning Jane's marriage to Hayes while she doted on a fiddler. I contrived to speak with her privately and hope to see her Sunday, though I doubt her prospects. At noon I dined at the Swan and kissed the girl there, and later bought Hooke's microscopy book, proud of it. With my wife I discovered our Doll had gone off, and on the way home a hare's foot from Mr. Batten cured my colic, so I spent my evening quietly at home.
levels.summary:
I rose early and went to Westminster, where I spoke with Sir Ph. Warwicke. From there I went to Jervas, where I found everyone in great disorder over Jane.

Her mistress took me aside and, after swearing me to secrecy, confessed that Jane had thrown herself away on a fellow who comes to the house—a mere fiddler—and that Jane had vowed never to leave him for anyone else.

They were contriving that very day to marry Jane off to one Hayes who was present, and I seemed to persuade her to it, but I managed to get them to allow me to advise her privately.

In that private conference I had her company and believe I shall meet her again next Sunday, though I truly doubt she will be undone in marrying this fellow. I gave her my advice and let her do as she pleases, so that I may enjoy her company now and then.

At noon I went to the Swan, where I dined on a bit of meat and had a kiss from the girl of the house, but nothing more. Then I took a coach to my Lady Sandwich's, and from there to my bookseller's, where I took home Hooke's book of microscopy—a most excellent piece, and one I am very proud to own.

I went home briefly, then abroad again with my wife on several businesses, and we met at the New Exchange. There we found, to our trouble, that our pretty Doll is gone away, said to live with her father in the country, but I suspect something worse.

On my way homeward I bought a hare, which came from my discourse earlier that day with Mr. Batten in Westminster Hall. He showed me my mistake: my hare's foot has not the joint to it, and he assured me he never had his colic since he carried such a one about him.

It is strange how fancy works, for I no sooner handled his foot than my belly began to loosen and break wind, and whereas I had been in some pain yesterday and the day before and feared more today, I became very well and so continue.

At home I went to my office for a while, then to supper, read, played cards, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of Feb 15

levels.sentence: Despite a painful finger from last night's struggle, I attended to business, dined with friends, discussed ticket abuses with Mr. Wayth, and spent the evening with Lady Sandwich talking of daughters, husbands, and the state of the times.
levels.paragraph: I woke with a mighty pain in my left forefinger, strained last night in a struggle with the woman I mentioned yesterday. I still went to the office and was busy till noon, while my wife, long confined indoors in the dirt, went to a hot-house to bathe and now pretends to a resolution of cleanliness. I dined with Sir W. Batten and his Lady, who are now very fond of me. Then, after the Exchange, I dined again with Mr. Wayth to discourse about Hamaccos and ticket abuses, and of Mr. Fen's great profit and dissatisfaction. Later, Lord Brunkerd took me to Lincolne's Inne Fields, where I talked with my Lady Sandwich about good housewifery, husbands for her daughters, and the luxury and looseness of the times, until past ten, and she told me of Lord Castlemayne's coming from France and of the mad freaks of the Maids of Honour. Finally, I returned home, spent a little time at my office, then supped and went to bed.
levels.summary:
I rose with a mighty pain in my left forefinger, strained last night in a struggle 'avec la femme que je' mentioned yesterday. Notwithstanding, I went to the office and was busy until noon.

Meanwhile, my wife, having been long indoors in the dirt, went with her woman to a hot-house to bathe herself, and now pretends to a resolution of being hereafter very clean—though I know how long that will hold.

I dined with Sir W. Batten and my Lady, who are nowadays very fond of me. Then I went to the 'Change, and from there with Mr. Wayth to a cook's shop, where we dined again for discourse about Hamaccos and the abuse now practised in tickets, which grows daily. We also spoke of the great profit Mr.

Fen makes of his place, he demanding but 5 per cent of all he pays, yet very little pleased with any man that gives him no more.

After returning to the office, my Lord Brunkerd carried me to Lincolne's Inne Fields, where I talked with my Lady Sandwich (good lady) of innocent discourse concerning good housewifery, husbands for her daughters, and the luxury and looseness of the times, until past 10 o'clock at night.

She told me how my Lord Castlemayne is coming over from France, and is believed will be made friends with his Lady again, and also of the mad freaks the Mayds of Honour at Court have, including something about Mrs. that I did not note fully.

Then I came home by coach, spent a little time at my office, and so to supper and to bed.

periods.label: Week of Aug 2

levels.sentence: Having been dressed and having my head combed by my little girle, I confess I was too kind with her, putting my hands on her breasts, but I resolve to leave it to avoid a greater inconvenience, and after settling my papers I ride to Woolwich through the rain to bed.
levels.paragraph: This morning I dressed and had my head combed by my little girle. I confess I was too familiar with her, touching her breast, but I know I must stop to avoid serious trouble. So I turned to my business, looking over and settling more of my papers than I could in the past two days. In the evening, as it rained hard, I went down to Woolwich, and after a little talk, I went to bed.
levels.summary:
I dressed and had my head combed by my little girle, and I must confess that I have been too kind to her—indeed, I put my hands upon her breasts. But I realize I must stop this behavior, lest it lead me into a greater inconvenience or scandal.

I am aware of the risk, and though I am tempted, I resolve to leave it be.

After that, I went to my business in my chamber, spending the day looking over and settling more of my papers than I could manage over the last two days.

In the evening, the rain came down hard, so I went to Woolwich. Once there, I had a little talk, and then I went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Aug 9

levels.sentence: Amidst the rising plague deaths and unsettling rumors, I tended to my cousin's distress, attended a dinner full of contradictions, and resolved to redraw my will before the town's unhealthiness could claim me.
levels.paragraph: I was called upon early by my she-cozen Porter, whose husband had been taken to the Tower for buying the King's powder, but I dared not help. At the office, the weekly bill showed over 4,000 dead, mostly of the plague, and I heard a harrowing tale of Alderman Bence stumbling over a corpse and his pregnant wife dying from fright. Later, at Sir G. Smith's dinner, Bence himself denied the story, yet confessed his wife was ill and he had left her, which troubled me all through the meal. I returned to business, wrote letters, and then went home to redraw my will, bound by oath to finish by tomorrow night, for the town grows so unhealthy that no man can count on living two days.
levels.summary:
This morning, my she-cozen Porter, the turner's wife, came to me early, telling me her husband had been carried to the Tower for buying some of the King's powder, and she begged for my help.

But I could give her none, not daring to appear any more in that business, having already had too much trouble lately with such matters. I went to the office, where we sat all morning, greatly troubled to see the weekly Bill rise so high—above 4,000 dead in all, and of them above 3,000 from the plague.

There was a strange story about Alderman Bence, who stumbled over a dead body in the street at night, and going home told his wife; she, being with child, was so frightened that she fell sick and died of the plague.

We sat late, and then by invitation my Lord Brunker, Sir J. Minnes, Sir W. Batten, and I went to Sir G. Smith's to dinner, where there was very good company and cheer.

Captain Cocke and Jacke Fenn were there, and to our great wonder, Alderman Bence himself came and told us that not a word of the story was true—others said so too.

But by his own telling, his wife has been ill, and he was fain to leave his house and not come near her, which continued to trouble me all the time I was there.

Thence to the office, and after writing letters, I went home to draw over anew my will, which I had bound myself by oath to dispatch by tomorrow night, for the town is growing so unhealthy that a man cannot depend upon living two days to an end. So having done something of it, I went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Sep 27

levels.sentence: After a night sail to Chatham, I inspected the yard with Commissioner Pett—shaming his four-horse team by carrying the timber myself—and, having found Sir W. Pen a false rogue in bed, I went on to Rochester, where the castle ruins gave me three pretty maids' kisses until the frightful precipice checked my pleasure, and I ended with a reverend magistrate at the Crowne.
levels.paragraph: We sailed all night to Gillingham and walked to Chatham, where I made Commissioner Pett's four horses take off a timber one man could carry, and he was ashamed. At Hill-house we found Sir W. Pen in bed and full of dissembled kindness, yet my presence won his consent to carry away his silk before payment. In Rochester, while dinner waited, I walked the old castle ruins and, going up the stairs, overtook three pretty maids; I kissed and touched them to my great pleasure, but looking down the precipices so frightened me that I lost much of my enjoyment. I then viewed the cathedral and returned to the Crowne, where the Mayor, Mr. Fowler, came in his gown, a very reverend magistrate.
levels.summary:
We sailed all night, and I wondered how the sailors could find their way in the dark; by morning we got to Gillingham, then all walked to Chatham.

There I viewed the Yard with Commissioner Pett, and among other things a team of four horses came close by us dragging a piece of timber that I am confident one man could easily have carried on his back.

I made the horses be taken away and a man or two carry the timber with their hands, which the Commissioner saw but said nothing to; I think he had cause to be ashamed.

From there Pett, Cocke, and I walked to the Hill-house, where we found Sir W. Pen in bed. There was much talk and much dissembled kindness from him, but I know he is a false rogue and shall not trust him.

My being there did procure his consent to have his silk carried away before the money was received, which I am sure he would not have done for Cocke. Thence we went to Rochester and walked to the Crowne, and while dinner was getting ready, I walked to visit the old Castle ruins, which have been a noble place.

Going up the stairs, I overtook three pretty maids or women and took them up with me, and I kissed their mouths and touched their hands and necks to my great pleasure; but, Lord, what a dreadful thing it was to look down the precipices, for it frightened me mightily and hindered much of the pleasure I would have made with those three.

The place was very noble, great, and strong in former ages.

I walked up and down the Cathedral and then returned to the Crowne, where Mr. Fowler, the Mayor of the town, came in his gown — a very reverend magistrate.

From there Pett, Cocke, and I walked to the Hill-house, where we found Sir W. Pen in bed. There was much talk and much dissembled kindness from him, but I know he is a false rogue and shall not trust him.

My being there did procure his consent to have his silk carried away before the money was received, which I am sure he would not have done for Cocke. Thence we went to Rochester and walked to the Crowne, and while dinner was getting ready, I walked to visit the old Castle ruins, which have been a noble place.

Going up the stairs, I overtook three pretty maids or women and took them up with me, and I kissed their mouths and touched their hands and necks to my great pleasure; but, Lord, what a dreadful thing it was to look down the precipices, for it frightened me mightily and hindered much of the pleasure I would have made with those three.

The place was very noble, great, and strong in former ages.

I walked up and down the Cathedral and then returned to the Crowne, where Mr. Fowler, the Mayor of the town, came in his gown — a very reverend magistrate.

periods.label: Week of Oct 4

levels.sentence: Amid the raging plague I tended to business, dallied with women, admired Evelyn's gardens, and renewed my vows.
levels.paragraph: I lay late talking with my wife, who agreed to give my sister Pall £400 and wished her married, though the plague makes it unfit to fetch her up. After office business and a visit to the Duke of Albemarle, I read Evelyn's gift on library-keeping, walked to the Swan to spend time with Sarah, and went by water to Deptford to see my Valentine, not valuing the plague around me. At Evelyn's we discussed the tortured business of prisoners and sick seamen, and he showed me his evergreen gardens and holly hedge, the finest I ever saw. Later I wrote late letters to Sir W. Coventry, found my wife gone home to Woolwich, and was comforted that the plague Bill had fallen by 740; then I renewed my promises to observe my vows.
levels.summary:
This day began lazily in bed, where my wife showed herself very willing that I should give my sister Pall £400 as her portion and have her married soon, though the great sickness makes it unfit to send for her up. I went abroad to the office and then to the Duke of Albemarle, reading on the way a book sent me by Mr.

Evelyn — directions for gathering a Library, above my reach, but with a very fine epistle to my Lord Chancellor. At the Duke we dealt with the victuallers' business, and I advised putting it into other or more hands, hoping to do myself a jobb of work in it.

Walking through Westminster, I stopped at the Swan and spent some time with Sarah, then took water to Deptford to see my Valentine, though the plague was on every side; I did not value it, but did what I would with her. From there I went to Mr.

Evelyn's to discourse of our confounded business of prisoners and sick and wounded seamen, which is so out of order. Evelyn then showed me his gardens, whose variety of evergreens and hedge of holly are the finest things I ever saw in my life.

We rode in his coach to Greenwich, talking all the way of trees and the nature of vegetables, and I went to my office to write letters, ending very late with a letter of great concernment to Sir W. Coventry.

I found my wife had gone home to Woolwich; but the Bill, blessed be God! is less this week by 740 than last week.

Having eaten little all day, I got something at my lodging and so to bed, having renewed my promises of observing my vows as I used to do; for since I left them off my mind has run a-wool-gathering and my business neglected.

periods.label: Week of Oct 11

levels.sentence: Roused before dawn in horrid cold, I went to Lord Bruncker's ship and found that the King's severe examination of the prize-goods revealed shameful abuse of my Lord Sandwich's order, with goods spoiled and broken in the hold and Sir W. Berkeley chiefly to blame, everyone saying my Lord's back was broad enough to bear it.
levels.paragraph: I was called up before day in horrid cold and went by water to Lord Bruncker's ship, where he showed me the King's severe command to examine all prize-goods removals without respect to my Lord Sandwich. Bruncker was already examining one man, and I saw that my Lord's order had been extremely ill used. The men tossed, tumbled, spoiled, and broke things in the hold — a great loss and shame — all to come at the fine goods. Sir W. Berkeley was the chief hand, and they all said my Lord Sandwich's back was broad enough to bear it.
levels.summary:
I was called up before day, in horrid cold, and dressed and went by water to my Lord Bruncker's ship.

He had advised me to come, and he civilly showed me what the King had commanded about the prize-goods: to examine most severely all that had been done in taking any out, with or without order, without respect to my Lord Sandwich at all. He had been carrying out the examination, and I found him questioning one man.

What I discovered was that extreme ill use had been made of my Lord's order. They tossed and tumbled and spoiled, and broke things in the hold, to great loss and shame, in order to come at the fine goods. They even took a man who knew where the fine goods were, and did this over and over again for many days.

Sir W. Berkeley was the chief hand in it, though others did the like at other times. And in doing it they said that my Lord Sandwich's back was broad enough to bear it.

periods.label: Week of Jan 3

levels.sentence: Riding up to London with Lord Bruncker and Mrs Williams, I found the city stirring back to life, did business at Whitehall and the Exchange, dined with Mr Povy at Sir George Smith's, heard Lord Bellases's complaints, studied the silting of the Thames at Mr Boreman's, and ended the night at home with little Mrs Tooker.
levels.paragraph: I came up to London with my Lord Bruncker and Mrs Williams and was delighted to see the town full of people again, with shops beginning to open even though many were still shut. I went with my Lord to Sir G. Carteret at Whitehall, where we talked openly about the Act and credit, and later I met Mr Povy at the Exchange and dined nobly at Sir George Smith's. After waiting for my Lord and returning to Greenwich, I tried in vain for Mrs Knipp, then passed an hour or two at Mr Boreman's reading a satisfying discourse about the Thames. At home I supped late with little Mrs Tooker and did what I would with her before bed.
levels.summary:
I rode to London that day with my Lord Bruncker and Mrs Williams in a coach with four horses. At my Lord's house in Covent Garden I was struck by the staring, porters bowing to us, and beggars on every side; it was a delight to see the town full of people again, shops beginning to open though many still stood shut.

Covent Garden and Westminster were still empty, with no Court or gentry there.

After setting Mrs Williams down, my Lord and I went to Sir G. Carteret's chamber at White Hall; he had come to town the night before for one day. We talked much about the Act and what credit we found upon it, but he and I had no private talk.

Then I went to the Exchange, met Mr Povy newly come to town, and dined nobly with him at Sir George Smith's. Povy told me how Lord Bellases complains for want of money and blames him and me for it, but I value it not, knowing I do all that can be done; we had no time for particulars and left it to another day.

Afterwards I waited at my stationer's on Cornhill for my Lord Bruncker, who took me up and carried me to Greenwich; after sitting a while at his house I went home.

" So I went to Mr Boreman's for pastime and spent an hour or two talking with him and reading a discourse about the River Thames, which explained that the river is choked with shelves because of encroachments and causeways running out into it at every wood-wharf—something that was not the case when Westminster Hall, White Hall, and Redriffe Church were built, though they are now sometimes overflowed.

This gave me great satisfaction.

Home I went to my papers for lack of company, but by and by little Mrs Tooker came and supped with me. I kept her very late, talking and making her comb my head, and did what I would with her, so that it was late when I went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Jan 10

levels.sentence: I spent the day troubled over my Lord Sandwich's need for a pardon and my own bond for him, while ordering shoes and clothes and enduring Sir W. Pen's obstructive behaviour at the office.
levels.paragraph: I went by coach to the Duke of Albemarle's, where only Sir W. Batten and I met, and I was troubled to see how things are ordered there without consideration or understanding. Then I called at Wotton's, my shoemaker, to bespeak shoes and to find me a tailor, which he did in Mr. Penny against St. Dunstan's Church. At the Exchange I met Mr. Moore and took him home to dinner, and we concluded my Lord Sandwich's case is very bad unless he gets a pardon before going for Spain; I pressed him to get my Lord to pay my cousin Pepys, since I am bound for L1000. At the office my paper about pursers was well approved by all except Sir W. Pen, who objected without remedying anything and declined Sir W. Batten's proposal to mend the victualling.
levels.summary:
This morning I went by coach to the Duke of Albemarle's, where only Sir W. Batten and I met. I was troubled at heart to see how things are ordered there without consideration or understanding.

On my way back I called at Wotton's, my shoemaker, lately come to town, and bespoke shoes; since my own clothes are not yet in town, nor Pym, my Lord Sandwich's tailor, I got Wotton to find me a tailor, and he recommended a pretty man, one Mr. Penny, against St. Dunstan's Church.

After that I went to the Exchange and met Mr. Moore, newly come to town, and took him home to dinner with me, where we talked.

He and I concluded that my Lord's case is very bad and may be worse if he does not get a pardon for his doings about the prizes, his business at Bergen, and other things done by him at sea, before he goes for Spain.

I used all the art I could to get Moore to persuade my Lord to pay my cousin Pepys, for it is a great burden to my mind that I am bound for my Lord in L1000 to him. I directed Moore to go express to my Lord tomorrow to get his pardon perfected before his going, because of what I read the other night in Sir W.

Coventry's letter.

At the office there was an extraordinary meeting of Sir J. Minnes, Sir W. Batten, Sir W. Pen, and my Lord Bruncker with me to hear my paper read about pursers. They all received it with great goodwill and great approbation of my method and pains, except Sir W.

Pen, who must except against everything and remedy nothing.

He objected to my proposal for reasons I could not understand, nor my Lord Bruncker neither, though he did detect a failure or two in my report about the ill condition of the present pursers, in one or two little things where I had magnified; to that I think he did with reason except.

Yet at last he declared with all respect that it was the best thing he ever heard of this kind.

When Sir W. Batten proposed that those who know the practical part of the Victualling—Sir J. Minnes, Sir W. Pen, and I—should meet and see what could be done to mend all, Sir W. Pen was so far from offering or furthering it that he declined, saying he must be out of town.

So he never attempts to mend anything, but rather lets all things go on in the way they are, though never so bad, instead of improving his experience to the King's advantage. That is the character I have ever known of him.

This morning I went by coach to the Duke of Albemarle's, where only Sir W. Batten and I met. I was troubled at heart to see how things are ordered there without consideration or understanding.

On my way back I called at Wotton's, my shoemaker, lately come to town, and bespoke shoes; since my own clothes are not yet in town, nor Pym, my Lord Sandwich's tailor, I got Wotton to find me a tailor, and he recommended a pretty man, one Mr. Penny, against St. Dunstan's Church.

After that I went to the Exchange and met Mr. Moore, newly come to town, and took him home to dinner with me, where we talked.

He and I concluded that my Lord's case is very bad and may be worse if he does not get a pardon for his doings about the prizes, his business at Bergen, and other things done by him at sea, before he goes for Spain.

I used all the art I could to get Moore to persuade my Lord to pay my cousin Pepys, for it is a great burden to my mind that I am bound for my Lord in L1000 to him. I directed Moore to go express to my Lord tomorrow to get his pardon perfected before his going, because of what I read the other night in Sir W.

Coventry's letter.

At the office there was an extraordinary meeting of Sir J. Minnes, Sir W. Batten, Sir W. Pen, and my Lord Bruncker with me to hear my paper read about pursers. They all received it with great goodwill and great approbation of my method and pains, except Sir W.

Pen, who must except against everything and remedy nothing.

He objected to my proposal for reasons I could not understand, nor my Lord Bruncker neither, though he did detect a failure or two in my report about the ill condition of the present pursers, in one or two little things where I had magnified; to that I think he did with reason except.

Yet at last he declared with all respect that it was the best thing he ever heard of this kind.

When Sir W. Batten proposed that those who know the practical part of the Victualling—Sir J. Minnes, Sir W. Pen, and I—should meet and see what could be done to mend all, Sir W. Pen was so far from offering or furthering it that he declined, saying he must be out of town.

So he never attempts to mend anything, but rather lets all things go on in the way they are, though never so bad, instead of improving his experience to the King's advantage. That is the character I have ever known of him.

periods.label: Week of Feb 28

levels.sentence: On a cold morning I walked to White Hall, shared ominous talk with Warwicke, transacted Navy business, dallied with several women, dined with Knipp, visited Carteret who fears a general catastrophe, lent money to Lane, and ended the month resolved to apply myself better to business.
levels.paragraph: I walked to White Hall on a dry cold morning, met Sir Ph. Warwicke in the Park, and we spoke gloomily of the nation's divisive state and the new Act that hampers raising money. After business with the Duke of York, I idled at Westminster Hall, talked with Michell and Howlett, and later had my way with Mrs. Martin. At home I dined with the delightful Mrs. Knipp, then visited Norwood and Carteret, who fears a general catastrophe. I lent Mrs. Lane money and lay with her, though she grows dangerous, and I went to bed early, resolved to reform my neglected business.
levels.summary:
After rising and doing a little business at my office, I walked through the curiously dry and cold morning to White Hall. Entering the Park, I met Sir Ph. Warwicke and took a turn with him in the Pell Mall, where we talked of the melancholy posture of affairs.

Everywhere people are snarling at one another, and the new Act has taken away our power of raising money. Warwicke fears the situation as I do, but he is fearful of enlarging on the ill condition of the State. We appointed another time to meet seriously about Navy business, and so parted.

At White Hall I did business with the Duke of Yorke, then walked to Westminster Hall, where I talked at length with Mrs. Michell and Howlett and her daughter, who has become a mighty pretty woman. As I was going out, Mrs.

Martin called to me, so I bought two bands from her, and later met at her chamber, where I did what I would with her. Then I went home and found Mrs. Knipp there; we dined together, and she is the pleasantest company in the world. After dinner I gave my wife 20s. to lay out on Knipp.

I went abroad to White Hall to visit Colonell Norwood, and then Sir G. Carteret, with whom I have brought myself right again. He was very open with me, but very melancholy; matters go down with him, and he seems most afeard of a general catastrophe to the whole kingdom, thinking all things will come to nothing.

Thence I went to the Palace Yard and the Swan, staying until dark.

After that I went to Mrs. Lane’s chamber and lent her L5 upon L4 01s. in gold. Then I did what I would with her. I perceive she is come to be very bad, offering anything, so it is dangerous to have to do with her, and I will not see her again for a good while.

I took a coach home, went to the office for a while, and then went to bed by ten o’clock, sooner than I have done many a day.

Thus this month ends with my mind full of resolution to apply myself better from this time forward to my business than I have done these six or eight days, which has been visibly to my prejudice both in quiett of mind and setting backward of my business, so that I cannot give a good account of it as I ought.

periods.label: Week of Mar 14

levels.sentence: After church and dinner I wandered about Westminster in fair dry weather, visited Mrs Martin and enjoyed her while her husband fetched wine, heard of my former sweetheart Betty Howlet's marriage, and came home to accounts, with Sir Christopher Mings returning from Hambro empty-handed but for pipe-staves.
levels.paragraph: I rose with my cold better, went to church and dined at home, then walked out toward St James's in fine dry weather, hoping to see fair Mrs Butler, but she was not there. I went on to Westminster, drank at Herbert's, then visited Mrs Martin and had my will with her while her husband fetched wine, promising to try to get him a purser's place. She told me Betty Howlet, my old sweetheart called my second wife, has married a younger son of Mr Michell's, which pleased me; then I came home by coach, did accounts, and went to bed, while Sir Christopher Mings returned from Hambro with little but pipe-staves.
levels.summary:
I got up with my cold better, went to church, and then home to dinner. Afterwards I walked out to St James's Church hoping to see the fair Mrs Butler, but she was not there, and I believe she no longer lives in that area. The weather was very fine and dry, though everyone cries out for lack of rain.

I went to Herbert's and drank, then to Mrs Martin's, where I did what I would with her while her husband went to fetch us some wine. The poor man would take pains, I think, if I can get him a purser's place, which I intend to endeavour.

She told me as a secret that Betty Howlet of the Hall, my little sweetheart whom I used to call my second wife, is married to a younger son of Mr Michell's; his elder brother, who should have had her, died in the plague, and I am glad. They are to live nearer me in Thames Streete, by the Old Swan.

Then I came home by coach and to my chamber about some accounts, and so to bed. Sir Christopher Mings has come home from Hambro without anything done, except bringing home some pipe-staves for us.

periods.label: Week of Apr 4

levels.sentence: A rainy day of trouble getting to Whitehall, where the Duke judged a captain's complaint, while news of Tom Cheffin's sudden death and the spreading plague darkened the Court.
levels.paragraph: Raining and coachless, I walked to the Old Swan and took a scull to Whitehall, where the Duke of Yorke heard Sir Thomas Allen's complaint against Mr. Wayth and settled it with rare judgement. The Court buzzed with news of Tom Cheffin's sudden death, and the plague is feared to be increasing again. I saw the Archbishop of Yorke preach, carried Mrs. Hunt home to dinner, and heard old Protectoral stories. The evening ended quietly with Mercer combing my head, a psalm, and bed.
levels.summary:
I rose in great trouble, for it rained and no coach could be had to carry me to White Hall; so I walked to the Old Swan and got a scull instead. At the Duke of Yorke's, we all met to hear the debate between Sir Thomas Allen and Mr.

Wayth — Allen complaining of Wayth's ill usage of him at the late pay of his ship, though he had but a sorry poor occasion for it.

The Duke determined the matter with great judgement, chiding both, yet encouraging Wayth to continue as a check to all captains in anything touching the King's right; indeed, I never saw the Duke do anything more orderly or with more judgement.

The Court was full this morning of the news of Tom Cheffin's death, the King's closet-keeper. He had been well last night, playing at tables in the house, and not very ill at six o'clock this morning, yet dead before seven; they think an imposthume in his breast.

It looks fearfully among people nowadays, the plague, as we hear, increasing everywhere again. I went to the Chappell but could not get in to hear well; yet I had the pleasure once in my life to see an Archbishop — this was of Yorke — in a pulpit.

Being at a loss how to get home to dinner, having promised to carry Mrs. Hunt thither, I at last got my Lord Hinchingbroke's coach, he staying at Court, and took her up in Axe-yard, and home we dined.

We had good discourse of the old matters of the Protector and his family, she having a relation to them; the Protector lives in France and spends about L500 per annum.

I carried her home again, then went to Court and walked over to St James's Chappell, thinking to hear a Jesuit preach, but came too late; so I got a hackney and went home to business. At night I had Mercer comb my head, and so to supper, sang a psalm, and to bed.
