periods.label: Week of May 16

levels.sentence: After church and a noble dinner, I sent my wife off to a christening, enjoyed Mrs. Martin's favours, discussed preferment and bribes with Blagrave and Yeabsly, inspected the navy's ships, read Bacon on fortune, and retired satisfied to bed.
levels.paragraph: I began the day with my wife at church, and we dined nobly at home alone. Afterward, my wife went to Greenwich for a christening while I visited Mrs. Martin for pleasure, though her loose company displeased me. I then spoke with Mr. Blagrave and later with Mr. Yeabsly, who had bribed Lord Ashby, and after inspecting ships and reading Bacon, I returned home to find my wife pleased with her role as godmother.
levels.summary:
In the morning I went with my wife to church, and at noon we dined mighty nobly, just the two of us alone. After dinner, my wife and Mercer took a coach to Greenwich, where she was to be gossip to Mrs. Daniel's new child. I went out to Westminster, and straight to Mrs.

Martin's house, where she had stayed at home all day for me, and I did what I would with her. Yet I was not well pleased with her over-free and loose company, so I left, heading to Westminster Abbey.

At the Abbey I fell into discourse with Mr. Blagrave, whom I find a sober, politique man who gets money and increase of places. Then I went by coach home, and met Mr. Yeabsly, whom I took up in my coach.

He told me he had presented my Lord Ashly with £100 to bespeak his friendship in his accounts now before us; my Lord received it, so I believe he is as bad as to bribes as what the world says.

I then called on all the Victualling ships to know what they had of their complements, and so to Deptford to enquire after a little business.

All the way coming and going by water, I read my Lord Bacon's "Faber Fortunae," which I can never read too often. Back home, I found my wife come home, much pleased with the reception she had there; she was godmother, held the child at the font, and it is called John.

After setting my papers in order and supping, I went to bed, desirous to rise betimes in the morning.

periods.sentence: After church and a noble dinner, I sent my wife off to a christening, enjoyed Mrs. Martin's favours, discussed preferment and bribes with Blagrave and Yeabsly, inspected the navy's ships, read Bacon on fortune, and retired satisfied to bed.
periods.paragraph: I began the day with my wife at church, and we dined nobly at home alone. Afterward, my wife went to Greenwich for a christening while I visited Mrs. Martin for pleasure, though her loose company displeased me. I then spoke with Mr. Blagrave and later with Mr. Yeabsly, who had bribed Lord Ashby, and after inspecting ships and reading Bacon, I returned home to find my wife pleased with her role as godmother.

periods.label: Week of Jun 6

levels.phrase: From expected triumph to bitter defeat
levels.sentence: I rose expecting to celebrate a great victory, but by nightfall the truth emerged—we were beaten, with ships, captains, and friends lost—and I had to write a sad letter to Lady Sandwich instead of a triumphant one.
levels.paragraph: What began as a day of anticipated triumph turned into one of grim disillusionment. Astonishing news from Court revealed that we had not won at all: the Prince was burned on the Galloper, Sir G. Ascue was taken, and our losses were heavy. The town's mood changed, and even the Duke of York spoke with dampened spirits. I spent the night drawing abstracts of the fleet's needs, and ended by writing a sorrowful letter to Lady Sandwich.
levels.summary:
I rose early and went to my office, expecting any moment to congratulate ourselves on the victory I had believed won the day before. Sir W. Coventry had already gone down to the fleet, and I awaited his return with the same hopeful expectation. But my Lord Bruncker and Sir T.

, coming from Court, brought news that astonished and troubled me deeply: we had been beaten, lost many ships and good commanders, taken none of the enemy's ships, and could only claim a victory on paper. Worst of all, the Prince had run ashore on the Galloper, stuck fast, and was burned by the Dutch; Sir G.

Ascue was taken prisoner and carried into Holland.

At noon I went to the Exchange, where the talk of the town and the countenances of the people were much changed, though not yet openly despairing. I dined at home alone, for my father and the rest were gone to Woolwich to see the launching of the new ship the Greenwich, built by Chr. Pett.

I was left alone with little Mrs. Tooker, whom I kept with me in my chamber all the afternoon and did what I would with her. Later Mr.

Wayth came, and from Captain Page's own mouth—he who has lost an arm in the fight—he told me plainly that the Dutch pursued us for two hours before they left off, and then allowed us to make for home while they retreated to their own coast. That was very sad news.

In the evening I went to White Hall, late, to the Duke of York, to learn his commands and to press for a Tangier meeting on behalf of Mr. Yeabsly. I found the Duke much damped in his discourse touching the late fight, and all the Court talked sadly of it. The Duke gave me several letters from the fleet—from Sir W.

Coventry and Sir W. Pen, who had gone down thither—directing me to pick out works needed for setting out the fleet again. I took them home and worked on an abstract of them till midnight.

As to the news, I find great reason to think we are beaten in every respect, and the losers. The Prince lay on the Galloper, where the Royal Charles and Royal Katharine had also struck twice but got off.

The Essex was carried into Holland; the Swiftsure, with Sir William Barkeley, has been missing since the start of the fight. Captains Bacon, Tearne, Wood, Mootham, Whitty, and Coppin were slain. The Duke of Albemarle writes that he never fought with worse officers in his life—not above twenty behaved like men.

Sir William Clerke lost his leg and died two days after. The Loyal George, Seven Oakes, and Swiftsure are still missing, never having engaged, as the General himself writes.

It was as great an alteration to find myself required to write a sad letter instead of a triumphant one to my Lady Sandwich this night as ever I experienced in my life. So I came home late and went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Jun 13

levels.sentence: After my usual business at St James's, I heard from Sir H. Cholmly of the growing quarrel between the Duke of Yorke and the Duke of Albemarle over the turning out of Yorke's commanders, and observed Sir W. Coventry's sharp reflections on Albemarle's captains.
levels.paragraph: I went by coach to St James's and did our usual business before the Duke. Before he rose, I walked in an ante-chamber with Sir H. Cholmly, who told me of great jars between the Duke of Yorke and the Duke of Albemarle over Albemarle's turning out Yorke's commanders. I also observed Sir W. Coventry's late reflections on Albemarle and his captains, especially old Teddiman, who was rightly turned out after the fight but replaced, Coventry says, by one as bad.
levels.summary:
Up early, I took a coach to St James's and there did our usual business before the Duke. While waiting in an ante-chamber before the Duke came out of bed, I walked with Sir H.

Cholmly, who told me there are great jars between the Duke of Yorke and the Duke of Albemarle about the latter's turning out one or two of the commanders put in by the Duke of Yorke.

Among the officers in question was Captain Du Tell, a Frenchman, put in by the Duke of Yorke and mightily defended by him. Yorke is therein led by Monsieur Blancford, who seems to have the same command over the Duke of Yorke as Sir W. Coventry hath, which raises ill blood between them.

I did in several little things observe that Sir W. Coventry hath of late, by the by, reflected on the Duke of Albemarle and his captains, particularly in that of old Teddiman, who did deserve to be turned out this fight and was so; but I heard Sir W.

Coventry say that the Duke of Albemarle put in one as bad as he is in his room, and one that did as little.

Thus the factions at court are stirring, and I took particular notice of the ill blood and discontent among these great men.

levels.sentence: After a colicky start caused by my cold-catching thin waistcoat, I gave my father money for his journey, attended the Duke of York, gained £25 from Colonel Fitzgerald on a £700 payment, pressed my Exchequer tally business through to completion, and went on to the Hall.
levels.paragraph: Up with colic, which I blame on washing my feet and wearing a thin silk waistcoat with an open breast and no coat over it. Father leaves tomorrow, so I gave him £20 for a horse and other needs for himself, my mother, and my sister, and promised about £3 more — the poor man received it with infinite kindness, and I think it money well spent. On the way to St James’s I spoke with Colonel Fitzgerald about paying him some £700, and he bid me deduct £25 for myself — very good. levels.summary:
I woke this morning feeling the grip of the colic, and I believe I have brought it on by washing my feet and going about in nothing but a thin silk waistcoat, open-breasted, with no other coat over it. It is a sharp discomfort, but I hope it will pass.

This morning, knowing my father goes away tomorrow, I gave him money to buy himself a horse, and further sums for his own use and for my mother and sister — £20 in all, besides undertaking to pay about £3 more for other things for them.

The poor man took it with infinite kindness, and I do not think I could bestow it better. Then I rode by coach toward St James’s, and on the way met Colonel Fitzgerald, who returned with me to Westminster. We discoursed about paying him a sum of £700-odd, and he bade me defalk £25 for myself — a very good thing for me.

At St James’s I waited on the Duke of York, as usual. Afterwards I went to the Exchequer and, after much ado, quite got over the difficulty of breaking a great tally into little ones; it shall be done tomorrow. Thence I went to the Hall, and with Mrs. —

levels.sentence: After settling my accounts to a record £5,700 and being delayed by Sir W. Pen so that the Duke's business stood still, I walked with Sir W. Coventry to hear his discontent with the late fight, then spent the fast-day afternoon in mirth at Mrs Martin's with a dissembling widow and her companions, and came home pleased with my wife's drawing.
levels.paragraph: I rose betimes to settle last month's accounts and found myself worth £5,700, the most my book ever made out. Delayed by Sir W. Pen's return from Sheerness, I came late to St James's and found everything stood still for want of me; walking with Sir W. Coventry, I heard his discontent with the late fight and the news that the Dutch had lost 5,000 men to our 400 or 500. On this common fast-day I went fearfully to church, dined at the Swan on rabbit, and spent the afternoon at Mrs. Martin's with Mrs Burroughs, a merry widow named Mrs Eastwood, and Mrs Fenton, toying with them and carrying them home. I was mightily pleased with the mirth, though uneasy in the coach for fear of being seen, and at home I was pleased with my wife's drawing before going to bed.
levels.summary:
Up betimes this morning I settled my last month's accounts, and I bless God I find them very clear, for I am worth £5,700, the most that ever my book did yet make out. As I was going to attend the Duke of York as usual, Sir W.

Pen came home from Sheerness and held me in discourse about public business till I came by coach too late to St James's, where I found that everything stood still and nothing was done for want of me.

Walking over the Park with Sir W. Coventry, I clearly saw he is not thoroughly pleased with the late management of the fight, nor with anything that the Generals do. He was only glad to hear that De Ruyter is out of favour and that this fight hath cost the Dutch 5,000 men, as they themselves report.

He observed how strangely the slaughter runs on one hand, there being 5,000 killed on theirs and not above 400 or 500 killed and wounded on ours, with as many flag-officers lost on theirs as ordinary captains on ours: Everson and the Admiral and Vice-Admiral of Freezeland on theirs, and Seamour, Martin, and another on ours.

Leaving him going to chapel, it being the common fast-day and the Duke of York at chapel, I went to Mrs Martin's, but she was abroad; so I sauntered to the Abbey and then to the parish church, fearful of being seen doing so, and after the parish church ended I dined at the Swan upon a rabbit.

After dinner I returned to Mrs Martin's and found Mrs Burroughs; by and by came a pretty widow, one Mrs Eastwood, and one Mrs Fenton, a maid. There was merry kissing and looking on their breasts, and all the innocent pleasure in the world. But, Lord!

to see the dissembling of this widow — when Doll, Mrs Martin's sister, sang a certain jigg that her husband, who died this last sickness, had loved, she seemed to be sick and fainted and God knows what.

Yet I soon made her as merry as possible, and towzed and tumbled her as I pleased, then carried her and her sober pretty kinswoman Mrs Fenton home to their lodgings in the new market of my Lord Treasurer's, and left them there.

I was mightily pleased with this afternoon's mirth, but in great pain to ride in a coach with them for fear of being seen. So I came home, and there much pleased with my wife's drawing today in her pictures; then to supper and to bed very pleasant.

to see the dissembling of this widow — when Doll, Mrs Martin's sister, sang a certain jigg that her husband, who died this last sickness, had loved, she seemed to be sick and fainted and God knows what.

Yet I soon made her as merry as possible, and towzed and tumbled her as I pleased, then carried her and her sober pretty kinswoman Mrs Fenton home to their lodgings in the new market of my Lord Treasurer's, and left them there.

I was mightily pleased with this afternoon's mirth, but in great pain to ride in a coach with them for fear of being seen. So I came home, and there much pleased with my wife's drawing today in her pictures; then to supper and to bed very pleasant.

periods.label: Week of Sep 12

levels.sentence: After attending to naval business and helping friends, I moved goods, then indulged my lust with Martin and Bagwell, only to feel self-loathing afterward.
levels.paragraph: After a morning of naval business with the Duke of Yorke and a helpful conversation with Michell and Howlett, I visited Martin for my own pleasure. I dined at home with Balty and his wife, then took Balty to Deptford to send away half my goods. In the dark I went to Bagwell and gratified my desire, but came away hating her and the act, and ended the evening late at Sir W. Pen's in a foolish humour.
levels.summary:
This morning I went by water with Sir W. Batten and Sir W. Pen to St. James's, where we did our usual business with the Duke of Yorke. Afterwards I walked to Westminster and spoke with Michell and Howlett.

They told me their poor young ones are going to Shadwell's, and Howlett mentioned the unkindness of the young man to his wife, which is now over. I promised to act as a counsellor to him, and I am glad she is like to be so near us again.

From there I went to Martin and had my way with her, then drank and returned by water home to dinner, with Balty and his wife. After dinner I took Balty down with me to Deptford, and by the Bezan I loaded above half my goods and sent them away.

We came back home, and then I found occasion to return in the dark to Bagwell's house, where I did all I desired. But although I had intended to stay with her, once it was done I hated both her and the deed. Taking the opportunity of her husband's return to leave, I went away home late to Sir W.

Pen's, where Balty and his wife were lying at my house. There I found Sir W. Pen in the same simple humour, and so went late to bed.

periods.label: Week of Sep 26

levels.sentence: Though Sir W. Warren balked at our Scotch motion, I finished the Parliament lists, found mighty satisfaction with Sir W. Coventry in the navy accounts above L3,000,000, and ended the day happily fetching my wife’s new flowered tabby gown.
levels.paragraph: At our first office meeting since the fire, Sir W. Batten, Sir W. Pen, and I conferred with Sir W. Warren about the Scotch motion, but he stalled us with a previous proposal, so we parted unresolved. I nevertheless completed the lists for the Parliament Committee by night, and at St. James’s Sir W. Coventry and I rejoiced to find wages, victuals, wear and tear would come to above 3,000,000, with extraordinaries more than justifying our declared expense of L320,000. Satisfied, I fetched my wife and her new flowered tabby gown from Unthanke’s, gave my people extra work writing over the lists in a new method, and went to bed in good humour.
levels.summary:
I met Sir W. Batten, Sir W. Pen, and myself at the office for a little meeting, the first since the fire. We rose soon, and Sir W. Warren came by our desire. Sir W. Pen and I talked with him about our Scotch motion, but Sir W.

Warren seemed stumbled at it and gave no ready answer; instead he proposed something previous to it, which he knew would find us work, or writing to Mr. Pett to be informed how matters go there as to cost and ways of providing sawyers or saw-mills.

We parted without coming to any good resolution, and I discerned plainly that Sir W. Warren had no mind to it, but that he was surprised at our motion.

After he left, I did some office business, went home to dinner, returned to the office, and by night got done the lists that are to be presented to the Parliament Committee of the ships, number of men, and time employed since the war. Then I took them with me to St. James’s, leaving my wife at Unthanke’s, where Sir W.

Coventry staid for me. , L320,000. He and I were both mightily satisfied, and he said that if God send us over this rub we must take another course for a better Comptroller.

We parted, and I went to my wife, who had stayed for the finishing of her new best gowne — the best that ever I made her, coloured tabby, flowered — and so took it and her home. , the writing over the lists in a new method, I went home to bed, being in good humour and glad of the end we have brought this matter to.

periods.label: Week of Oct 10

levels.sentence: On a foul October day, after taking leave of my poor father as he set out to see the burned city and fetch my brother, I went from St. James's to Westminster to Deptford and home, hearing of Parliament's L150,000 cut, indulging myself with Mrs. Martin, meeting my wife's poor new girl, and ending the night with my neglected Tangier accounts.
levels.paragraph: I rose and took leave of my poor father, who was setting out for Brampton by the Cambridge coach after coming to see the burned city and to bring my brother to town, and then went through foul weather to St. James's, where Sir W. Coventry told me the House had cut us L150,000 of wear and tear, though they intend to allow 28,000 men and will today declare the money they will give the King. At Westminster, with the Hall and the House both full, I found people eager to fling at the Vice-Chamberlain, and I hoped he would weather it by fate rather than by any dexterity of his. I paid a ticket for little Michell, dined alone at the Swan and played with Sarah, then went to Mrs. Martin's lodging and did what I would with her, she being very big and resolving I must be godfather. After a dark trip to Deptford to order a press for my tools, I came home to find my wife had brought the new girl from Mr. Falconbridge's—wretched poor and plain, needing seven or eight pounds of clothes, with a furred voice but a promising manner of singing—and I finished the night by shutting myself in my chamber to make up my Tangier accounts, which were clear enough but hard to recover because I had left them so long.
levels.summary:
This morning I took leave of my poor father, who was setting out for Brampton by the Cambridge coach. He had made the journey to see the burned city and to bring my brother to town, and after he was gone I went by water and then coach to St. James's through foul weather. There Sir W.

Coventry told me the House had cut us off L150,000 of our wear and tear, on the ground that the King had saved that money while the fleet lay in harbour during the winter.

He seemed pleased, and so was I, that they had abated no more; they intend to allow 28,000 men for the next year, and this very day they have appointed to declare the sum they will give the King and to propose the way of raising it. It is likely to be the great day.

From his chamber I walked with him to Westminster Hall, where the Hall was mighty full and the House likely to be very full about the money business.

I met several people and found they have a mighty mind to have a fling at the Vice-Chamberlain, if they could lay hold of anything; his place, they think, is too much for such a man, or for any single subject of no greater parts and quality than he.

I hope he may weather it all, though I dare say it will not be by any dexterity of his—if he stands, it will be by his fate only, and by people's being taken off by other things.

Then I went home by coach in mighty dirty weather, and then to the Treasurer's office, where I got a ticket paid for my little Michell, and so again by coach to Westminster, coming presently after the House rose. I went to the Swan, sent for a piece of meat, dined alone, and played with Sarah.

Afterwards I spent a while in the Hall and then went to Mrs. Martin's lodging, where I did what I would with her. She is very big, and she resolves I must be godfather.

From there I went by water with Cropp to Deptford, and it was almost night before I got thither. I only gave directions concerning a press I am having made there to hold my turning and joiner's tools, which were lately given me and will make a very handsome piece, and then came back in the dark.

At home I found my wife had come back and brought her new girl, whom I helped her to, from Mr. Falconbridge's. She is wretched poor and but ordinary favoured, and we are fain to lay out seven or eight pounds' worth of clothes upon her back, which goes against my heart.

I do not think I can ever esteem her as I could have done another who had come fine and handsome; her voice, for want of use, is so furred that it does not at present please me, but her manner of singing is such that I think I shall take great pleasure in it. She is come, and I wish us good fortune in her.

At home I met with notice of a meeting of the Commissioners for Tangier tomorrow, and so I must have my accounts ready for them.

That made me confine myself to my chamber presently and set to making up my accounts, which I found very clear, but with much difficulty by reason of my not doing them sooner, things being out of my mind.

It was a day of public cuts and private pleasures, and it ended, fittingly, in a reckoning with my own neglected books.

periods.label: Week of Oct 17

levels.sentence: I balanced a day of church, a frustrating Tangier money plea before the King, court gossip, moving my iron chests out of the damp cellar, and an unlooked-for encounter with Doll Martin.
levels.paragraph: This morning I went to church with my wife and her new woman Barker, then dined merrily with Lady Pen and Peg. In the afternoon I attended the Cabinet to plead again for Tangier money, and found the King immovable as an image, which left me uneasy. Later I moved my iron chests and money out of the damp cellar, read a book on Purgatory, and heard Cholmly's ill-news of court banishments and elections. I also indulged myself unexpectedly with Doll Martin, which sits uneasily with all the rest.
levels.summary:
Up and to church with my wife and her new woman Barker, who I think will do very well; the sermon was lazy, but we dined at home with my Lady Pen and Peg, while Sir William was below with the fleet, and were mighty merry.

After dinner, though the day was mighty cool, I took a coach to White Hall and attended the Cabinet, where I was called in before the King and the lords to account for our want of money for Tangier.

It troubles me that it is my place so often to be the solicitor for what they least love to hear; the King sat like an image and said not one word, and only my Lord Chancellor asked whether it was in nature to help us at this time.

I was referred to another meeting of the Lords Commissioners for Tangier and my Lord Treasurer, and so went away.

I spent the evening reading Stillingfleet's defence of the Archbishop, especially the part about Purgatory, a point I had never fully weighed; though I believe we are in the right, I saw no great matter in the book.

Then, with my people mostly abed, my boy and Jane and I brought two iron chests out of the damp cellar into my closet, and I was much satisfied to see my money safe there again. This being done, and I weary, I went to bed.

This afternoon walking with Sir H. Cholmly in the gallery, I learned that Harry Killigrew has been banished from Court for saying my Lady Castlemayne was a little lecherous girl when she was young.

She complained to the King, who had the Duke of York turn him away; the Duke did it but takes it ill that she did not complain to him first, and ill blood is made.

Cholmly also told me that Mr.

Williamson could not get into the House of Commons, the people crying "No courtier," and that Bab May went down to Winchelsea with the Duke of York's letters but was defeated by a private gentleman, the people crying they would have no Court pimp to be their burgesse—things that bode very ill.

This afternoon, between these things, I went to see and sat a good while with Mrs. Martin, and there was her sister Doll, with whom, contrary to all expectation, I did what I would, and might have done anything else.

periods.paragraph: This morning I went to church with my wife and her new woman Barker, then dined merrily with Lady Pen and Peg. In the afternoon I attended the Cabinet to plead again for Tangier money, and found the King immovable as an image, which left me uneasy. Later I moved my iron chests and money out of the damp cellar, read a book on Purgatory, and heard Cholmly's ill-news of court banishments and elections. I also indulged myself unexpectedly with Doll Martin, which sits uneasily with all the rest.

periods.label: Week of Oct 24

levels.sentence: I went to church, dined with Captain Guy who lamented the fleet's spent valour and foolish commanders, tumbled women all afternoon, supped merrily with the Wights, and ended the day hearing of more disasters among the King's ships.
levels.paragraph: I went to church with my wife, then dined at home with little Michell and his wife and Captain Guy, who cried out that the true English valour is almost spent and that the fleet is governed by fools. After he left, I went with my brother toward White Hall, sent him to Westminster Abbey, and at Mrs. Martin's tumbled widow Burroughes and Doll all afternoon before giving them wine. That evening my wife and I supped with uncle and aunt Wight, saw Woolly's pretty wife, and made merry abusing my aunt with Dr. Venner. I then did accounts and went to bed, while news came of the Revenge's forecastle blown up, the Diamond overset, and other disasters among the King's ships.
levels.summary:
I rose and went to church with my wife, then came home, where I had sent for little Michell and his wife, and also Captain Guy, to dine with me. He and I talked much together.

He cried out against the discipline of the fleet, and confessed that the true English valour we boast of is almost spent and worn out; few commanders do their duty, and he much fears we shall be beaten the next year.

He assured me we were beaten home in the last June fight, and that the whole fleet was ashamed to hear of our bonfires. He commends Smith, and cries out of Holmes for an idle, proud, conceited though stout fellow.

He tells me we are to owe the loss of so many ships on the sands not to any fault of the pilots but to the weather; but I have good authority to fear there was something more. He says the Dutch fight in very good order, and we in none at all.

He says that in the July fight, both the Prince and Holmes had their belly-fulls and were fain to go aside, though if the wind had continued, we had utterly beaten them. He confesses the whole is governed by a company of fools, and fears our ruin. I was much troubled by all this.

After dinner he went, and I with my brother to White Hall; he went to Westminster Abbey. I presently to Mrs. Martin's, and there met widow Burroughes and Doll, and did tumble them all the afternoon as I pleased, and having given them a bottle of wine I parted and came home by boat (my brother going by land).

Thence with my wife to sit and sup with my uncle and aunt Wight, and see Woolly's wife, who is a pretty woman. After supper, being very merry, we abused my aunt with Dr. Venner. We came home, and I did something in my accounts, and so to bed.

There are further marks of the method all the King's work is now done in: the Revenge had her forecastle blown up with powder, killing some men in the River, and the Diamond was overset in careening at Sheerness.

The Foresight also and another came to disasters in the same place this week in the cleaning, which is strange.

periods.label: Week of Oct 31

levels.sentence: I began with a noble cake and a plan to house-warm Betty Michell, but the day turned on want of money, a stolen afternoon with Mrs Bagwell, and a gloomy conference with Sir W. Coventry about the ruined state of the King's service.
levels.paragraph: Burton's wife gave me a noble cake this morning, and I sent my wife with wine to house-warm Betty Michell while I sat at the office answering people who wanted money. In the afternoon I took Mrs. Bagwell into my office and did what I would with her. That evening I found Sir W. Coventry as melancholy as myself: he expects all will be ruined and all discipline lost in the fleet, and we agreed to lay the truth plainly before the Duke of York. I came home to the comfort of my wife and brother, but with a thousand sad reflections upon the times.
levels.summary:
Burton, one of our smiths' wives, presented me with a very noble cake this morning, and I resolved at once that my wife should carry it, with some wine, to house-warm Betty Michell. She readily agreed, and after dinner she went off to Shadwell with my brother, W. Hewer, and Barker.

I stayed at the office, where the morning was spent answering people about want of money—little service to the King and great disquiet to myself, for I do not enjoy my employment as I should when my pains can do no better service.

In the afternoon I took Mrs. Bagwell into my office and did what I would with her, and she went away. I remained there almost until night. When my wife came back, I carried her to her brother's, who is very sick, and then went on to White Hall, where I was alone a good while with Sir W. Coventry.

He was melancholy under the same considerations of the King's service that I am; he confessed he expects all will be undone and ruined, and said himself that all discipline is lost in the fleet—no order, no command.

We agreed that we must again and again lay everything plainly before the Duke of York, to guard ourselves when things grow worse.

He told me the House goes on slowly in finding money, and that the discontented party say they have not done with us: they will have a further bout with us over our accounts, and they are exceedingly well instructed where to hit us.

I left him with a thousand sad reflections upon the times and the state of the King's matters.

I took up my wife and came home, did a little at the office, then supped, and talked with my wife—with whom I have much comfort—and my brother, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of Nov 21

levels.sentence: Though the Great Fire was over, my days were still a whirl of office work, a tiff with my wife over a lascivious handkerchief, a tumble with Doll Lane, a failed rendezvous with Mrs. Burroughs, a weighty parliamentary case against Lord Mordaunt, and a disturbing talk with Cousin Roger about the nation's ruin.
levels.paragraph: This week was a jumble of duties and diversions. At the office, Lord Bruncker showed me Hollar's print of the burned City, and I was glad to learn the King had commanded him to continue his great map. At home I quarrelled with my wife about a low-cut handkerchief, though we quickly made up. Later, I dallied with Doll Lane at the Swan, pursued Mrs. Burroughs in vain, and heard serious charges against Lord Mordaunt in Parliament. Cousin Roger's talk of inevitable ruin left me much shaken.
levels.summary:
On the 22nd, I spent the morning at the office, where Lord Bruncker showed me Hollar's new print of the City, with a fine representation of the burnt part. Hollar had just been sworn the King's servant and commanded to continue his great map, news that pleased me greatly.

At dinner, my wife and I fell out over her cutting a lace handkerchief down to her breasts, which she thought fashionable and I thought unreasonable; we exchanged harsh words but were friends again soon after. I returned to the office and worked late, then supped and played cards at home with Mr. Batelier.

On the 26th, after some morning business, I met Mrs. Burroughs by appointment, but she was with her aunt and could not leave. Earlier, at the Swan, I drank burnt claret with Doll Lane, talked of her sister's lying-in, and tumbled her, doing almost what I would with her.

In Parliament, I heard the great case against Lord Mordaunt for arbitrary proceedings against Taylor; my old chamber-fellow Mr. Sawyer argued against him, and I was glad to see him in good play.

I also met my cousin Roger Pepys for the first time this parliament; he promised to dine with me on Friday and bring Madam Turner, who had lost everything in the fire.

Roger, resolved to retire into the country, asked me to help him find a rich widow, for he is confident we shall all be ruined speedily, and I am much in his mind.

The day ended with me hungry, having missed Mrs. Burroughs, so I went home to eat, did a little office work, and then went to Sir W. Batten's, where Sir J. Minnes and Captain Cocke had no news from the North, only that the rebels are dispersed, which I pray God may prove so. Then home to bed.

periods.sentence: Though the Great Fire was over, my days were still a whirl of office work, a tiff with my wife over a lascivious handkerchief, a tumble with Doll Lane, a failed rendezvous with Mrs. Burroughs, a weighty parliamentary case against Lord Mordaunt, and a disturbing talk with Cousin Roger about the nation's ruin.
periods.paragraph: This week was a jumble of duties and diversions. At the office, Lord Bruncker showed me Hollar's print of the burned City, and I was glad to learn the King had commanded him to continue his great map. At home I quarrelled with my wife about a low-cut handkerchief, though we quickly made up. Later, I dallied with Doll Lane at the Swan, pursued Mrs. Burroughs in vain, and heard serious charges against Lord Mordaunt in Parliament. Cousin Roger's talk of inevitable ruin left me much shaken.

periods.label: Week of Nov 28

levels.sentence: Amidst splendid dinners and flirting with women, I attended to business while the king's troubles in Scotland cast a shadow over everything.
levels.paragraph: This week I hosted two sumptuous dinners, enjoying fine food and noble company. I also indulged in flirtations, first with Pegg and later with Mrs. Burroughs, who proved willing. Business at Whitehall kept me busy, but court fears over Scotland weigh on my mind. Each night I went to bed mightily pleased with the day's entertainment.
levels.summary:
On the 28th I hosted a magnificent dinner for Lord Hinchingbroke and other gentlemen, with six dishes prepared by a man-cook that all praised. I felt that such pleasures as eating in silver with fine company were the height of life.

Afterwards, at Gresham College, Henry Howard was admitted as a Fellow, proud of his Norfolk title. That evening I played cards with Lady Pen and others, and Pegg allowed me to kiss and touch her breast, which gave me great pleasure.

On the 30th, St Andrew's Day, I attended the Duke of York, but most people showed no respect for the Scottish saint, and Parliament sat anyway. I dined with my cousin Roger Pepys and Mrs. Turner, who had lost everything in the plague and was angry with me for not writing. I promised to mend my ways. Later I met Mrs.

Burroughs and took my pleasure with her. On the 3rd, Lord Peterborough's man pressed me for money, and I heard that the Duke of York would go north to raise an army, though nobles would not serve without pay. Kate Joyce came to dinner, distressed about her husband's situation, while my wife lay ill.

I spent the evening with Mrs. Burroughs again, riding in a coach and stopping at a cake house.

periods.label: Week of Dec 12

levels.sentence: After hearing at the office that poor Batters was drowned in the Thames, I dined at home, visited Lord Bellasses in vain, saw Mrs Martin at Westminster Hall, made merry at the Swan with Sarah, fetched another dozen of plates from Sir Robert Viner, invited Mr Thomas Andrews to Christmas dinner, and returned late from the office to bed, sorry for Batters.
levels.paragraph: This morning I heard that poor Batters, a born seaman who had brought his ship in only yesterday, was drowned in the Thames as he went from me to his ship—a sad fortune that makes me more afraid than ever. I dined at home, then went by coach to my Lord Bellasses, but he was not at home, so I went to Westminster Hall to see Mrs. Martin, who is very well and goes abroad tomorrow after her childbed; she told me about the child's coming. I went to the Swan, sent for Sarah, and was mighty merry, then called on Sir Robert Viner about my plate and carried home another dozen, bringing my stock to 2½ dozen. At home I found Mr. Thomas Andrews, talked with him, and invited him to dine with me at Christmas. I then worked late at the office, and went to bed sorry for poor Batters.
levels.summary:
Up and to the office, I heard the ill news that poor Batters—bred a seaman and only yesterday brought his ship up from sea—was drowned in the Thames as he went down from me to his ship. It is a sad fortune, and it makes me afeard, more than ever I was.

At noon I dined at home, then took a coach to my Lord Bellasses, but he was not at home. From there I went to Westminster Hall, where the Lords are still sitting, and I stepped in to see Mrs. Martin. She is very well and intends to go abroad to-morrow after her childbed.

She told me that this child did come the same day that it ought to, after my being with her before her husband came home.

Thence I went to the Swan, where I sent for Sarah, and mighty merry we were. After that I called on Sir Robert Viner about my plate, and carried home another dozen of plates, which makes my stock of plates up to 2½ dozen. At home I found Mr.

Thomas Andrews, with whom I stayed and talked a little, and invited him to dine with me at Christmas. Then I went to the office and stayed late doing business, and so home and to bed.

I am sorry for poor Batters; his drowning has struck me with a fear I cannot shake.

periods.label: Week of Dec 19

levels.sentence: After granting a favor for a boat command and taking a liberty with the daughter, I spend the day on small office business, arranging pictures, and putting accounts in order.
levels.paragraph: I lay long this morning, and upon rising found Mrs. Clerk of Greenwich and her daughter Daniel waiting, their business being a request that I help the daughter's husband gain command of a new pleasure boat, which I promised to do. In my chamber, I took the opportunity to kiss her and touch her breasts. The rest of the day passed in small matters: a little office business, the Exchange, dinner at home, and an afternoon spent arranging pictures and pasting Lady Castlemayne's print onto a handsome frame. In the evening I marshalled my parliamentary accounts papers for future reference, did some Tangier work, and went to bed.
levels.summary:
I lay long in bed, and when I rose I found Mrs. Clerk of Greenwich and her daughter Daniel waiting. Their business included a request from the daughter: to help her husband get command of a little new pleasure boat that was building.

I took her into my chamber and promised to assist, and there I had the opportunity to kiss her and touch her breasts.

Then I went to the office and did a little business, and afterward to the Exchange for similar small matters. I came home to dinner and spent all the afternoon putting things in order, especially pictures, and pasting my Lady Castlemayne's print on a frame I have made handsome; it is a fine piece.

In the evening I went back to the office to marshal my papers of accounts presented to the Parliament, so that I might recur to them on any future occasion, which I did to my great content. Then home, where I did some Tangier work, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of Dec 26

levels.sentence: I spent New Year's Eve settling my accounts and paying debts, meeting Doll Lane for burnt wine, then found I had earned less and spent far more than the year before even though my worth grew, while the kingdom slipped toward public ruin.
levels.paragraph: I rose resolved to settle my accounts for the year, and walked through the hard frost paying off debts, stopping at the Fleece Tavern and later meeting Doll Lane and a young woman named Scott at the Half Moon Tavern for burnt wine. Home again, I cast up my books and found them right, yet the news was bitter: I had earned L2,986, a full L573 less than last year, and had spent L1,154, more than double the L509 of the year before. Still, blessed be God, I found myself worth above L6,200 in good money, which is over L1,800 more than last year, and I resolved to be thankful and more careful. The work left my eyes sore, and I ended the year looking out at a sad public condition: unpaid seamen, a backward Parliament, French and Dutch enemies, a vicious Court, and fears of the kingdom's ruin.
levels.summary:
Rising this day with my full design to mind nothing but my accounts for the year past, I took money and walked out in the great frost to pay all my debts, going as far as the New Exchange. I stayed at the Fleece Tavern in Covent Garden while my boy Tom went to W.

Joyce's to pay what I owed for candles, and then I went on to the New Exchange to clear my wife's score. Coming back, I met Doll Lane, Mrs.

Martin's sister, with another young woman of the Hall named Scott, and took them to the Half Moon Tavern, where we drank burnt wine together, though without more pleasure, and then I came home by coach.

After dinner I turned to my accounts, and at last found them clear and right; but to my great discontent I found that my gettings this year had been L573 less than my last, being this year in all but L2,986, whereas last year I got L3,560.

My spendings this year also exceeded last year's by L644: my whole spendings last year were but L509, whereas this year I have spent L1,154, a sum not fit to be said that ever I should spend in one year before I am master of a better estate. Yet, blessed be God!

I found myself worth in money, all good, above L6,200, which is above L1,800 more than I was the last year, and I pray God make me thankful and careful to make up next year by care what my negligence and prodigality have lost and spent this year.

The doing of this account, entering it fair, and sorting all my expenses to see how and in what points I had exceeded, kept me at work late, till my eyes became very sore and ill; and then I gave over, had supper, and went to bed.

Thus this year of publick wonder and mischief to the nation ends, and is generally wished by all people to have an end. Publick matters stand in a most sad condition: seamen are discouraged for want of pay and are become not to be governed, nor, as matters are now, can any fleet go out next year.

Our enemies, French and Dutch, are great and grow more by our poverty; the Parliament is backward in raising because jealous of the spending of the money; the City is less and less likely to be built again, everybody settling elsewhere and nobody encouraged to trade.

A sad, vicious, negligent Court makes all sober men fearful of the ruin of this whole kingdom next year, from which good God deliver us.

For my own condition, I reckon it remarkable that I am come to abound in good plate, so as at all entertainments to be served wholly with silver plates, having two dozen and a half.

Myself and family are well, with four maids and one clerk, Tom, in my house, and my brother now with me to spend time in order to his preferment; our healths all well, only my eyes are sore as candlelight comes to them, and not else.

periods.label: Week of Jan 2

levels.phrase: Fears, politics, and a bad play
levels.sentence: Amidst Court fears of a French invasion and political tensions with Parliament, I attended conferences, met acquaintances, dallied with Doll Lane, and suffered through the worst play I ever saw.
levels.paragraph: This day was filled with anxiety and frustration. The Court buzzed with fears of a French invasion, while Parliament and the King clashed over accounts. I heard a conference on the Wine Patent, drank with Doll Lane, and then wasted time at a truly dreadful play, which left me displeased and feeling guilty toward my wife.
levels.summary:
I walked to White Hall this morning to attend the Duke of York as usual, while my wife went walking with Mrs. Pen in the frosty fields. The Court is full of great apprehensions about the French, who have certainly shipped many landsmen at Brest, with most guessing their design is Ireland.

We have orders to send all possible ships to the Downes, but we can send no ships without men, nor will men go without money, and every day brings news of new mutinies among the seamen—so our condition is like to be very miserable.

At Westminster Hall I met all the Houblons, who laugh at the French talk and think it is merely a sending to their plantations in the West Indies, suggesting the Court is blowing up an invasion scare to make Parliament hasten money matters. I do not believe we have any such plot. Later, Mr.

George Montagu, whom I have not seen long, was mighty kind.

He tells me all is like to go ill: the King is displeasing the House of Commons by evading their Bill for examining Accounts and putting it into a Commission, leaving out Coventry and me, though naming all the rest Parliament named, all country Lords and not one Courtier.

He also finds the enmity almost over for my Lord Sandwich, and that now all is upon the Vice-Chamberlain, who bears up well.

Thence I went up to the Painted Chamber and heard a conference between the Lords and Commons about the Wine Patent, which I was exceeding glad to attend for the excellent discourses, especially from the Commons—Mr. Swinfen and Sir Thomas Meres—who do outdo the Lords infinitely.

Then down to the Hall and to the Rose Taverne, where Doll Lane came to me, and we drank a good deal of wine, and I gave her twelve sols to buy herself some gloves as a New Year's gift. After that, I went with Sir W.

Pen by coach to the Temple, ate a bit at an ordinary, and then alone to the King's House, where I saw "The Custome of the Country," the second time of its acting.

Knipp does the Widow well, but it is of all the plays that ever I did see the worst—having neither plot, language, nor anything acceptable; only Knipp sings a little song admirably. Fully the worst play that ever I saw or believe I shall see.

I went away home much displeased for the loss of so much time and for disobliging my wife by being there without her. So, by link, I walked home, it being mighty cold but dry, yet bad walking because very slippery with the frost.

Home and to my chamber to set down my journal, and then to thinking upon establishing my vows against the next year, and so to supper and to bed.

periods.full:
I walked to White Hall this morning to attend the Duke of York as usual, while my wife went walking with Mrs. Pen in the frosty fields. The Court is full of great apprehensions about the French, who have certainly shipped many landsmen at Brest, with most guessing their design is Ireland.

We have orders to send all possible ships to the Downes, but we can send no ships without men, nor will men go without money, and every day brings news of new mutinies among the seamen—so our condition is like to be very miserable.

At Westminster Hall I met all the Houblons, who laugh at the French talk and think it is merely a sending to their plantations in the West Indies, suggesting the Court is blowing up an invasion scare to make Parliament hasten money matters. I do not believe we have any such plot. Later, Mr.

George Montagu, whom I have not seen long, was mighty kind.

periods.phrase: Fears, politics, and a bad play
periods.sentence: Amidst Court fears of a French invasion and political tensions with Parliament, I attended conferences, met acquaintances, dallied with Doll Lane, and suffered through the worst play I ever saw.
periods.paragraph: This day was filled with anxiety and frustration. The Court buzzed with fears of a French invasion, while Parliament and the King clashed over accounts. I heard a conference on the Wine Patent, drank with Doll Lane, and then wasted time at a truly dreadful play, which left me displeased and feeling guilty toward my wife.

periods.label: Week of Jan 9

levels.sentence: This week I balanced my office duties with small stolen pleasures, refused a play to work, and fretted over wasteful sales, yet ended each day with a light mind.
levels.paragraph: This week I kept busy with office affairs, dining with Lord Bruncker to discuss the King's losses from poor officers, and meeting with the Trinity House about the loss of The Prince Royall. Amidst the work, I stole a kiss and later touched Mrs. Burroughs' breasts, small pleasures in the midst of business. I refused a play to stay diligent, though I worried about the Prize Office selling valuable goods cheaply. Despite these troubles, I went to bed with my mind at ease, seeing the fruits of my diligence.
levels.summary:
On January 10th, I spent the morning at the office and dined with Lord Bruncker, complaining about the Controller and Surveyor's poor performance and the King's losses. In the afternoon, we met with the Trinity House to examine the master and mates about the loss of The Prince Royall, and I took their examinations.

I also stole a kiss from Mrs. Burroughs when she came on business, a small pleasure amidst affairs. I ended the day with letters and an easy mind.

On January 15th, I refused Lord Bruncker's invitation to see Knipp act in 'The Indian Emperour' to stay at work, though I later got Mrs. Burroughs alone and touched her breasts.

That evening we were troubled about the Prize Office's candle sale, which would sell good hemp and timber at low prices, forcing us to buy them back at higher ones — a horrid evil and shame. Still, I went to bed with a mighty light mind, satisfied with my diligent work.

periods.label: Week of Jan 23

levels.phrase: A merry office, a grave Sunday
levels.sentence: I filled our office with music and dancing for a merry meeting, then spent a Sunday on sermons and fruitless Tangier business, still stealing a kiss from Michell's wife.
levels.paragraph: On Thursday I turned the office into a scene of revelry, with fiddlers, dancing, and good company, including Harris and Knipp. On Sunday I sent my wife to a sermon, kissed Michell's wife, and spent the day on business and worship, though I got no money for Tangier. I felt merry at the feast, ashamed about neglecting Lady Jemimah, and frustrated that Sir Warwicke would not talk business on the Sabbath.
levels.summary:
On Thursday I examined the loss of The Bredagh, which was plainly negligence, then prepared the office for a merry meeting. My guests included Mercer, Batelier, Lady Pen, Captain Rolt, and Mr. Harris, along with Mrs. Pierce and Knipp in a straw hat.

We danced, sang, and Harris sang an Irish song that was the prettiest I ever heard. We supped in the office, wondrous merry, though Mrs. Turner was sad about her lodgings.

On Sunday I sent my wife to hear Mr. Frampton preach, while I went to the Old Swan and kissed Michell's wife, whom I love mightily. I met Sir W. Coventry and Bruncker about office business, heard an anthem at the King's closet, and dined with Sir G. Carteret, ashamed that I had not seen Lady Jemimah.

Later I saw Sir Philip Warwicke, but he would not discuss business on Sunday, so I read Erasmus. Lord Bellasses and I talked of Tangier, but got no hope of money. I walked in the Park with Roger Pepys.

periods.label: Week of Jan 30

levels.sentence: This week I balanced my books, refused a hundred-pound bribe, enjoyed a moonlit walk to the Michells', and secretly took liberties with Betty Michell after the play.
levels.paragraph: On Monday I settled my accounts to my content, though I gained little beyond my salary, and I blessed God for that. That evening my wife, Mercer, Barker, and I walked to little Michell's house with gifts, and sat talking and drinking with them, much pleased by their pretty home. Later, after singing with Mercer in the garden until reminded it was the King's fast-day, I went inside and played cards, kissing Mercer several times before bed. On Tuesday, I refused a box of gold from the flagmakers, heard good news of the Prince and the peace with Spain, and learned of Lord Bellasses's base dealings. After dinner, I went to a play where Knipp sang admirably, then bought gifts for Betty Michell and took her hand, doing whatever I wished with her, which pleased me greatly.
levels.summary:
This week I found myself a small gainer from my month's accounts, yet thanked God I could save from my salary. I enjoyed a pleasant evening walk with my wife, Mercer, and Barker to the Michells' pretty house, carrying neats' tongues, cake, and wine.

Back home, I sang with Mercer in the garden until reminded it was a fast-day for the King's death, then stopped and played cards, stealing a few kisses from Mercer before bed.

The next day I refused a bribe of £100 in gold from the flagmakers, wanting to keep my hands clean. I heard that the Prince was better and that Lord Sandwich had perfected the peace with Spain, but also heard of Lord Bellasses's underhanded dealings with Sir H. Cholmly.

After dinner I saw a good play, was delighted by many fine ladies, and bought Betty Michell gloves and a dressing-box. Later, despite a bruise, I made my wife shift sides and sat with Betty, where she gave me her hand freely and I did whatever I wished, which pleased me greatly.

periods.label: Week of Feb 6

levels.sentence: I went to Westminster for Tangier tallies, heard that Prince Rupert is better, Lord Sandwich is ordered home, and the King's speech hints at peace, then met Betty Michell at the New Exchange and bought her a dressing-box when my wife did not appear.
levels.paragraph: This morning I went to Sir Philip Warwicke about my Tangier warrant for tallies, meeting Lord Bellasses and Creed, but we had no hopes from the Poll Bill. At Westminster Hall I heard that Prince Rupert is better, that Lord Sandwich is ordered home, and that Rupert is hunting stolen prize-goods again; I also bought the King's speech, which hints at peace. After dinner I went with Lord Bellasses to Povy's house to speak with Vernatty, a cunning knave. Then at the New Exchange I met Betty Michell, found my wife was not there, bought Betty a dressing-box, and since she would not come to a drinking-house, I passed the time walking and visited Drumbleby, the best flageolet-maker in town.
levels.summary:
Up by water to the Temple, and thence to Sir Philip Warwicke about my Tangier warrant for tallies.

There I met my Lord Bellasses and Creed, and we discoursed about our business of money; but we were defeated as to any hopes of getting anything upon the Poll Bill, which did not much trouble me, since it concerned me little.

Then with Creed to Westminster Hall, where I walked up and down and heard that Prince Rupert is still better and better, and that he told Dr. Troutbecke expressly that my Lord Sandwich is ordered home.

I hear, too, that Prince Rupert hath begged the having of all the stolen prize-goods which he can find, and that he is looking out anew after them; this at first troubled me, but I do see it cannot come to anything, but is done by Hayes, or some of his little people about him.

Here I bought the King's speech at proroguing the House, wherein are some words which cannot but import some prospect of a peace, which God send us!

After walking a good while in the Hall, it being Term time, I went home by water, calling at Michell's and giving him a fair occasion to send his wife to the New Exchange to meet my wife and me this afternoon. So home to dinner.

After dinner, by coach to Lord Bellasses, and with him to Povy's house, where we found Auditor Beale and Vernatty about their accounts still, which is never likely to have end. Our business was to speak with Vernatty, who is certainly a most cunning knave as ever was born.

Having done what we had to do there, my Lord carried me and set me down at the New Exchange, where I stayed at Pottle's shop till Betty Michell came about five o'clock, and I was surprised not to find my wife there; but I made a good enough excuse. , but it would require an hour's time to make fit.

I was glad of this, thinking to have got her into a drinking-house, but she would not, so I did not much press it, but allowed her to go to her brother's house; and so I passed my time walking up and down, and among other places, to one Drumbleby, a maker of flageolets, the best in town.

    - Took her over the water to the cabinet-maker's
    - Bought her a dressing-box for 20s.; needed an hour to make fit
    - Hoped she would go to a drinking-house, but she refused; I did not press
    - She went to her brother's house while I walked about
    - Visited Drumbleby, the best flageolet-maker in town

periods.paragraph: This morning I went to Sir Philip Warwicke about my Tangier warrant for tallies, meeting Lord Bellasses and Creed, but we had no hopes from the Poll Bill. At Westminster Hall I heard that Prince Rupert is better, that Lord Sandwich is ordered home, and that Rupert is hunting stolen prize-goods again; I also bought the King's speech, which hints at peace. After dinner I went with Lord Bellasses to Povy's house to speak with Vernatty, a cunning knave. Then at the New Exchange I met Betty Michell, found my wife was not there, bought Betty a dressing-box, and since she would not come to a drinking-house, I passed the time walking and visited Drumbleby, the best flageolet-maker in town.

levels.paragraph: At White Hall I joined my brethren in a hot encounter before the Duke of York, insisting that without money no fleet could be expected; I was disgusted that hardly anyone spoke but Sir W. Coventry, while Sir G. Carteret afterward fell stark mad with me. The Lord Treasurer's failure to consult counsel on the Poll act seemed a prodigious danger, and Coventry even said settling it was better work than going to church. levels.summary:
On the seventeenth I rose and called at Michell's, taking him and his wife along to Westminster, though I had no pleasure in her company. At the Duke's we came to a hot encounter over the Ticket Office payments, where I urged that we had nothing to do with the pay and that money had not been sent to us in time.

I was disgusted by my brethren's baseness: hardly a man spoke but Sir W. Coventry, though they were like devils at the office on this point. I declared plainly that without money no fleet could be expected, and desired the Duke of York to take notice; he did, but I doubt it will do any good.

I also noted it as a prodigious thing that my Lord Treasurer had not consulted counsel about the Poll act, and Sir W. Coventry said it would be a better work for the King than going to church to send for the Attorney General; the Duke promised to speak to the King. We broke up having done almost nothing, and Sir G.

Carteret was stark mad at what passed, heartily vexed with me; then I went home by water and to dinner with W.

The next morning I went to my bookbinder's and was mightily pleased to see the Navy account papers sewn together, prettier than I could conceive. At the Exchequer I met Mr. Weaver and discoursed on our law business, which eased my mind, for I had feared I had omitted something prudent.

After dinner at the office I had Mrs. Burrows all alone in my closet and did kiss and touch her breasts. Then with my wife I went to the Duke's playhouse expecting a new play, but we removed to the King's house to see The Mayd's Tragedy.

There I was vexed all the while by two talking ladies and Sir Charles Sedley, yet pleased to hear their discourse; one masked lady, exceeding witty and seemingly virtuous, made sport with him very inoffensively, giving him leave to find her out but not to pull off her mask.

By that means I lost the pleasure of the play wholly, though his exceptions against words and pronouncing were very pretty. So home, to the office for much business, then supper and bed.

periods.label: Week of Feb 27

levels.sentence: I went by barge with Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten to Deptford and Woolwich, where Sir W. Batten's stumble into a tar-drain hole ended in only a sprained foot and the King's business ended in rejecting the ballast wharf, before a merry dinner with Captain Cocke at the White Hart.
levels.paragraph: I rose early and took barge with Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten to Deptford, where we did business at the King's yard and then inspected some of Sir W. Batten's cordage. There Sir W. Batten stepped into a hole made for tar drainage, full of stinking water, and though it might have broken his leg, thanks be to God he only sprained his foot. After he changed his stockings at a strong-water shop, we went on to Woolwich, looked at the ballast wharf but rejected it because the fee-simple could not be bought, and finished with business at the Dockyard and a merry dinner at the White Hart with Captain Cocke.
levels.summary:
Up early, I went by barge with Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten and reached Deptford by eight in the morning. At the King's yard we looked after a little business, and then we went to a private storehouse to view some of Sir W. Batten's cordage.

In that storehouse there was a hole formerly made for tar to drain into, and a barrel stood in it full of stinking water. Sir W. Batten happened to step with one leg into that hole; it might have been very bad for him, breaking his leg or some other hurt, but, thanks be to God, he only sprained his foot a little.

He shifted his stockings at a strong-water shop close by, and then we took the barge again.

We went on to Woolwich, where our chief business was to look at the ballast wharf offered for the King's use to hire. I did not think it worth laying out much money upon unless we could buy the fee-simple of it, but the fee-simple could not be sold to us, so we wholly flung it off.

We went to the Dockyard and stayed a while talking about the business of the yard, then to the Rope-yard, and so to the White Hart, where we dined. Captain Cocke was with us, whom we had found at the Rope-yard, and we were very merry at dinner. Sir J. Minnes told many pretty tales, which I have entered in my tale book.

periods.label: Week of Mar 13

levels.sentence: Amidst public fears of war and want of victuals, I find comfort in family, music, and stolen kisses, while trying to do my duty.
levels.paragraph: This week brought a mix of public anxiety and private pleasure. At court, I heard troubling news about the fleet and the Dutch demands, which alarmed me and made me resolve to examine the Victualler's stores. Yet I also enjoyed friendly dinners with the Carteret ladies, made progress with my wife's music, and stole kisses from Betty and little Mis. Tooker. The cares of state weigh on me, but I manage to balance them with these small comforts.
levels.summary:
On the 13th, I attended the Duke of York with W. Batten, fearing Lord Bruncker's revenge, but instead heard Sir G. Carteret quarrel with him. Mr. Gawden told me of the Council's doubts about setting out a fleet for want of victuals, which alarmed me, so I resolved to draw up a state of the Victualler's stores.

I dined at Carteret's with the ladies, kissed Betty at Michell's, and received Mr. Holliard's advice to bring my father to town for his health. The day ended with public cares and private comforts mixed.

On the 15th, I rose pleased with Tom teaching Barker to sing. At the Exchange, I learned that letters suggest war with the Dutch and France, leaving merchants uncertain. I visited the Carterets, where Lady Carteret spoke of coming afflictions, and walked with Dr. Fuller, who thinks matters will be bad.

I tried unsuccessfully to see Doll Lane at Westminster Hall. Little Mis. Tooker came and I kissed her. Also, Sir John Winter called early about the King's timber business, and I resolved to speak well of him to the Duke.

periods.label: Week of Apr 3

levels.sentence: Amid frustrating dealings with false men and the city's cries for a bad peace, I found myself haunted by Betty Michell's beauty, yet managed my accounts and read a fine book on Turkish policy.
levels.paragraph: I had troubles with Mr. Carcasse and found Sir W. Pen false. I did business, settled accounts, and heard of corruption in church building. Later I enjoyed a play, tried to meet Knipp, and was captivated by Betty Michell, whose image lingered. I also heard of Lady Batten's jewels found suspiciously, and read a good book.
levels.summary:
On April 5th, I was troubled by Mr. Carcasse's ill manners and discovered Sir W. Pen's falseness. After office business and a quiet dinner with my wife, I ran errands: found no council at White Hall, bought snuffers, saw Mrs.

Howlett, and settled my accounts at Sir Robert Viner's, though their books were not kept regularly. Later, Mr. James Houblon gave me no hope of peace, and at Sir W. Batten's, Mr. Young showed how even new churches were placed for the advantage of the great, not the city.

On April 9th, a holiday, I walked to the Exchange where the town cried for peace, and heard of tenants throwing up land. After dinner I saw a mediocre play, attempted in vain to meet Knipp, and kissed a little miss at the Swan.

Then at the Old Swan I saw Betty Michell and did not kiss her, but her beauty ran in my mind all evening and night. Later, Sir W. Batten told me how his lady's jewels were found under a china cup, though we suspected she had hidden them herself. I ended the day reading a well-regarded book on Turkish policy.

periods.label: Week of Apr 10

levels.sentence: I spent the morning foiling Pett's scheme against Lord Bruncker, worked late with sore eyes, wrote to my father, and fondled Mrs Lowther when she came to my office.
levels.paragraph: I went to the office this morning and sat all morning, keeping Pett from forcing Carcasse's business on to spite Lord Bruncker. After dinner I sang a little with my poor wife, then worked at the office until late, troubled by my eyes. I wrote to my father, longing to have him in town and to help him live. This afternoon Mrs Lowther came to my office, and I touched and kissed her breasts and mouth, which she took willingly.
levels.summary:
Up and to the office, where we sat all morning.

That false fellow Commissioner Pett was eager to have Carcasse's business brought on today, so that he might give my Lord Bruncker a cast of his office in pleading for his man Carcasse; but I know Bruncker hates Pett and has spoken against him to the King, so I prevented the business being brought on, and so we broke up.

I went home to dinner, and after dinner had a little singing with some pleasure alone with my poor wife. Then back to the office, where I sat all afternoon until late at night, then home to supper and to bed. My eyes still trouble me after candle-light, which worries me.

This afternoon Mrs Lowther came to me at the office, and I did touch her breasts and kiss them and her mouth, which she took willingly.

periods.label: Week of Apr 17

levels.sentence: Jollity at Whitehall for the Swedish ambassadors gave way to an office day spent awaiting news of Betty Michell's labour, and my wife's return brought the happy tidings of a pretty girl, after which I visited the child and also stole a moment with Mrs. Martin.
levels.paragraph: We kept the feast at Whitehall this day to show jollity to the Swedish ambassadors before they go to the treaty abroad. I sat at the office all morning, and word came that young Michell had called for my wife to attend his wife's labour. She came home at noon with the good news that she and the midwife had delivered poor Betty of a pretty girl, which made me mighty glad. After dinner and some office business, I set my wife at her mother's, went to Mrs. Martin's to do what I would with her, and then visited little Michell's to see the child, which I liked mightily.
levels.summary:
This day the feast was kept at White Hall, by design to make the best countenance to the Swede's Embassadors before their leaving us to go to the treaty abroad, to shew some jollity. We sat at the office all the morning.

Word is brought me that young Michell is come to call my wife to his wife's labour, and she went, and I at the office full of expectation what to hear from poor Betty Michell. This morning much to do with Sir W.

Warren, all whose applications now are to Lord Bruncker, and I am against him now, not professedly, but apparently in discourse, and will be.

At noon home to dinner, where alone, and after dinner to my musique papers, and by and by comes in my wife, who gives me the good news that the midwife and she alone have delivered poor Betty of a pretty girl, which I am mighty glad of, and she in good condition, my wife as well as I mightily pleased with it.

Then to the office to do things towards the post, and then my wife and I set down at her mother's, and I up and down to do business, but did little. So to Mrs.

Martin's, and there did hazer what I would con her, and then called my wife and to little Michell's, where we saw the little child, which I like mightily, being I allow very pretty, and asked her how she did, being mighty glad of her doing well, and so home to the office, and then to my chamber, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of May 15

levels.sentence: A day of lessons, errands, and city wanderings, filled with news of Treasury appointments, a visit to see my pretty mercer and her wife, a fond encounter with Betty Michell, and a private tryst with Mrs. Martin, all rounded off with music and my wife's lingering cold.
levels.paragraph: I rose early to learn a new flagelette tune, then hurried through my business at the Excise and Westminster Hall, where I heard the King had named Treasury Commissioners, though no one could agree who. On my way home I consulted Mr. Commander about coach-houses and stables for my planned building, and we looked at ground by Mr. Hide's. Later, enjoying a broken day, I walked over the Hill to see my young mercer and his pretty wife, spied them but said nothing, then found Betty Michell looking lovelier than ever. I ended at Mrs. Martin's for a stolen pleasure, then home to play flagelets with my wife, who still suffers from her cold.
levels.summary:
I began the day with my flagelette master, who set me a new tune, and I played it presently, feeling that in a month I should be as good as I desire. Then I went by coach to the Commissioners of Excise and to Westminster Hall, where I spoke with several persons on business.

There I heard that the King named the Commissioners for the Treasury yesterday, but nobody could agree who they were: some said the Lord Chancellor, the two Secretaries, Lord Ashly, and others said Sir W.

Coventry and Sir John Duncomb, while all concluded the Duke of Albemarle; reports differed, but it would be known in a day or two.

After my business, I overtook Mr. Commander and took him in a coach to Lincoln's Inn Fields to look at coach-houses, to see what ground was necessary for my planned building. We then went to Mr.

Hide's to look at the ground behind our house again, and he agreed to go with us tomorrow to see some stables, though he thought we demanded more than necessary.

It being a broken day, and having power by my vows, I walked abroad, first through the Minorys — the first time I had been over the Hill to the postern-gate since the fire — to find where my young mercer with his pretty little wife lives, who lived in Lumbard Street.

I did espy them but took no notice, saving that for hereafter.

Then I went down to the Old Swan and saw Betty Michell, whom I had not seen since her christening. Lord, how pretty she is, and looks as well as ever I saw her, and her child, which I am fain to seem very fond of, is pretty also, I think, and will be.

Thence by water to Westminster Hall, where I walked a while talking at random with Sir W. Doyly, and then away to Mrs. Martin's lodging, who was gone before expecting me, and there I did what I wished with her and drank.

I forgot to mention that in the morning I went to the Swan and tumbled a little girl, whose uncle found her with her neckcloth off, which I was ashamed of but let pass with a laugh. Then home, where I spent the evening with my wife at our flagelets, and so to supper, and after a little reading to bed.

My wife is still troubled with her cold.

I find it everywhere now doubted whether we shall have peace or no; the captain of one of our ships that went with the ambassadors says the seamen of Holland to his hearing did defy us, called us English dogs, and cried out against peace, though the common people there do wish it.

periods.label: Week of May 22

levels.sentence: On a sweltering Sunday I managed my usual pleasures — church, a perspective glass, an hour with Mrs. Martin, and reading by the river — only to come home and find my poor father recovering from a fearful fit of his fallen bowel, bearing it all with a patience that went to my heart.
levels.paragraph: This hot Sunday began with a walk in the garden and a crowded church, where I passed the service by ogling fine women with my perspective glass when I was not sleeping. After dinner I went to Westminster, where I spent an hour or two with Mrs. Martin and did what I would with her, then took a pleasant boat ride reading Evelyn and Boyle and watching gallant people sup by the river. But coming home I found my father in terrible pain from a fallen bowel, and his patient, good-humoured endurance under it saddened me more than anything.
levels.summary:
On this hot Sunday I rose earlier than usual and went to walk, for the night had been so hot that I left off my waistcoat for the year. After walking in the garden until church time, my wife and I went to church, where our pew was quite full with several strangers of good condition.

At noon we dined at home with little Michell and his wife, who continues mighty pretty.

After dinner I went alone by water to Westminster. Not finding Mrs. Martin within, I walked toward the parish church and overtook her on the way; she planned to go into church with Mrs. Hargrave (the little crooked vintner's wife of the Dog) and then come out again.

I followed, but when I saw her return I tried to leave, only to meet Mr. Howlett, who offered me a pew in the gallery; I could not refuse, and so against my will I stayed through the whole service in pain while she expected me at home.

I diverted myself with my perspective glass up and down the church, gazing at a great many very fine women, and with that and sleeping I passed the time until the sermon ended. Then I went to Mrs. Martin and stayed an hour or two, and there did what I would with her.

Afterwards I took my boat up as far as Barne Elmes, reading Mr. Evelyn's new book against Solitude, in which I found little excess of good matter, though it was pretty enough for a by-discourse.

I walked the length of the Elmes and took great pleasure seeing gallant ladies and people come with bottles, baskets, chairs, and forms to sup under the trees by the waterside. Back in the boat I read more, then took up Mr. Boyle's book of Colours, where I laughed at many fine things worthy of observation.

I landed at the Old Swan and came home.

There I found my poor father newly recovered from an unexpected fit of pain that had made them fear he would die. They had sent for me to White Hall and everywhere, and for Mr. Holliard, but W. Hewer, being here, did the business of getting my father's bowel, which had fallen down, back into his body.

What made me more sensible was that my father had that very morning shown me the place where his bowel used to fall down and swell, which troubled me to see.

Above all, the poor man's patience under it, and his good heart and humour as soon as he was out of it, worked so upon me that my heart was sad to think of his condition; yet I hope a steel truss will be found to relieve him.
