periods.label: Week of Jun 5

levels.sentence: A day spent rowing between White Hall, Southwark, and Westminster to keep up acquaintance, present a gift of maps, hear news of a recovering duke, and see Betty Michell at church.
levels.paragraph: This morning I took a boat to White Hall and walked to St James’s, where I heard good news of the Duke of Cambridge’s recovery. I visited Sir W. Coventry and talked with him at length, glad to keep my acquaintance with him visible to the world. Lord Barkeley came in with the Duke of Monmouth and other young Hectors, and I offered to give my Lord a set of pocket maps. Later I went to chapel with Creed, but the preacher was dull, so we crossed to Southwark and then home to dinner. In the afternoon I delivered the maps to Captain Aldrige, went to Westminster Church, and saw Betty Michell there.
levels.summary:
This morning I took a boat to White Hall and walked to St James’s, where I heard that the Duke of Cambridge—whom the doctors had long given over—is now likely to recover, for which God be praised. I then went to Sir W.

Coventry and talked with him a great while; I was mighty glad of my good fortune to visit him, because it keeps me in his acquaintance, and the world sees it and reckons my interest accordingly.

While I was there, Lord Barkeley came in, going down to Harwich to look after the militia, and with him came the Duke of Monmouth and many young Hectors—Lord Chesterfield, Lord Mandeville, and others—whom I fear will do little but debauch the country women thereabouts.

When Lord Barkeley said he wanted some maps, Sir W. Coventry recommended the six maps of England bound up for the pocket, and I offered to present them to my Lord, which he accepted, and so I intended to send them to him.

From there I went back to White Hall and to the Chapel, where I met Creed. We stayed to hear who preached, but the man began so dully that we took water and landed in Southwark, going to a church in the street where we take water beyond the bridge; it was so full and the weather so hot that we could not stand there.

So we came to my house, where we found my father and wife at dinner. After dinner Creed and I went by water to White Hall, and there we parted. I then went to Sir G. Carteret’s; he was busy, so I went up into the house and met Captain Aldrige, one of Lord Barkeley’s men, and gave him the book of maps for my Lord.

From there I went to Westminster Church and stayed a good while, and I saw Betty Michell there. —and there the entry breaks off.

periods.brief: A day spent rowing between White Hall, Southwark, and Westminster to keep up acquaintance, present a gift of maps, hear news of a recovering duke, and see Betty Michell at church.
periods.full:
This morning I took a boat to White Hall and walked to St James’s, where I heard that the Duke of Cambridge—whom the doctors had long given over—is now likely to recover, for which God be praised. I then went to Sir W.

Coventry and talked with him a great while; I was mighty glad of my good fortune to visit him, because it keeps me in his acquaintance, and the world sees it and reckons my interest accordingly.

While I was there, Lord Barkeley came in, going down to Harwich to look after the militia, and with him came the Duke of Monmouth and many young Hectors—Lord Chesterfield, Lord Mandeville, and others—whom I fear will do little but debauch the country women thereabouts.

When Lord Barkeley said he wanted some maps, Sir W. Coventry recommended the six maps of England bound up for the pocket, and I offered to present them to my Lord, which he accepted, and so I intended to send them to him.

From there I went back to White Hall and to the Chapel, where I met Creed. We stayed to hear who preached, but the man began so dully that we took water and landed in Southwark, going to a church in the street where we take water beyond the bridge; it was so full and the weather so hot that we could not stand there.

So we came to my house, where we found my father and wife at dinner. After dinner Creed and I went by water to White Hall, and there we parted. I then went to Sir G. Carteret’s; he was busy, so I went up into the house and met Captain Aldrige, one of Lord Barkeley’s men, and gave him the book of maps for my Lord.

From there I went to Westminster Church and stayed a good while, and I saw Betty Michell there. —and there the entry breaks off.

periods.paragraph: This morning I took a boat to White Hall and walked to St James’s, where I heard good news of the Duke of Cambridge’s recovery. I visited Sir W. Coventry and talked with him at length, glad to keep my acquaintance with him visible to the world. Lord Barkeley came in with the Duke of Monmouth and other young Hectors, and I offered to give my Lord a set of pocket maps. periods.label: Week of Jun 12

levels.sentence: A day of office business, a bold letter about want of money, Roger Pepys's visit, and secret dalliances with Nell and Mrs. Markham.
levels.paragraph: I rose to office business and looked out old letters to justify our warnings about the want of money. Roger Pepys came with his foolish son Talbot, and we dined and discoursed on the kingdom's misery and maladministration. In the evening I wrote a bold letter to Sir W. Coventry about our lack of money, feared it might give offence, and wished Sir W. Batten had not signed with me. After Roger left, I dallied with Mrs. Markham in the garden, then read and wrote before bed.
levels.summary:
I was up early and called on by several on office business; then I went to the office to look out old letters to Sir W. Coventry, preparing to justify this office in our frequent foretelling of the want of money.

By and by Roger Pepys came with his son Talbot, whom he had brought to town to settle at the Temple, but because of our present stirs he would carry him back again this week; the lad seemed but a silly lad. I sent them to church this morning, while I stayed at home at the office, busy.

At noon I came home to dinner and had much good discourse with Roger, who was mighty sensible of our misery and maladministration. Talking of our straits, he told me that my Lord Arlington did the last week take up £12,000 in gold, which was very likely, for all was taken up that could be.

Afterwards, discoursing of our family, he said that when I come to his house he would show me a decree in Chancery wherein there were twenty-six men, all housekeepers in Cottenham in Queen Elizabeth's time, of our name.

In the afternoon he went to church again, while I stayed at home busy and showed some dalliance to my maid Nell, speaking to her of her sweetheart which she had, silly girl. After sermon Roger Pepys came again.

I spent the evening with him, much troubled with the thoughts of the evils of our time, whereon we discoursed. By and by occasion offered for my writing to Sir W.

Coventry a plain bold letter touching lack of money; when it was gone I was afeard it might give offence, but upon two or three readings over again the copy of it I was satisfied it was a good letter; only Sir W. Batten signed it with me, which I could wish I had done alone.

Roger Pepys gone, I went to the garden and dallied a while all alone with Mrs. Markham, and then home to my chamber to read and write, and then to supper and to bed.

periods.label: Week of Jun 26

levels.sentence: Though I put on a fine new silk camlet vest, the day was mostly stalled by lack of money, softened by walks with Mrs. Turner and my wife, and clouded by news of poor Tooker's death.
levels.paragraph: I put on my new silk camelott suit, made from my old cloak and now turned into a vest, and went to a rare office meeting with W. Pen and Sir T. Harvy. Our only business was with the owners of six merchantmen we had been taking up, but everything stands still for want of money—we cannot advance them what they need, nor pay for grapnells we promised ready money for in our hour of need. After dinner my wife and Jane went to see Jane's old mistress, and I dallied a little with my maid Nell before returning to the office. In the evening Mrs. Turner walked with me and told me that the King, the Prince, and the Duke of Albemarle speak badly of our whole office except me, which I was glad to hear; then my wife and I walked in the garden, joined by Sir W. Pen with a bottle of cider. I also heard that poor Tooker is dead, a very painful poor man as ever I knew.
levels.summary:
This morning I put on my new silk camelott suit, made out of my cloak and now turned into a vest, and went to the office. There W. Pen, Sir T. Harvy, and I met for the first time since the Dutch came upon this coast.

We had little else to do, because nobody is willing to trust us for anything; our only business was to speak with the owners of six merchantmen we have been taking up this fortnight, and they are still not ready.

They will not fit out their ships without money advanced to them, and we owe them for what their ships earned last year. So every thing stands still for money, while we cannot even pay for the most necessary things we promised ready money for in the height of our wants, such as grapnells.

At noon I went home to dinner, and after dinner my wife and Jane—mighty fine the girl—went to see Jane's old mistress, who had seen my wife the other day.

It is pleasant to hear with what kindness her old mistress speaks of this girl, and how she would still have her; and the wench cried when she told her that she must come to her old mistress my wife.

After they were gone, I went to my chamber and dallied a little with my maid Nell, and then to the office, where I was busy till night. Then Mrs. Turner came and walked with me in the garden to talk about her husband's business.

She told me she hears at the other end of the town how badly our office is spoken of by the King, the Prince, and the Duke of Albemarle, and that there is not a good word said of any of us but of me; and me they all do speak mightily of.

Whether it be true or no, I am mighty glad to hear it, and from all I hear from other people I am likely to pass as well as anybody.

After Mrs. Turner was gone, my wife came and we walked in the garden; Sir J. Minnes is still ill, and so we could not sing. By and by Sir W. Pen came and walked with us and gave us a bottle of cider, and so we went home to supper and to bed.

This day I am told that poor Tooker is dead—a very painful poor man as ever I knew.

periods.label: Week of Jul 3

levels.sentence: A sudden report of peace lightens my heart, but the afternoon brings Doll's strange false fury, Captain Vandener's violence, an ominous nosebleed, and a false deathbed report, before I end the day at home with news of a new-born boy.
levels.paragraph: The report of peace reached me at dinner through Creed, and my heart lightened at once; I carried the news to Batten and Pen and spent a merry afternoon in Westminster. At Mrs. Martin's I was relieved to learn she is not with child, though her sister Doll's loud complaint against Captain Vandener struck me as false, since she has granted me far greater liberties. I confirmed the peace at White Hall, came home to weigh whether to go to Epsom, and stayed, troubled only by my own wavering; the day closed with the welcome news that my Lady Jemimah has borne a boy.
levels.summary:
At the office this morning passed quietly, but at noon home to dinner everything changed: Creed came with the first report of peace. The King has letters saying it is concluded, and Mr. Coventry is coming over for the King's satisfaction. The news was so sudden and glad that I hurried to tell W. Batten and W.

Pen, then sat down to a merry dinner. My heart was light because a continuing war must undo us; though peace may still ruin us if we do not reform and gather money, at least it gives us an opportunity — and for myself, I can hold out until I get my money into my hands, and then shift for myself.

After dinner, leaving Creed, I went by coach to Westminster. I drank at the Swan, talked joyfully of peace in the Hall, and then went to Mrs. Martin's. There I received the other good news I had been dreading: she is not with child. I sent for wine, and her sister Doll and Mrs. Cragg came in.

But then came the worst instance of woman's falseness I ever saw: Doll, sent out for the bottle, came home blubbering and swearing against Captain Vandener, a Dutchman of the Rhenish Wine House, who pulled her into a stable by the Dog tavern and tumbled and tossed her — yet she has suffered me to do anything with her a hundred times.

Her rage, in that light, seemed a strange hypocrisy.

From there I went to White Hall with a joyful heart and asked Mr. Williamson for the news. He said Mr.

Coventry was coming over with a project of peace; if the States and our King agree when their ministers have seen it, we shall agree, and that is all; but the King already gives it out plainly that peace is concluded. Then by coach home, where I wrote a few letters and consulted my wife about going to Epsom to-morrow.

I wavered, but at last bethought myself of business at home and stayed — a little troubled, especially since the Duke of York and W. Coventry are out of town, though it was my own judgment.

I met Mr. Rolt this afternoon, who is going Cornett under Colonel Ingoldsby, his old acquaintance, and I thought it a handsome way for him; but just as he bade me his last adieu, his nose fell a-bleeding, which ran in my mind a good while as an ominous thing.

Also Sir Alexander Frazier, who had been of counsel for Sir J. Minnes and had given him over for a dead man, told me bluntly, "Sir J. " I said no, there is hope of his life, and methought he looked very sillily and went away. Late home to supper, a little troubled about Epsom, but to bed at last.

This day brought great satisfaction too: I hear my Lady Jemimah is brought to bed at Hinchingbroke of a boy.

periods.label: Week of Jul 10

levels.sentence: I took my wife, Mrs Turner, and W. Hewer to Epsom on a dusty July morning, drank the waters, dined and napped, heard praises from James Houblon and stories from Tom Wilson, showed them my cousin's house, and sprained my foot leaping out of the wood.
levels.paragraph: I was up before four with my wife, and after being kept waiting by her dressing until past five, we set out for Epsom in a coach and four, with wine, beer, and cold fowl. At the well I drank four pints of water and had good stools, then we went to the King's Head, where we heard that Lord Buckhurst and Nelly were keeping a merry house nearby. I walked to church, met the Houblons, and was told by James that I was the only happy man of the Navy, which gave me great joy. We dined, napped, listened to Tom Wilson on Dr Fuller's art of memory, filled bottles of water, saw my cousin Pepys's house, and I sprained my right foot leaping out of the wood, though the pain soon went away.
levels.summary:
Up before four with my wife, and after my wife’s slow dressing vexed me by keeping Mrs Turner and me waiting until past five, we set out in a coach and four, carrying wine, beer, and cold fowl.

The day was fine but dusty, and we talked pleasantly all the way, particularly of Mrs Lowther’s pride and ignorance in having her train carried up. We got to Epsom by eight, where I drank four pints of the water and had some very good stools, while the women walked among the company.

I met several tradesmen of the office but spoke little with them, for the sun grew hot.

At the King’s Head we took the best room the house could spare and bespoke dinner. We heard that Lord Buckhurst and Nelly were lodged next door with Sir Charles Sidly, keeping a merry house; I pitied poor Nelly, but thought more of the loss of her at the King’s house. I also saw Gilsthrop, Sir W.

Batten’s clerk, looking like a dying man of consumption, though he said he was better since coming thither. W. Hewer rode with us, but I left him and the women and walked to church, where there were few people and none I knew except all the Houblon brothers.

James Houblon told me I was the only happy man of the Navy, against whom not one bad word had been spoken during all the freedom of treasonous talk; this was a great joy to me, for I know I have deserved as well as most.

Back at the inn, we got a better room and a good dinner, and Pendleton came to us, and we were merry. After dinner, the day being wonderfully hot, we all lay down and took a good nap.

Tom Wilson then came to see me and talked for an hour of his acquaintance with Dr Fuller and Dr Pierson and several great cavalier parsons, and much of Dr Fuller’s art of memory, with several instances.

Afterwards we took coach to take the air, filled bottles of water at the well, and talked with the two women who farm the well at £12 per annum of Mr Evelyn, whose lady and Lord George Barkeley’s lady and their fine jewel-dressed daughter—the one the King of France liked so well—were at church that morning. W.

Hewer’s horse broke loose, and we had the sport of seeing it caught. Then I carried the women to see my cozen Pepys’s house, which they liked very well, and led them into the wood, where we got lost among the thickets and I could not find the walks.

Coming out of the wood by leaping down a little bank, I sprained my right foot, which gave me great present pain, but it went away with walking; and so the women and W. Hewer... The text breaks off there.

periods.label: Week of Aug 21

levels.sentence: After church and a pleasant dinner with Pelling, I went by water to Westminster, where my hope of seeing Betty Michell was dashed when the turned head revealed her mother, but I found consolation in Putney church and the infinite delight of Boyle's Hydrostaticks before a quiet supper with W. Hewer.
levels.paragraph: I began the day at church and then dined at home with Pelling, whose pleasant discourse cheered me. Afterward I traveled by water, landing Pelling at White Hall and going on to Westminster, where I kissed Frank but missed Betty Michell, mistaking her mother for her and feeling vexed. My boat's oar had broken but was mended, and I went up to Putney, where I admired the fine people and young ladies in church. Then I walked to Barne-Elmes, reading Boyle's Hydrostaticks with great delight, and returned home leisurely, supping with W. Hewer and talking of the Office before bed.
levels.summary:
I rose and went to church, then home, where Pelling came by invitation to dine with me, and we had much pleasant discourse. After dinner I took water to White Hall, landed Pelling (who was going to his wife in the country at Parson's Greene), and went myself to Westminster.

At the Swan I kissed Frank, and then went to the parish church hoping to see Betty Michell; I stayed an hour in the crowd, thinking from the end of a nose I saw that it was her, but when the head turned toward me it was her mother, which vexed me.

Returning to my boat, I found one of her oars had broken in rowing but had been fastened again.

I then went up to Putney, stepped into the church to look at the fine store of people and young ladies there, and walked to Barne-Elmes, sending Russel on while I read Boyle's Hydrostaticks, which gave me infinite delight. I walked in the Elms a good while before taking my boat leisurely home with great pleasure.

There I supped with W. Hewer, with whom I had a great deal of good talk touching the Office, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of Sep 4

levels.sentence: I attended to business, dallied with Doll Lane, dined at Sir W. Batten's, and finished the day at Bartholomew Fair, where I pitied a crippled dancer and my wife was accosted by Sam Hartlib.
levels.paragraph: I began the day at the Exchequer and bought heraldry for my wife, then dallied with Doll Lane at the Swan. Finding my wife gone to Walthamstow, I followed with Mrs. Turner, discoursing about Sir W. Pen's baseness. We dined at Sir W. Batten's and inspected his well-furnished house, though I was tired of the company. Later, at Bartholomew Fair, I saw a legless dancer and a clockwork show, and my wife was briefly accosted by Sam Hartlib before we went home.
levels.summary:
I rose and went to the Exchequer at Westminster, then to the Hall, where I bought Guillim's Heraldry for my wife. Afterwards, at the Swan, Doll Lane came to me, and I did touch her, and we drank together before I took a coach home. Finding my wife had gone to Walthamstow with Sir W. Batten, I followed, picking up Mrs.

Turner on the way. She and I talked all the journey about the baseness of Sir W. Pen and the sluttishness of his family, and how the world suspects his son Lowther, sick of a sore mouth, has got the pox.

We arrived at Sir W. Batten's, where Sir W. Pen and his lady and Mrs. Shipman were present. We walked and had an indifferent good dinner, the victuals very good and cleanly dressed with good linen, but no fine meat.

After dinner we went up and down the house, and I liked it well, it being furnished with a great deal of very good goods. I stayed, tired with the company, until almost evening, then took leave, Turner and I together, and my wife with W. Pen.

At Aldgate I took my wife into our coach and went to Bartholomew Fair. It was very dirty and now night.

We saw a poor fellow whose legs were tied behind his back dance upon his hands with his arse above his head, and also upon his crutches, which he did with that pain that I was sorry to see it, and did pity him and give him money.

Then we saw a piece of clockwork made by an Englishman, very good, showing the several states of man's age to 100 years, pretty and solemn, along with several other more cheerful things.

We took a link, the women resolving to be dirty, and walked up and down to find a coach. My wife, being a little before me, had been like to be taken up by one whom we saw to be Sam Hartlib.

My wife had her wizard on, yet we cannot say he meant any hurt, for it was as she was just by the coach-side which he had or had a mind to take up, and he asked her if she went in that coach. But soon as he saw a man come to her (I know not whether he knew me), he departed apace.

By and by we got a coach, went home, had supper, and to bed.

levels.sentence: After a morning of committees and a Council debate where I spoke well and Lord Anglesey defeated Ashly's scheme to borrow the City's credit for seamen's pay, I visited Mrs Martin, promised my goddaughter a coat, found the grave little Willet come to serve my wife, and heard Mr Turner's plan for sending Franke to the Indies.
levels.paragraph: I went by water to White Hall, where the Tangier committee at first had not met and then did little, and afterwards I attended the Duke of York's Council, speaking for the Navy on seamen's tickets and pleasing the King in the debate over Ashly's motion and Anglesey's opposition. After dinner I returned to White Hall, heard of musique before the King, and then at Mrs Martin's bespoke linen, had all with her, and promised my goddaughter her first coat. At home I found Willet, brought by Mr Batelier, very pretty and grave, and I began to be full of thought for my Brampton journey. Mr Turner and his wife came in the evening about sending their son Franke to the East Indy Company, which I very well like.
levels.summary:
By water I went to White Hall for the Tangier committee, but they had not met; I went to St James's with the thought of petitioning the Duke of York for some reward for my service in this war, yet I waived it.

Returning to White Hall, the committee met and did little; then we officers of the Navy attended the Duke of York's Council about discharging seamen by tickets. Several lords spoke, and I was the only one of our number to speak, and I did so in a manner that pleased the King and Council.

In the debate about how to give the seamen assurance they should be paid their arrears, Lord Ashly moved that an assignment for money on the Act might be put into the hands of the East India Company or the City of London, thinking the seamen would believe them.

Lord Anglesey handsomely opposed this, and I think carried it that it would not be. I agreed it was mean for the King to own his want of credit by borrowing theirs; Anglesey told Ashly this was the way to teach Parliament to trust the King no more, and to have a kingdom's Treasurer distinct from the King's.

Home at noon to dinner, I expected our new girle, my wife's woman, but she was not yet come. After dinner I went abroad to White Hall, and there heard there will be musique tomorrow night before the King.

Then to Westminster, where I drank at the Swan, went to the Hall, and then to Mrs Martin's to bespeak linen, and there had all with her; I drank, and promised my goddaughter a new coat—her first coat.

By coach I came home, and there found our pretty girl Willet, who was brought by Mr Batelier. She is very pretty, and so grave as I never saw a little thing in my life; indeed I think her a little too good for my family, and she is so well-carriaged I hardly ever saw. I wish my wife may use her well.

Now I begin to be full of thought for my journey the next week, if I can get leave, to Brampton.

Tonight Mr Turner and his wife came and sat with me, and told me of a design of sending their son Franke to the East Indy Company's service if they can get him entertainment, which they are promised by Sir Andr. Rickard. I do very well like of it. So the company broke up and to bed.

After dinner I returned to White Hall, heard of musique before the King, and then at Mrs Martin's bespoke linen, had all with her, and promised my goddaughter her first coat. At home I found Willet, brought by Mr Batelier, very pretty and grave, and I began to be full of thought for my Brampton journey. Mr Turner and his wife came in the evening about sending their son Franke to the East Indy Company, which I very well like.

periods.label: Week of Oct 2

levels.sentence: From the Council's long hearing on Pett's neglect, through a cheap dinner, Yeabsly's abatement, a stolen touch at Mrs Martin's, and Lord Crew's anxious talk of Sandwich's unanswerable expenses, I came home only to hear that Sir W. Batten was not expected to live till tomorrow.
levels.paragraph: I went up to Whitehall for the Council's hearing on Commissioner Pett, where the Chatham Masters gave him the lie and I thought him a weak, silly man; the matter was put off to Monday. After a scanty dinner and settling Yeabsly's claim with Lord Ashly, I slipped to Mrs Martin's and then to Lord Crew's, who talked of Lord Sandwich's monstrous spending and the difficulty of getting him money or home. Returning, I found Sir W. Batten asleep and soon heard he was not expected to live till tomorrow, which troubled my wife and me both for kindness and for the money he owes me.
levels.summary:
Up, and to White Hall to attend the Council about Commissioner Pett's business, along with my Lord Bruncker and Sir W. Pen. In the Robe-chamber the Duke of York came to us, the officers of the Navy, and we met about Navy business, Sir W. Coventry being with us.

Among other things, he nobly recommended to his Royal Highness, now the prizes were disposing, to remember Sir John Harman to the King for some bounty, and also for my Lady Minnes.

Then we all attended the Council, where there was a long hearing of Commissioner Pett; the two Masters Attendant of Chatham were called in and denied having any order from Pett about bringing up the great ships, which gave the lie to what he says.

In general, I find him but a weak, silly man, guilty of horrid neglect in this business all along. The Council broke off without coming to an issue, ordering another hearing on Monday next.

After the Council rose, I stayed walking up and down the galleries till the King went to dinner, and then I went to my Lord Crew's; but he having dined, I took a very short leave, confessing I had not dined, and so went to an ordinary hard by the Temple-gate, where I have heretofore been, and dined, costing me 10d.

Then I went to my Lord Ashly's, where after dinner Sir H. Cholmly, Creed and I, with his Lordship, handled Mr. Yeabsly's business, coming to agreement with him abating him L1000 of what he demands for ships lost. I then went to Westminster, to Mrs.

Martin's lodging, whither I sent for her, and there heard that her husband is come from sea, which is sooner than I expected; and here I stayed and drank, and so did toucher elle and away.

By coach I went to my tailor's, and thence to my Lord Crew's, where I stayed with him an hour till almost night, discoursing about the ill state of my Lord Sandwich—that he can neither be got to be called home, nor money got to maintain him there, which will ruin his family.

And the truth is, he does almost deserve it, for by all relation he hath, in a little more than a year and a half, spent L20,000 of the King's money, and the best part of L10,000 of his own; a most prodigious expense, more than ever Ambassador spent there, and more than these Commissioners of the Treasury will or do allow.

They demand an account before they will give him any more money, which puts all his friends to a loss what to answer. But more money we must get him, or call him home. I offered to speak to Sir W. Coventry about it, but my Lord would not advise to it without the consent of Sir G. Carteret.

So home, and I went to see Sir W. Batten, who fell sick yesterday morning. He was asleep, so I could not see him, but in an hour after, word was brought me that he is so ill it is believed he cannot live till tomorrow.

This troubles me and my wife mightily, partly out of kindness, he being a good neighbour, and partly because of the money he owes me upon our bargain of the late prize. So home, and to supper and to bed.

periods.label: Week of Nov 13

levels.sentence: I called on Alderman Backewell to settle the £6,000 Tangier remittance, and heard him boast how, after the Sheerness disaster nearly ruined him, he instantly honoured £7,000 to the Swedes' ambassadors and offered to answer any further drafts.
levels.paragraph: I went to Alderman Backewell's to arrange the £6,000 remittance to Tangier, which he promised to send by Monday's post; we agreed I should note his diligence for the Lords Commissioners. Then he fell to boasting of his condition, saying the Sheerness business drove him mad and might well have undone him. Yet the very next day he paid and took up bills to answer his promise of £7,000 to the King for the Swedes' ambassadors, and told the bankers they might draw on him for all their money and £10,000 more. He also told me Serjeant Maynard and many others came to demand money, and his only question to each was "What countrymen are you?"
levels.summary:
This morning I went to Alderman Backewell's and spoke with him about remitting the £6,000 to Tangier. He promised to do it by the first post, Monday the 18th, and I agreed to take notice of it so that he might be seen to have done his best at the desire of the Lords Commissioners.

From that we fell to talking of his condition, and he told me with some vain glory how the business of Sheerness made him quite mad and might well have undone him.

Nevertheless, the very next day he paid here and got bills to answer his promise to the King for the Swedes' ambassadors (who were then doing our business at the treaty at Breda) £7,000, and promised the bankers there that if they would draw upon him for all that he had of theirs and £10,000 more, he would answer it.

He also told me that Serjeant Maynard came to him for a sum of money he had in his hands, and so did many others, and his answer was, "What countrymen are you?" This shows his shrewdness and confidence in the face of demands.

periods.label: Week of Nov 20

levels.sentence: From Cooling I learned that the Lords' stiffness toward Lord Clarendon springs from self-interest and fear, and that this may drive the King to a packed court; then, unable to shake off Creed, I went to the Excise Office and the Temple, noted Selden's plain tomb beside his executor's better one, and came home to dinner.
levels.paragraph: This morning I drank strong water with Betty Michell, though I had no chance to kiss her, and then went by water to White Hall, where I met Creed. At Westminster Hall we met Cooling, Lord Chamberlain's Secretary, who told me the truth behind last night's report: the Lords' stiffness toward my Lord Chancellor is no kindness but fear for their own skins, and it may actually prejudice him by pushing the King toward a packed court. Later, though I wished to be rid of Creed, I was forced to carry him to the Excise Office and the Temple, where I compared Selden's plain tomb with his executor's finer one. At last I parted with him, took coach, and went home to dinner.
levels.summary:
I rose betimes and took my morning draught of strong water with Betty Michell, though I had no opportunity to kiss her. Then I went by water to White Hall, met Creed, and walked with him to Westminster Hall, where we talked long together of news.

There we met Cooling, my Lord Chamberlain's Secretary, and from him I learned the truth of all I had heard last night.

Cooling explained that the Lords' stiffness is in no manner of kindness to my Lord Chancellor, for he neither hath obliged, nor doth, nor for the future likely can oblige any of them, but rather the contrary; they fear what the consequence may be to themselves should they yield in his case.

Moreover, he shewed me how this is rather to the wrong and prejudice of my Lord Chancellor, for it is better for him to come to be tried before the Lords, where he can have right and make interest, than, when the Parliament is up, be committed by the King and tried by a Court on purpose made by the King, of what Lords the King pleases, who have a mind to have his head.

So that my Lord's own son, Cooling tells me, hath moved, that if they have Treason against my Lord of Clarendon, they would specify it and send it up to the Lords, that he might come to his trial. So full of intrigues is this business!

Having now a mind to go on and be rid of Creed, I could not, but was forced to carry him with me to the Excise Office, and thence to the Temple, where we walked a good while in the Temple church, observing the plainness of Selden's tomb and how much better one of his executors, buried by him, hath.

At last I parted with him, took a coach, and went home to dinner.

periods.label: Week of Dec 25

levels.sentence: I spent the last day of 1667 in the long suspense of White Hall and the Tangier committee, came home to a mournful dinner with my uncle and uneasy talk of the Act for Accounts, and ended the year at Westminster, going to Mrs. —.
levels.paragraph: I rose in a silent mood, said scarcely a word to my wife, and spent the morning at White Hall waiting while the Duke of York was with the King in the Cabal, hearing all the talk of the great lords being turned out of power over the Chancellor's business. Then came a dull meeting of the Tangier committee, where Lord Middleton seemed a heavy, needy man. Back home, Uncle Thomas dined with us in mourning for his daughter, and the Act for Accounts hung over the table like a threat I dared not examine. Afterwards I took my wife to Unthanke's and went on to Westminster, to Mrs. —.
levels.summary:
I rose this last day of the year and said little to my wife—not from anger, but from my own silenced mood—then made for White Hall. There I waited for a long time while the Duke of York was closeted with the King in the Cabal, and Creed and I talked in the Vane-Room.

I could feel everyone's expectation turning on the great business of thrusting those powerful lords out of the council; the quarrel, as I perceived it, was only that they stood against the King's will in the Chancellor's affair.

When the Duke at last came out, we went into the Tangier committee, where my Lord Middleton made his first appearance. He struck me as a dull, heavy man, though a stout and needy soldier—and I feared that his neediness would keep that poor garrison from ever yielding any real value to the King.

After a short meeting we broke up, and I went home to the office, found them sitting, and joined them until our business was done.

At dinner with my people, my uncle Thomas was there, wearing a mourning hat-band for his daughter Mary.

We fell to discoursing on the Act for the Accounts, which, by report of those who had read it—I have not read it, and have no mind to, for fear of meeting something in it to trouble me—gives a greater power to those commissioners than was ever given to any subjects; indeed, too much.

After dinner I walked with my wife and the girl to Unthanke's, left her there, and then went on to Westminster, and from there to Mrs. —, where the day's record breaks off.

  - Walked with my wife and the girl to Unthanke's; left my wife there
  - Went to Westminster and on to Mrs. —, where the record breaks off
periods.sentence: I spent the last day of 1667 in the long suspense of White Hall and the Tangier committee, came home to a mournful dinner with my uncle and uneasy talk of the Act for Accounts, and ended the year at Westminster, going to Mrs. —.
periods.paragraph: I rose in a silent mood, said scarcely a word to my wife, and spent the morning at White Hall waiting while the Duke of York was with the King in the Cabal, hearing all the talk of the great lords being turned out of power over the Chancellor's business. Then came a dull meeting of the Tangier committee, where Lord Middleton seemed a heavy, needy man. Back home, Uncle Thomas dined with us in mourning for his daughter, and the Act for Accounts hung over the table like a threat I dared not examine. Afterwards I took my wife to Unthanke's and went on to Westminster, to Mrs. —.

periods.label: Week of Jan 1

levels.sentence: Despite a mix-up that brought Mr. Pierce and Mr. Harris to my house for dinner instead of supper, and a thwarted hope of seeing Mrs. Bagwell, I went on to enjoy a play and then a splendid night of dancing, singing, and music with a large company at home.
levels.paragraph: I left home in the morning to do business at White Hall, only to learn from Mr. Pierce that my wife’s folly had made him expect dinner instead of supper. Coming home, I found Mr. Harris there by the same mistake, and was delighted by his excellent conversation. After seeing The Tempest and gathering Mrs. Pierce and others, I brought a great company back to my house, where we danced and sang to the Duke of Buckingham’s music until two in the morning. The night was full of joy, though afterward I found Mrs. Hollworthy but a mean, conceited woman.
levels.summary:
I rose early and left my wife to make herself ready and the maids to prepare supper for our evening company, then went by coach to White Hall. While there I met Mr.

Pierce and discovered, to my chagrin, the folly of my wife: he understood that he and his wife were to dine at my house today, when in truth they were invited to sup. Having done my business at court, I went home to dinner and found Mr. Harris there by the like mistake.

Nevertheless we got a pretty dinner ready, and I found him an excellent person, one of the best qualified for converse I have ever known—great understanding, observation, and most civil and agreeable in discourse. I was mightily pleased with his company.

After dinner I took coach with Mr. Harris, my wife, and the girl, intending to go to a play and then carry him to his own house. But I alighted on the way to look for Mrs.

Bagwell, whom I had seen that day in our entry, newly come from Harwich and not seen above a year; I would have liked to have had my way with her, but she was gone. So I took coach again and joined my wife at the Duke of York’s house in the pit, then fetched Mrs. Pierce, her cousin Corbet, Knepp, and little James.

, besides oranges, which troubled me, though their company pleased me. The play acted was The Tempest.

After the play we stayed until Harris was dressed again, then all went by coach to my house. There I found good fires and candles ready, and the Office likewise, with the two Mercers, Betty Turner, Pendleton, and W. Batelier.

With much pleasure we fell to dancing, with extraordinary music—two violins, a bass viol, a theorbo, and four hands—the Duke of Buckingham’s music, the best in town, sent me by Greeting.

By and by we went into my house to a very good supper, mighty merry, with good music playing; after supper we danced and sang till about midnight, when we had a good sack posset and an excellent cake of our Jane’s making, which cost near 20s. and was cut into twenty pieces.

There were by now so many company, for young Goodyer and some other young neighbours who could dance came in upon hearing of our dancing. Anon Mrs. Turner the mother came in and brought with her Mrs. Hollworthy, which pleased me mightily.

So we danced and sang again with extraordinary great pleasure until about two in the morning, and then broke up.

Mrs. Pierce and her family, with Harris and Knepp, went home by coach as late as it was. After they were gone, I took Mrs. Turner and Mrs. Hollworthy into my house and gave them wine and sweetmeats. But I found Mrs.

Hollworthy a mean woman in understanding, only a little conceited, proud, and talkative, with nothing extraordinary in person, discourse, or understanding.

periods.label: Week of Jan 22

levels.sentence: I spent the Lord's Day in church with my wife, then labored late over my Tangier and East India accounts with Mr. Poynter transcribing them fair, supped with W. Hewer, and had the girl comb my head till I slept.
levels.paragraph: I went with my wife to church and dined at home with no strangers. All the afternoon and evening I was deep in serious business over my Tangier and East India accounts, with Mr. Poynter transcribing them fair. After supper with W. Hewer, I let the girl comb my head until I fell asleep, and so to bed.
levels.summary:
On January 26th, I rose and went with my wife to church, then returned home for dinner, where no strangers were present. The rest of the day I gave to serious business: settling my Tangier accounts and examining my East India accounts.

Mr.

Poynter worked with me all day, employed to transcribe the accounts fair. In the evening W. Hewer supped with us.

Afterwards the girl combed my head until I slept, and then I went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Feb 26

levels.sentence: After a morning spent preparing our parliamentary defence with Sir W. Coventry, I made plans with my wife, called on Betty Michell’s family and Mrs. Martin, admired the King’s starling, and went to bed troubled by Carcasse’s confession about "The Flying Greyhound".
levels.paragraph: This morning I went to Sir W. Coventry and we went over our whole defence on the ticket business before Thursday’s House, though I found him anxious about Parliament and helped him with the flag-maker’s place. At home I persuaded my wife to accept having her closet made up and a summer visit to my father’s instead of a coach. In Westminster I missed Betty Michell at St. Margaret’s but met her parents, then found a chance at Mrs. Martin’s and was charmed by the King’s starling. That evening Carcasse confessed his old complaint about "The Flying Greyhound", which weighed on me so much I went to bed without supper.
levels.summary:
Up betimes, I went by coach to Sir W. Coventry’s, carrying all my notes and papers, and we ran through our whole defence in the business of tickets, to answer the House on Thursday. I thought we should make a good defence unless they were set on ruining us.

I found Coventry very anxious about Parliament’s proceedings, though he tried to hide it, and he wanted his name kept out of our discourse as much as possible.

He is now having to defend himself in the matter of selling places, and I helped him with his defence concerning the flag-maker’s place that had been named in the House.

We also went over the complaint about want of victuals in the fleet in 1666, which will lie on me to defend, so my head was full of care and weariness in my employment.

Then home, where my mind was a little lightened by the better method I had laid together for our defence. , and Jane to accompany her. I did this partly to entertain her and to prevent the falling out she usually has with my father or Deb. when she goes into the country.

After dinner I went by coach to Westminster, to St. Margaret’s church, thinking to see Betty Michell, but she was not there.

I met her father and mother instead, went with them to her father’s house, where I had never been before, and was made much of, with good strong waters they have from their son Michell; they are mighty good people. Thence to Mrs.

Martin’s, where I had not been in a good while, and though company was there, with great difficulty I got an opportunity to have my will with her. I was mightily taken with a starling she has, which formerly belonged to the King and was kept in his bedchamber; it whistles and talks the most and best that ever I heard.

Thence to visit Sir H. Cholmly, who is still sick of his cold, and then called at Sir G. Carteret’s house in Lincoln’s Inn Fields, but spoke with nobody, and so home.

At home I spent the evening talking with W. Hewer about the business of the House, declaring my expectation that we should all be turned out. Then Carcasse came to me on business, and of his own accord confessed that he had formerly discovered a complaint against Sir W. Batten, Sir W.

Pen, and me, that we preferred paying some men to man "The Flying Greyhound" over others, by order under our hands. Upon recollection I believe the thing is true, but I hope no great matter can be made of it; yet I would be glad to have my name out of it, and I shall labour to do so.

In the mean time it weighs as a new trouble on my mind, and troubled me all night. I went to bed without supper, my eyes also being a little overwrought of late that I could not stay up to read.

periods.label: Week of Mar 11

levels.sentence: I navigated a week of political accusations, dinner preparations, and social visits, ending with a surprising painting that brought me rest.
levels.paragraph: This week I resolved to speak less in Parliament and instead answer only objections, but I found myself caught up in rumors of enemies and the stress of arranging a grand dinner. I faced a rebuke to my cousin Roger, dined poorly at Chatelin's, met Lord Hinchingbroke's lady for the first time, and struggled to find a cook until Mr. Levett kindly agreed. Later I walked with Sir W. Coventry, dined with great men at Sir Thomas Clifford's, spent an afternoon at Mrs. Martin's, and was utterly delighted by a picture so realistic it astonished me. Despite the worries, I went to bed with my mind at rest.
levels.summary:
Parliament occupied my mind this week. I resolved to make no more speeches while my fame is good, only to answer objections. My cousin Roger Pepys told me he had been rebuked for supporting the King's supply, and that there were whispers of great things against me.

I stayed calm, knowing I was prepared to answer, and we waited in the Hall but were not called. Later I dined badly at Chatelin's with my colleagues and then attended to the Duke of York, complaining that we stood still for want of money.

Much of my energy went into preparing for a feast at my house. I invited Sir Thomas Crew and met Lord Hinchingbroke's lady for the first time; she seemed comely and good-humoured. I found my napkins laid in pretty figures, bought new pewter, and after a long search secured Mr. Levett as cook.

My wife was unwell with a breast breakout, which troubled me, but I hoped it would be for her good. We set everything in order late that night.

On the fifteenth I walked to Sir W. Coventry and discussed the Commissioners of Accounts, who had laid little blame on us but were dissatisfied with Sir G. Carteret's bookkeeping.

I walked with the King and Duke in the Park, and later enjoyed an excellent dinner with Sir Thomas Clifford and Lord Arlington, where we spoke of Spain and the Escuriall. That afternoon I visited Mrs. Martin and her companions, and in the evening I was astonished by a picture W.

Hewer brought—a painting on a deal board so lifelike that I could not remove my fancy. I went to bed very sleepy, but my mind was at good rest.

    - Afternoon: visited Mrs. Martin and her sister and Mrs. Burrows

periods.sentence: I navigated a week of political accusations, dinner preparations, and social visits, ending with a surprising painting that brought me rest.
periods.paragraph: This week I resolved to speak less in Parliament and instead answer only objections, but I found myself caught up in rumors of enemies and the stress of arranging a grand dinner. I faced a rebuke to my cousin Roger, dined poorly at Chatelin's, met Lord Hinchingbroke's lady for the first time, and struggled to find a cook until Mr. Levett kindly agreed. Later I walked with Sir W. Coventry, dined with great men at Sir Thomas Clifford's, spent an afternoon at Mrs. Martin's, and was utterly delighted by a picture so realistic it astonished me. Despite the worries, I went to bed with my mind at rest.

I rose betimes and went to Westminster, where I met my cousin Roger and Creed.

Roger continues to insist that the only way to save the nation is to dissolve this Parliament and call another, but there are so many among the King's courtiers who would be ruined by a new Parliament that they will never persuade the King to it.

I spent most of the morning walking about with one or other of them, and presently met Doll Lane at the Dog tavern, where I had my desire of her, and gave her 20s. as my valentine.

Coventry argued against it, and I was wholly silent, because I saw the King, by the Prince's earnestness, was willing to it, and he cried very sillily that if we ever intended to man the fleet without being cheated by captains and pursers, we might go to bed and resolve never to have it manned.

So it was overruled, like other things, that all volunteers should be presently entered. There was then another great business about our signing of certificates to the Exchequer for goods upon the £1,20,000 Act, which the Commissioners of the Treasury all opposed, laying the fault upon us.

I spoke in justification of what we had done, even to the angering of Duncomb and Clifford, which vexed me, but for all that I set the Office and myself right and went away with the victory, my Lord Keeper saying he would not advise the Council to order us to sign no more certificates.

Pepys making of another speech to them," which made all the Lords, and the Attorney- and Solicitor-General, look upon me.

Thence Sir W. Coventry, W. Pen, and I took a hackney-coach to Hyde Park for a little air, the first time I have been there this year; we met many coaches going and coming, the weather being mighty pleasant. Coming back again, I alighted in the Pell Mell and went to see Sir H.

Cholmly, who continues very ill of his cold. There came in Sir H. Yelverton, whom Sir H. Cholmly commended to my acquaintance, but neither of us remembered that we had been school-fellows, and I said nothing of it.

He took notice of my speech the other day at the bar of the House, and indeed I perceive he is a wise man by his manner of discourse.

He says the town is full of it that now the Parliament hath resolved upon £300,000, the King, instead of fifty, will set out but twenty-five ships, and the Dutch as many; and that Smith is to command them, who is allowed to have the better of Holmes in the late dispute, and is in good esteem in the Parliament, above the other.

Thence home, and there, in favour to my eyes, I stayed at home, reading the ridiculous History of my Lord Newcastle, wrote by his wife, which shows her to be a mad, conceited, ridiculous woman, and him an ass to suffer her to write what she writes to him, and of him.

Betty Turner sent my wife the book to read, and it being a fair print, to ease my eyes, which would be reading, I read that. Anon comes Mrs.

Turner and sat and talked with us, most about the business of Ackworth, which comes before us to-morrow, that I would favour it, but I do not think, notwithstanding all the friendship I can show him, that he can escape, and therefore it had been better that he had followed the advice I sent him the other day by Mrs.

Turner, to make up the business. So parted, and I to bed, my eyes being very bad; and I know not how in the world to abstain from reading.

periods.label: Week of Mar 25

levels.sentence: In the last days of March 1668 I tried silence to calm my wife, saw the great stone cut from Sir Thomas Adams, and answered Parliament about the fleet's provisions.
levels.paragraph: This week I walked about London on small errands while Parliament sat, kissed Frank at the Swan, and had a quiet dinner after trying a new tactic of silence with my wife when she was cross. In the afternoon I went to Mrs. Martin's and had my way with her, then rode about with my wife looking for plays that were not acting, ending at Hyde Park in the dust. I heard of the cowardice of Smith and Allen, and of the brave Charles Wager whom even the Moors remember with tears. I also paid my uncle his quarterly pension, gave the Committee of Parliament a full account of the victualling for Harman's fleet, and watched Mr. Hollier come in fuddled and talk Latin. That night I gave Deb good advice while she wept, because my wife thought her sullen writing was a fault.
levels.summary:
On the 27th I walked to White Hall and learned that my Lord Sandwich is coming from Spain to see to Tangier, which is much out of order. I wandered through Westminster Hall without speaking to anyone, drank and kissed Frank at the Swan, and then showed myself at the Exchange before going home to dinner.

My wife and I had a small squabble, but I tried staying silent instead of provoking her, and it worked wonderfully—she calmed down and became fond. That afternoon she went to buy lace while I visited Mrs.

Martin and had my way with her, and then we rode to the Nursery and the New Cockpit, but no play was acting, so we went to Hyde Park, which was so dusty it was troublesome.

At noon Mr. Pelling showed me the stone cut from Sir Thomas Adams' body—it weighs over twenty-five ounces, bigger than my fist, yet the old alderman never had a fit from it and died of something else.

Creed also told me how Sir Jeremiah Smith and Sir Thomas Allen are known for cowardice and ill-government in the Straits, while poor Charles Wager behaved so well that even the Moors mention him with tears. On the 31st I paid Uncle Thomas his quarterly pension, and Mr.

Hollier came in fuddled, talking Latin and laughing. A summons took me to a Committee of Parliament, where I gave a full account of the victuals sent to Harman's fleet, though I saw how fixed they are in their jealousy, wanting to blame Brouncker. That night, after Mr.

Pelling left, I called Deb to write down things for my wife's journey; she cried because her writing was poor, and my wife took it as sullenness. But when she undressed me for bed, I gave her good advice and kissed her while she wept.

periods.label: Week of Apr 1

levels.sentence: Between sending off my wife and struggling with office business, I found time to kiss Deb and later Knipp, and heard the scandal that Lady Castlemayne has taken the actor Hart as her lover.
levels.paragraph: On the second I kissed Deb after giving her ten shillings, saw my wife off toward my father's house (longing to kiss Deb again), and then spent the day on office matters. On the seventh, after a frustrating morning trying to fit forth a fleet, I went to the playhouse and afterward with Knipp heard the news of Lady Castlemayne's affair with Hart. I kissed Knipp, but her paint held me back, and I went home to my letters.
levels.summary:
On April 2, after a pleasant talk with my wife, I resolved on house alterations. Betty Turner, her mother, W. Batelier, Deb, and Jane arrived, and I gave Deb ten shillings and kissed her.

Later, as my wife and the others set out for my father's house, I had to alight in Cheapside on meeting Lord Anglesey, and though I had a great mind to kiss Deb again, I did not. The rest of the day was taken up with office business and dining with Mr. Pierce.

On April 7, I spent the morning in a great hurry fitting forth the little fleet, but was hindered by want of money and people's distrust. At noon my solicitor and the Auditor's men dined with me over my account.

In the afternoon I went to the King's playhouse for "The English Monsieur," sitting in an upper box for privacy, and found much mirth.

After the play, I went down to Knipp and sat with her while she undressed.

She told me the mighty news that Lady Castlemayne is mightily in love with Hart of their house, giving him presents, and that Becke Marshall is the only one privy to it and the means of bringing them together—so Castlemayne is even with the King's love for Mrs. Davis.

I kissed Knipp in the Park, but not more because of her paint, and then set her down at Mrs. Manuel's and went home to bed.

periods.label: Week of Apr 15

levels.sentence: I began learning the recorder, pursued my errands amid the political stir over Sir W. Pen's impeachment, visited Mrs. Martin, and ended the day writing to Lady Sandwich, displeased that my maid had brought her brother to lie at my house.
levels.paragraph: This day I began to learn the recorder from Th. Greeting's book, spent the morning at the office, and dined with my clerks, laughing at Sir W. Pen's calling himself the King's martyr. The great business was Pen's impeachment: at Westminster Hall I heard he was ordered to be impeached, and from G. Montagu I learned that the Coventrys were trying to save him by laying the blame on Lord Sandwich, which I silently believed was the only way. I ran errands to the Treasury Commissioners in vain, visited Mrs. Martin and did what I would, talked with Lord Crew and G. Carteret, and came home by moonshine after writing to Lady Sandwich—only to be displeased that my maid had brought her countryman brother to lie there.
levels.summary:
This morning I bought Th. Greeting's book, and began this day to learn the recorder. I was at the office all the morning, then dined with my clerks, and we were merry at Sir W. Pen's crying yesterday to the King that he was his martyr.

Afterward I took a coach to White Hall to see the Commissioners of the Treasury about certificates, but they did not meet; it cost me 2s. Then by water to Westminster, and at Westminster Hall I heard that W. Pen is ordered to be impeached, which cost 6d.

I spoke with many, particularly G. Montagu, and went with him and Creed to his house. He told me how W. Pen hath been severe to Lord Sandwich, and that the Coventrys are both labouring to save him by laying it on Lord Sandwich.

Our friends cry out upon this, but I remained silent, because I believe they did it as the only way to save him. It could not be carried to commit him; the House is thought to cool. W. Coventry's being for Pen provoked Sir R. Howard and his party, while the Court is all for W. Pen.

Thence to White Hall, but the Commissioners again did not meet; there I met Mr. Hunt, and from there went to Mrs. Martin's, where I did what I would. She was troubled for want of employment for her husband, and I spent 1s on her.

periods.label: Week of Apr 22

levels.sentence: I spent the day on political errands and personal longings, saw the woman I desired but lacked the courage to approach her, found Betty shy and her husband unhelpful, heard of Sir W. Pen's impeachment with the Duke's kindness, watched a play, and ended the evening at Sir W. Pen's because my eyes were too bad to read.
levels.paragraph: Up betimes and to White Hall, where I learned of the petition against Sir W. Coventry and secured Mr. Wren's favour for Mrs. Pett. After talking with Lord Brouncker about Parliament's dangerous violence, I went to Ducke Lane, bought a Spanish book from Fouquet's library, and saw my pretty woman but dared not approach her. Later I called on Betty Michell but got no opportunity, then returned to White Hall to hear of Sir W. Pen's impeachment. I finished the day at the playhouse and supped at Pen's, my eyes too sore for reading.
levels.summary:
This morning I rose early and took a boat to White Hall to see the Duke of York. There I heard that Hopis and Temple intend to bring in a petition against Sir W. Coventry, which troubles me, though I hope he will escape. I also presented Mrs. Pett's condition to Mr. Wren, who promised his favour.

Then I sat with Lord Brouncker, who fears the Parliament will, by their violence and delay over money, force the King to risk everything and dissolve them.

Afterwards I went to Ducke Lane, where a bookseller had bought much of Monsieur Fouquet's library.

" While there, I tried to see the pretty woman I had kissed in the dark a little while ago; I found her alone in the shop but lacked the confidence to speak to her, so my pains were lost—though I intend to try another time.

Returning home, I dined and then went to the Old Swan, stopping at Michell's to see Betty; but she seemed either shy or foolish, and her husband had no mind to let me see his wife, so I got little satisfaction.

Back at White Hall by water, I did some small business with the Duke of York. There I heard him tell how Sir W. Pen's impeachment had been brought into the House of Lords that day; the Duke spoke of him with great kindness, and the Lords would not commit him until they could find a precedent, inclining to favour him.

From there I went to the King's playhouse and saw a piece of "Beggar's Bush," which I had not seen in years. Then I went home, and having nowhere else to go and my eyes too bad to read, I supped at Sir W. Pen's and sat talking late before going to bed.

periods.label: Week of May 6

levels.sentence: From missing the Duke of York to finding Knepp on a pallet in the dark, this day was full of small disappointments and reminders of time's changes.
levels.paragraph: I rose and went to the office, then to White Hall, but came too late to see the Duke of York. At Westminster Hall I met old Mrs. Washington, whose husband has a place in the Excise at Windsor, and I saw plainly how time had aged her; I remembered that it must be the same with me. The House passed the City Bill, but I was sorry I had not thought to move for churches to be allotted for the convenience of the people. I dined poorly at Mrs. Pierce's with Knepp and Mrs. Foster, saw a disappointing girl's picture, and later enjoyed the music of "The Virgin Martyr." I ended by going back to Mrs. Pierce's and finding Knepp on a pallet in the dark.
levels.summary:
I was up and at the office, then went to White Hall, but came too late to speak with the Duke of York, so I went to Westminster Hall. There I talked with several people and learned that my Lord St. John is meant by Mr. " I also met Mrs.

Washington, my old acquaintance of the Hall, whose husband has a place in the Excise at Windsor and lives well; I had not seen her these eight or nine years, and I perceived visibly that she begins to grow old. This led me to reflect that time alters me too.

This morning the House was upon the City Bill, and they say it hath passed it; I was sorry I did not think to put somebody in mind of moving for the churches to be allotted according to the convenience of the people, and not to gratify this Bishop or that College.

Thence I went by water to the New Exchange, where I bought a pair of shoe-strings, and so to Mr. Pierce's, where I was invited. There were Knepp and Mrs. Foster, and we dined, but it was a poor, sluttish dinner, as usual, so I could not be heartily merry at it.

I saw her girl's picture, which is mighty far short of her boy's and not like her neither; but it makes Hales's picture of her boy appear a good picture.

Thence I went to White Hall and walked with Brisband, who dined there also, and then I went back to the King's playhouse, where I saw "The Virgin Martyr" and heard the music that I like so well. I had intended to have seen Knepp, but I let her alone; and having done there, I went to Mrs.

Pierce's back again, where she was, and there I found her on a pallet in the dark—that is Knepp.

periods.label: Week of May 13

levels.sentence: During a busy week of court business, office work, and social outings, I balanced official duties — including attending the Council and commissioning a new suit — with playgoing, music, and merry company, while learning of Sir Thomas Teddiman's death and enjoying a late night with Mrs. Horsfield and the others.
levels.paragraph: I spent the week shuttling between White Hall, the Office, and the playhouse, attending to the King's business and my own pleasures. The Council agreed to back Hemskirke's strange ship-building project, which I thought foolish, and I heard that poor Sir Thomas Teddiman had died of a thrush. Later I saw The Sea Voyage, kissed Knepp's pretty maid, and went on a long, merry excursion with Mercer, Mrs. Horsfield, and Gayet that ended with a broken coach trace and a late walk home.
levels.summary:
Early in the week I conferred with Sir W. Coventry, Sir H. Cholmly, and Sir Stephen Fox about the Excise and the payment of the Guards and Tangier. At the Council, the King approved Hemskirke's project for a swifter ship, granting him money, though I thought it a folly that could not keep its secret.

I also learned that Sir Thomas Teddiman had died of a thrush, which people murmured was hastened by Parliament's doings.

Later in the week I attended the Office, saw Knepp in The Sea Voyage, and had my hair cut close by Nell because of the heat. On the last day, I took Mercer, Mrs. Horsfield, and Gayet to a play at White Hall, but the play and music were poor, and I was vexed to see Sir Heneage Finch's son beating a dog to death.

We went to the Grotto at Kensington to sing, then on to Fox Hall to eat, drink, and be merry before a trying coach ride home, Mrs. Horsfield proving a silly, citizen-like companion.

periods.label: Week of May 20

levels.sentence: I was mistakenly congratulated for a purchase that was not mine, and soon after learned that a strange fire in the sky had alarmed the town, which made me recall my own sighting and the people's fears of burning and Papist plots.
levels.paragraph: I rose and busied myself sending things into the country, then went to the Office, where Sir Richard Ford congratulated me on a great purchase—though it was a mistake, for it was my cousin Tom Pepys who had bought Martin Abbey in Surrey. He advised me to forbear, fearing the world would envy me, and I grew sorry that the error might spread to my prejudice. At noon my clerks dined with me and told me how the whole town was talking of a meteor or fire that flew over the City on Saturday night. I then remembered that I myself had seen a sudden light in the sky while walking in the garden, which I took for a rocket; but the people are full of apprehensions of another fire and Papist plots, which God prevent. After dinner I went by coach to the Temple, bought a new book of songs, walked a little in Westminster Hall, and so to Mrs. —
levels.summary:
Up early, I sent several things into the country and then went to the Office. There I met Sir Richard Ford, who, like one or two others yesterday, congratulated me on what he called my great purchase. I soon discovered the mistake: it was my cousin Tom Pepys who had bought Martin Abbey in Surrey, not I.

Sir Richard advised me to forbear, saying the world would envy me, and I was sorry for the error, fearing it might spread to my prejudice.

All the morning I was at the Office, and at noon my clerks dined with me. From them I heard that the whole town was talking of a meteor, or some fire, which on Saturday last flew over the City at night.

This put me in mind that, being then walking in the dark in my garden after writing, I saw a sudden light before me coming from behind, which made me turn my head. I saw a sudden fire or light running in the sky towards Cheapside ward, and it vanished very quickly.

I bethought myself what holyday it was, and took it for a rocket, though much brighter than any rocket, and thought no more of it. But it seems Mr. Hater and Gibson, going home that night, met with many clusters of people talking of it, and many people from towns about the City did see it.

The world makes much discourse of it, their apprehensions being mighty full of the rest of the City to be burned, and the Papists to cut our throats; which God prevent!

After dinner I took a coach to the Temple, where I bought a new book of songs set to music by one Smith of Oxford, containing some songs of Mr. Cowley's. Thence I went to Westminster, walked a little in the Hall, and so to Mrs. — (the entry breaks off).

Sir Richard advised me to forbear, saying the world would envy me, and I was sorry for the error, fearing it might spread to my prejudice.

All the morning I was at the Office, and at noon my clerks dined with me. From them I heard that the whole town was talking of a meteor, or some fire, which on Saturday last flew over the City at night.

This put me in mind that, being then walking in the dark in my garden after writing, I saw a sudden light before me coming from behind, which made me turn my head. I saw a sudden fire or light running in the sky towards Cheapside ward, and it vanished very quickly.

I bethought myself what holyday it was, and took it for a rocket, though much brighter than any rocket, and thought no more of it. But it seems Mr. Hater and Gibson, going home that night, met with many clusters of people talking of it, and many people from towns about the City did see it.

The world makes much discourse of it, their apprehensions being mighty full of the rest of the City to be burned, and the Papists to cut our throats; which God prevent!

After dinner I took a coach to the Temple, where I bought a new book of songs set to music by one Smith of Oxford, containing some songs of Mr. Cowley's. Thence I went to Westminster, walked a little in the Hall, and so to Mrs. — (the entry breaks off).

periods.label: Week of May 27

levels.sentence: This week I balanced office drudgery and Tangier accounts, yet filled my days with singing, gardens, and loose company at Fox Hall, while Lord Sandwich's letter stung my conscience and I stole to Bagwell's wife in the dark.
levels.paragraph: This week I kept at my Tangier accounts and the office, but most of my hours were given to pleasure. I walked and sang in the gardens at Neat-houses and Fox Hall with Mercer and Gayet, and later with Harris, Rolt, and a pack of rogues whose bawdy talk made my heart ache. A gentle letter from Lord Sandwich reproached me for neglecting him, and I still found time for secret visits to Bagwell's wife and Mrs. Martin.
levels.summary:
All week I kept at my Tangier accounts and the office, and was sent by the Duke of York to cast up the charge of the summer fleet. Sir W. Coventry argued that we should obey Parliament and set out fifty sail even though it would spend all the money to little purpose—so wary is the world grown.

The King's birthday brought a dinner at Sir G. Carteret's, and Lord Sandwich's letter troubled me: he had noticed how rarely I wrote while he was abroad, and I had no good excuse.

My chief pleasures were with Mercer and Gayet: walking at the Neat-houses, singing at Fox Hall with gallants gathering about us, and merry evenings of song with Mr. Pelham and the swaggering Mr. Monteith.

I also fell in with Harris, Rolt, and a crew of town rogues—Harry Killigrew, young Newport, and others—whose loose, bawdy talk made my heart ache, though it was worth seeing once to know their lives. With them I first learned the meaning of the "Ballets" company and their naked dancing.

My private amours continued: at Westminster I did what I would with Mrs. Martin and touched her landlady's thigh; and at Deptford, in the dark, I went up to Bagwell's wife's chamber. There was also a pleasant supper at Mr. Mills's with Mrs. Hallworthy, Mrs. Andrews, and Mrs.

Turner, extraordinarily merry till one in the morning, and a country walk with Mercer and a pretty sober girl named Mrs. Knightly. Through all this, the thread of Lord Sandwich's reproach kept pricking my conscience.

periods.label: Week of Jun 24

levels.sentence: After a morning spent arranging coal shipments and money for Tangier with Creed and Colonel Atkins, I idled through the holyday, took my wife and companions to see "The Impertinents," supped at Spring Garden, and came home to sing in the garden with Mercer.
levels.paragraph: A holyday morning was swallowed up in Tangier business, first with Creed and Colonel Atkins about coals, then at Alderman Backewell's about money. Stopping at Michell's for a drink but no baisado, I found Westminster shut for the holyday and returned home. In the afternoon I took my wife, Mercer, Deb., and W. Hewer to the Duke of York's playhouse, where "The Impertinents" proved pretty good, and then we supped at Spring Garden. We came home not very merry, but Mercer and I sat and sang in the garden a good while before bed.
levels.summary:
Up early, I was met by Creed and Colonel Atkins about sending coals to Tangier, and that business took up most of the morning. Then Creed and I went to Alderman Backewell's to settle Tangier money matters.

I went by water to Westminster, calling at Michell's for a drink—though I did not baisado (kiss)—but because it was a holyday, no business was to be done; I only looked in at Martin's, and so came home by water. I was busy about small things till dinner.

, and W. Hewer to the Duke of York's playhouse and saw "The Impertinents," which I thought a pretty good play. From there we went by water to Spring Garden and supped.

We came home not very merry, yet once we were in, Mercer and I sat in the garden and sang together for a good while, and that made a pleasant end to the day; then we went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Jul 22

levels.sentence: After a busy morning at the office, I dined and then went out to my bookseller's, where I followed a pretty woman from Duck Lane to Newgate Market; I visited Lord Crew, saw my wife's almost-finished picture at Cooper's, and took my wife, Deb., and Mercer to Spring Garden, where I was troubled by gallants forcing themselves on women, before returning home with pleasure to receive my four costly little plates.
levels.paragraph: This morning I was busy at my office, and after dining at noon I went out to Duck Lane to see my bookseller, but his wife was not at home. There I spied a pretty woman with a wanton look and followed her round the streets until she turned back and I lost her. I then visited my Lord Crew, whose face is sore but hopeful, and afterwards saw my wife's picture at Cooper's, almost done and mighty fine. I took my wife, Deb., and Mercer to Spring Garden, where we ate and walked, though I was troubled by the rude gallants who almost forced women in the arbours. We returned by water with much pleasure, and my plate-maker brought me four little plates costing £5, which both troubled and pleased me.
levels.summary:
This morning I was busy at my office until noon, when I dined. Afterward I went out to my bookseller's in Duck Lane, but his wife was not at home.

While I was there, I noticed a pretty woman passing by with a wanton look, and I followed her around the streets from Duck Lane to Newgate Market, until she turned back and I lost her. From there I called on my Lord Crew, whom I found up; his face was sore, but he was hopeful of doing well again.

Next I went to Cooper's, where my wife's picture is almost done and looks mighty fine indeed. , and Mercer to Spring Garden. We ate and walked there, but I was troubled to see how rude some of the young gallants of the town have become—they go into people's arbours where there are no men, and almost force the women.

This confidence of the age's vice upset me. Yet we returned by water with much pleasure. Also this day my plate-maker came with my four little plates of the four Yards, which cost me £5; that troubles me, but it pleases me too.

periods.label: Week of Aug 5

levels.sentence: After being respectfully received by Lord Arlington and complimented by Lord Orrery, I paid for Cooper’s finished picture of my wife, bought a ridiculous book, and let Deb comb my head with great pleasure.
levels.paragraph: This morning I went by water to White Hall, only to find Sir W. Coventry gone out of town, so I visited Lord Arlington at Goring House for the first time; he received me with great respect before several Lords. There Lord Orrery discovered who I was and complimented my abilities, which made me mighty proud. After business at Westminster Hall and the old Exchange, I saw my pretty book vendor but had no chance with her. In the afternoon Cooper finished my wife’s picture; I paid him £30 plus £8 3s. 4d. for the crystal and cases, and though the resemblance and blue garment did not fully satisfy me, it is a rare piece of painting. At night my wife read a ridiculous book while Deb combed my head, and I touched her with my hand to my great pleasure before bed.
levels.summary:
Up, and by water to White Hall, and thence to Sir W. Coventry, but I found he was gone out of town this morning, so I went to my Lord Arlington’s house at Goring House, the first time I had been there since he came thither.

It is a very fine, noble place, and he received me in sight of several Lords with great respect.

While I waited, my Lord Orrery took notice of me and began discourse of hangings and the improvement of shipping; I had not thought he knew me, but he soon discovered it and made a mighty compliment of my abilities and ingenuity, which made me mighty proud, and he do speak most excellently.

Thence to Westminster Hall, and so by coach to the old Exchange, where I did several businesses, and so home to dinner. Then abroad to Duck Lane, where I saw my belle femme of the book vendor, but had no opportunity para hazer con her.

So away to Cooper’s, where I spent all the afternoon with my wife and girl, seeing him make an end of her picture, which he did to my great content, though not so great as I confess I expected, being not satisfied in the greatness of the resemblance nor in the blue garment; but it is most certainly a most rare piece of work as to the painting.

He hath £30 for his work, and the crystal, and case, and gold case comes to £8 3s. , which I sent him this night that I might be out of debt.

Thence my people home, and I to Westminster Hall about a little business, and so by water home, supper, and my wife to read a ridiculous book I bought today of the History of the Taylors’ Company, and all the while Deb. did comb my head, and I did toker her with my main para very great pleasure, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of Aug 26

levels.sentence: I spent the last days of August and the first of September enjoying plays, the fair, and several amorous encounters, while also attending to business and fitting up Deb's chamber.
levels.paragraph: This week I balanced my duties at the office with a round of pleasures. I saw Hamlet with Betterton, which delighted me mightily, and visited the fair, where a clever mare pointed me out for a kiss. At home, Deb's chamber was newly hung, and my wife received a pretty spaniel from Mrs. Batelier. Yet I also met with some frustrations, like finding Betty Michell's husband at home and a weeping woman at the bookseller's.
levels.summary:
