periods.label: Week of Sep 23

levels.sentence: A day of pressing duties—to the playhouse women, the Duke of York, and my Lord's family—was sweetened by a pretty maid's kisses but shadowed by Sidney Montagu's arrival with a demand for money.
levels.paragraph: I rose early to a day crowded with claims on me: Knepp's maid reminded me of the women's day at the playhouse; the Duke of York asked me to draft a plan for better managing our Office; and at Lord Burlington's house I found Sidney Montagu newly come from Mount's Bay, with news that Lord Sandwich needed money and expected me to supply L500. I paid the pretty messenger with half-a-crown and a kiss or two, promised the Duke what he asked, and felt my duty to my Lord more keenly because I had written to him so seldom during the voyage. Sir W. Godolphin arrived before I could think further.
levels.summary:
Knepp's maid Betty came to me this morning with word that it was the women's day at the playhouse, so I knew I must be there to increase their profit; I gave her half-a-crown for coming and had a kiss or two, for she is mighty pretty.

Then, going about my business, I took water to St James's, where I had good opportunity to speak with the Duke of York.

He again asked me to prepare something for him to do for the better managing of our Office, telling me that my Lord Keeper and he had talked of it yesterday and that my Lord Keeper advised him to originate the proposal, since it would come better from him than from me; this I promised to do.

From there I went to Lord Burlington's house for the first time—the house built by Sir John Denham, next to Clarendon House—to visit my Lord Hinchingbroke and his lady. There I found Mr.

Sidney Montagu, who had come up to town last night unexpectedly from Mount's Bay, where he had left my Lord Sandwich well eight days since, so we might hourly expect to hear of his arrival at Portsmouth.

Sidney is mighty grown, and I was glad to be there to see him at his first coming, though the visit cost me dear, for I found myself necessitated to supply them with L500 for my Lord.

Sidney had been sent up with a declaration to friends of the necessity of being presently supplied with L2000, but I do not think he will get it.

I felt it became my duty to my Lord to do something extraordinary in this, and the more because I had been remiss in writing to him during this voyage—more than ever I did in my life, and more indeed than was fit for me. By and by Sir W. Godolphin came to see Mr. Sidney Montagu.

periods.label: Week of Oct 7

levels.sentence: Despite the troubling news of James Southern's petition, I secured support from Lord Brouncker and the Duke of Albemarle, and wrote to the Duke of York, to make sure T. Hater and Mr. Turner got the places our clerks deserved.
levels.paragraph: This morning I got Lord Brouncker's assent for T. Hater to have Mr. Turner's place and also Sir J. Minnes's, but at the Board Mr. Wren told me that James Southern was petitioning the Duke of York for the Storekeeper's place at Deptford, which troubled me and the Board. After Wren left, we agreed to press hard for our clerks and for preferment by seniority and merit. That night, with Mr. Turner, I visited the Duke of Albemarle and asked him to befriend Turner before Wren; he took it kindly. I came away well pleased, stopped at Lord Brouncker's to get his signature on my letter to the Duke of York for T. Hater, and felt hopeful.
levels.summary:
This morning, before the Board sat, I spoke with Lord Brouncker and secured his ready assent for T. Hater to have Mr. Turner's place, as well as Sir J. Minnes's place. But once we were at the Board, Mr.

Wren came to town and told me that James Southern was petitioning the Duke of York for the Storekeeper's place of Deptford. This troubled me and the whole Board.

After Wren left, we reasoned together and resolved to move hard on behalf of our clerks, insisting that places of preferment should go according to seniority and merit.

After the Board rose, I went home with my people to dinner, then returned to the office and did some business. In the evening I went with Mr. Turner to the Duke of Albemarle's house, where I spoke to the Duke about appearing to Mr. Wren as a friend to Mr. Turner; he took my request kindly.

We came away well pleased with what we had done, and on the way home I stopped at Lord Brouncker's to get his hand to a letter I had written to the Duke of York for T. Hater. I felt hopeful that our efforts would keep the places in the hands of our own clerks.

periods.label: Week of Nov 18

levels.sentence: After pursuing my mistress Deb against my wife's suspicions, I was caught, confessed everything, and was forced to swear never to see the girl again, leaving me in shame and my wife in grief.
levels.paragraph: I spent a day of deceit, slipping away to find Deb while my wife suspected, and though I comforted myself with a stolen kiss, the very next morning my wife confronted me with the truth. I confessed everything, and she raged with threats to disfigure the girl and leave me, until my servant Hewer helped calm her. In the end I signed a promise never to see Deb again, and I lied about my intentions, but my heart was full of shame and my home was never the same.
levels.summary:
On November 18th, I rose late with my wife, who voiced her jealousy over Deb. I denied it, but as soon as I was out, I went searching for Deb, who had been sent away from our house.

I tracked her through porters and eventually found her at a coach near my tailor's, where I kissed her, gave her counsel and twenty shillings, and arranged a way to reach her through my bookseller.

I returned home and told my wife a fair tale, but she had been busy preparing our best chamber, and I felt a secret relief that all seemed safe.

The next morning, my joy turned to horror: my wife confronted me, knowing I had been with Deb. I denied it at first, but then confessed all, and she spent the afternoon cursing me, threatening to slit the girl's nose and to leave me, demanding money to keep quiet.

My servant Hewer, whom I was forced to trust, wept and persuaded her to stay on condition that I sign a promise never to see or speak to Deb again. I signed it, and even promised for Deb, though I lied to myself about keeping it.

The day ended in the most perfect confusion of face and heart, sorrow and shame, and I knew my peace was broken.

periods.label: Week of Mar 24

levels.sentence: I took a cold, windy day-trip to Maidstone, pleased by the countryside and old sights, then spent a late, flirtatious evening at Captain Allen's with the willing Mrs. Jowles before walking home through snow.
levels.paragraph: I set out with Gibson and Coney for Maidstone, stopping on the way to spy Mrs. Jowles through a window at Captain Allen's without letting on. I delighted in the Medway valley, Sir John Bankes's abbey-house, and the pretty town of Maidstone, where I watched flax-beating and bought fish for dinner. On the way back I viewed an ancient Saxon monument, then returned to Captain Allen's, where Mrs. Jowles allowed me great liberties. We stayed near midnight, and I walked through snow and darkness back to Chatham with Coney.
levels.summary:
Waking, I walked in the garden and found that Mrs Tooker had not brought any of her daughters as I had expected. I went to the yard, leaving Middleton at the pay, and after walking up and down I gave orders at the Hill-House for the coach to be made ready.

I took Mr Gibson with me, and Mr Coney the surgeon, and set out for Maidstone, which I had a mighty mind to see.

On the way, at St Margett's, I pretended to call on Captain Allen to see whether his daughter Mrs Jowles was there. His wife came to the door—he was in London—and I spied Jowles through a window but took no notice, excusing myself until night and promising to come again.

It was a mighty cold and windy but clear day, and I had the pleasure of seeing the Medway winding through a very fine country.

I went a little out of my way to visit Sir John Bankes, but he was in London; still I had a sight of his house, an old abbey just like Hinchingbroke and as good, finely placed by the river with handsome grounds and walls.

At Maidstone I walked all about the town and up to the top of the steeple for a noble view. I saw an old man beating flax, stepped into the barn to give him money, and found that piece of husbandry very pretty.

I bought a dish of fresh fish and sent it to our inn, the Bell, and after a good dinner a barber came and trimmed me so I should be clean to visit Mrs Allen at night.

Staying until about four, I set out alone in the coach, and on the way back stopped to see a Saxon monument near Aylesford—three upright stones with a great round one lying across them, a thing of great antiquity.

I stopped again at Captain Allen's, sent the coach and Gibson home, and stayed with Coney. Mrs Jowles came in, a very fine, proper, well-dressed lady, and there was also Major Manly and his wife, and later a pretty cozen of hers, daughter-in-law to Manly, who had such a cold she could not speak.

I set Coney and the Major to play while Mrs Jowles and I talked over all our old stories; I had the liberty to salute her often and pull off her glove, and found her mighty free and kind.

I do not doubt I might have had what I desired had there been time to carry her to Cobham, for she was very willing; she is certainly a whore, but a brave and comely one.

I got her to the street door and there kissed and touched her breasts without any force, and believe I might have had all else had it been time and place.

We stayed till almost twelve, and then with a lantern I walked with Coney over the fields,—dark as pitch, mighty cold and snowy,—to Chatham. Everyone was already in bed when I got home, and I presently went to bed.

I got her to the street door and there kissed and touched her breasts without any force, and believe I might have had all else had it been time and place.

We stayed till almost twelve, and then with a lantern I walked with Coney over the fields,—dark as pitch, mighty cold and snowy,—to Chatham. Everyone was already in bed when I got home, and I presently went to bed.

periods.sentence: I took a cold, windy day-trip to Maidstone, pleased by the countryside and old sights, then spent a late, flirtatious evening at Captain Allen's with the willing Mrs. Jowles before walking home through snow.
periods.paragraph: I set out with Gibson and Coney for Maidstone, stopping on the way to spy Mrs. Jowles through a window at Captain Allen's without letting on. I delighted in the Medway valley, Sir John Bankes's abbey-house, and the pretty town of Maidstone, where I watched flax-beating and bought fish for dinner. On the way back I viewed an ancient Saxon monument, then returned to Captain Allen's, where Mrs. Jowles allowed me great liberties. We stayed near midnight, and I walked through snow and darkness back to Chatham with Coney.

periods.label: Week of Apr 14

levels.sentence: I stole meetings with Bagwell’s wife and Deb today, and though each encounter gave me pleasure, guilt followed me even into the evening’s company.
levels.paragraph: I went out on business in the morning, but my true errands were secret ones: first to enquire after Deb’s aunt in Jewen Street, and then to keep a noon appointment with Bagwell’s wife in Moorfields, where the holiday crowd let us do no more than talk. Later I saw Deb on Holborne Hill, followed her into a blind alehouse, and took liberties with her, though she stayed coy and modest; I gave her twenty shillings and agreed to meet her again at Westminster. My coach had gone when I returned, and at Povy’s, among friends, I tried to be merry but could not shake my fear of what I had done. At last I carried my wife home by Islington, and we supped quietly.
levels.summary:
Being up early, I went to the office, and before the session sat with W. Hewer at the Excise Office, though business carried me another way to the Temple. By Deb’s direction I knew where in Jewen Street to send my hackney coachman while I waited in the coach in Aldgate Street, so I sent him to enquire whether Mrs.

Hunt, her aunt, was in town; the answer was that she was not. This was all I could do at that moment, and I went away troubled because I could do no more.

Coming to the office, I found Bagwell’s wife, who slipped a note into my hand inviting me to meet her in Moorfields at noon.

My wife had already gone to dine with my cozen Turner, so after the office was up I went to the place, and after walking up and down by the windmills I found her and talked with her; but being a holiday and the place full of people, we parted, leaving further discourse and doing to another time.

Then I drove through Jewen Street, my mind, God knows, running that way, but I did not stop; going down Holborne Hill by the Conduit I saw Deb on foot going up the hill. She saw me but would not stop or speak, so I alighted and followed, overtaking her at the end of Hosier Lane in Smithfield.

I led her into a little blind alehouse within the walls, and there we talked alone, and I kissed her and touched her breasts; but she was mighty coy and, I hope, modest. I gave her 20s. in a paper, and we agreed to meet again in the Hall at Westminster on Monday.

She gave me great hopes by her carriage that she continues modest and honest, and so we parted.

When I came back to where I had left my coach, it was gone, for I had stayed too long, and I was troubled to have abused the poor fellow; so I took another coach and directed him to find out the fellow and send him to me. At my cozen Turner’s I found they were all gone to dinner to Povy’s, and thither I went.

They were all there—W. Batelier and his sister—and had already dined, but good things were brought me. I was mightily pleased with the fine rooms, though in truth there are so many bad pictures that they lessen the pleasure of the good ones. The.

and Betty Turner were in new flowered tabby gowns, and we were pretty merry, only my fear of what I had newly done kept my content from being full.

About five or six o’clock I took my wife and the two Bateliers homeward; W. Batelier alighted, and I carried the women round by Islington and so down Bishopsgate Street home. We talked and supped, and then to bed.

periods.label: Week of May 5

levels.sentence: I was troubled by my wife's early May-dew outing, and then at White Hall I witnessed a sharp quarrel between the Duke of York and Sir T. Littleton over Mr Child, followed by the Duke chiding the Treasurers, before I dined with the much-broken Lord Crew and heard his old rule about country families and London.
levels.paragraph: I was troubled about three in the morning when my wife rose with her maid to gather May-dew by coach abroad; I feared some hurt from her going out so early, but she came home about six and went to bed again well. I then went by coach with Mr Gibson to St. James's and White Hall, where the Duke of York met the Office. There a hot dispute arose about the Council of Trade and Mr Child, the Duke answering Sir T. Littleton sharply, and I was sorry to see it go so far, fearing I might be observed to assent to Captain Cox. Afterwards the Duke chided the Treasurers, and I went with Mr Wren to Lambeth, but the gate was shut; so I walked with my boy Jacke to Lord Crew's and dined with him.
levels.summary:
About three in the morning I was troubled to find my wife calling her maid up and rising herself to go abroad in her coach to gather May-dew. I feared some hurt might happen to her by going out so betimes, but she came home about six and went to bed again all well.

I myself then got up, and with Mr Gibson took a coach to St. James's, and thence to White Hall.

At White Hall the Duke of York met the Office, and we discoursed of several things, particularly the Instructions of Commanders of ships. There happened by chance a discourse of the Council of Trade, against which the Duke is mightily displeased, and particularly against Mr Child.

Captain Cox seconded the Duke by saying that Child was talked of as an unfair dealer with masters of ships about freight. To this Sir T. Littleton very hotly and foolishly replied that he never heard any honest man speak ill of Child.

The Duke made a smart reply and was angry; I was sorry to hear it come so far, and feared that by seeming to assent to Cox I might be observed too much by Littleton, though I said nothing aloud. I felt this must breed great heartburnings.

After the meeting, the Duke took the Treasurers into his closet to chide them, as Mr Wren told me; for my Lord Keeper did last night at the Council say, when nobody was ready to say anything against the constitution of the Navy, that he did believe the Treasurers of the Navy had something to say.

This was very foul on their part, to be parties against us.

Then Mr Wren took boat, thinking to dine with my Lord of Canterbury; but when we came to Lambeth, the gate was shut, which is strictly done at twelve o'clock, and nobody comes in afterwards. So we lost our labour and returned to White Hall.

Thence I walked with my boy Jacke to my Lord Crew, whom I have not seen since he was sick, which is eight months ago, and I dined with him. He is mightily broke. A stranger, a country gentleman, was with him; and he was pleased with my discourse, accidentally, about the decay of gentlemen's families in the country.

He told us that the old rule was that a family might remain fifty miles from London one hundred years, one hundred miles from London two hundred years, and so farther, or nearer London, more or less years.

He also told us he had heard his father say that in his time it was so rare for a country gentleman to come to London that, when he did come, he used to make his will before he set out.

periods.label: Week of May 12

levels.sentence: I spent a busy day of legal business, an illicit meeting with Mrs. Martin, a painful visit to the playhouse, and ended with my brother's news of my sister's pregnancy.
levels.paragraph: We went to Westminster Hall, where I met old acquaintances and made arrangements for tomorrow. Afterwards, I visited Mrs. Martin and was intimate with her, despite her foolish talk about her husband's fortune. Later, my wife and I tried to see a new play, but my eyes troubled me in the candlelight, and we left. At home, I found my brother John, who told me my sister is pregnant, which left me with mixed feelings.
levels.summary:
This morning I rose and went to Westminster Hall, it being the first day of term. There I chanced upon Roger Pepys, just arrived from the country, and was glad to see him.

I also spoke with Sir Charles Harbord and Sidney Montagu, who is setting out tomorrow for Flanders and Italy; I invited them both to dine with me tomorrow.

After some talk, I went to Mrs. Martin's lodging, for she had come to town last night. I was intimate with her; she had spent a month at Portsmouth with her husband, newly returned from the Straits. But Lord!

how silly she talks of the great entertainment there, and how all the gentry visited her; she believes her husband is worth £600 or £700, which I am glad of, though I doubt they will spend it too quickly.

Returning home, after dinner my wife and I went to the Duke of York's playhouse, where we sat in the side balcony over against the music, and heard but did not see a new play, the first day acted, called "The Roman Virgin" — an old play and but ordinary, I thought.

The trouble of my eyes with the light of the candles almost killed me.

Thence I went to my Lord Sandwich's, and obtained a promise from Sidney to come and dine with me tomorrow. So my wife and I came home in our coach, and there found my brother John, come from Ellington as I expected.

Among other things, he told me the first news that my sister is with child and far gone — which I know not whether it troubled or pleased me more, having no great care for my friends to have children, though I love other people's. Glad to see John, we had supper and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of May 26

levels.sentence: I spent the morning finally making a satisfactory start on my neglected accounts in preparation for going abroad, then kissed Mrs. Michell in her mother's presence, advanced my business with the Duke of York, and finished the night merrily with my wife, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman at The World's End.
levels.paragraph: This day I made a satisfactory beginning at settling my long-neglected accounts, though my weak eyes had made the task troublesome. After dinner I went to Whitehall, stopping at Michell's, where I kissed her but found no opportunity to go further. I then met again with the Duke of York and advanced yesterday's business, before joining my wife, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman in the Park and at The World's End drinking-house, where we were merry until late.
levels.summary:
I rose very early and spent the whole morning with W. Hewer examining and stating my accounts, in order to fit myself to go abroad beyond sea.

The ill condition of my eyes, and my neglect for a year or two, had left me behindhand, making the work difficult and troublesome to my mind; but this day I made a satisfactory entrance therein, and so dined at home.

In the afternoon I took water to Whitehall, calling by the way at Michell's, where I had not been for many a day until the other day.

I met her mother there, and knew her husband to be out of town; and here I did kiss her, but had not the opportunity to do something more with her as I would have offered if I had had it. Then I had another meeting with the Duke of York at Whitehall, on yesterday's work, and made a good advance.

Being called by my wife, we went to the Park, Mary Batelier and a Dutch gentleman, a friend of hers, being with us. Thence to The World's End, a drinking-house by the Park, where we were merry, and so home late.

periods.full:
I rose very early and spent the whole morning with W. Hewer examining and stating my accounts, in order to fit myself to go abroad beyond sea.

The ill condition of my eyes, and my neglect for a year or two, had left me behindhand, making the work difficult and troublesome to my mind; but this day I made a satisfactory entrance therein, and so dined at home.

In the afternoon I took water to Whitehall, calling by the way at Michell's, where I had not been for many a day until the other day.

I met her mother there, and knew her husband to be out of town; and here I did kiss her, but had not the opportunity to do something more with her as I would have offered if I had had it. Then I had another meeting with the Duke of York at Whitehall, on yesterday's work, and made a good advance.

Being called by my wife, we went to the Park, Mary Batelier and a Dutch gentleman, a friend of hers, being with us. Thence to The World's End, a drinking-house by the Park, where we were merry, and so home late.

periods.paragraph: This day I made a satisfactory beginning at settling my long-neglected accounts, though my weak eyes had made the task troublesome. After dinner I went to Whitehall, stopping at Michell's, where I kissed her but found no opportunity to go further. I then met again with the Duke of York and advanced yesterday's business, before joining my wife, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman in the Park and at The World's End drinking-house, where we were merry until late.

periods.label: January 1660

levels.sentence: Mr. Downing told me he had made me a Clerk of the Council, but I feared his favour was only to save his own salary, and the rest of the day was spent in errands, a feast, and news that the other clerks were turned out.
levels.paragraph: This morning Mr. Downing surprised me by saying he had got me made one of the Clerks of the Council; I thanked him, but not heartily, for I suspected he only wanted to ease himself of the salary he pays me. After a morning draft with Sheply and Pierce, I went to Whitehall and got Sir Ant. Cooper's leave to keep our lodgings, so Sheply can go to the country. Later I was kept waiting at Downing's, where I read the Dutch Ambassador's answer contradicting my Lord's reasons for coming home. I dined on turkey with Mrs. Jem, then went to the French Ordinary where Downing feasted several Parliament men, and he gave me a note to invite more members to dinner tomorrow. At Whitehall I heard from the clerks that they are all turned out except the two Leighs, though my name was mentioned last night.
levels.summary:
I was sent for to Mr. Downing's bedside this morning, and he told me he had done me a kindness by getting me made one of the Clerks of the Council.

I was quite stumbled and did not know whether to thank him; I did at last, but not heartily, for I feared that he had done it only to ease himself of the salary he gives me. Mr. Sheply was waiting below, and we went with Mr. Pierce to the Harp and Ball for our morning draft, and then to Whitehall. There I met Sir Ant.

Cooper, gave him my Lord's answer, and he gave us leave to keep the lodgings still, so we resolved that Mr. Sheply could now go into the country, and would do so to-morrow.

By Mr. Downing's order I went back and stayed till noon expecting someone to come and read writings, but he never came; so I sat alone reading the Dutch Ambassador's answer to our State, which labour to contradict my Lord's arguments for coming home. Then I went to my office, and with Mr.

Sheply and Moore dined upon a turkey with Mrs. Jem. After that Mr. Moore and I went to the French Ordinary, where Mr. Downing this day feasted Sir Arth. Haselrigge and a great many more of the Parliament; he stayed to put him in mind of me. He gave me a note to go and invite some other members to dinner to-morrow.

I went to White Hall and stayed at Marsh's with Simons, Luellin, and all the rest of the Clerks of the Council, who I hear are all turned out, only the two Leighs. They all tell me that my name was mentioned last night, but that nothing was done in it.

I then left some of my notes at the lodgings of the members and went home to bed. All day I have been uneasy about Downing's true intent, and the news of the clerks being turned out makes me fear for my own place.

periods.label: August 1660

levels.sentence: After ordering a velvet coat, hearing Sir Samuel Morland’s secret service story, dining at the Tower, settling accounts, and going to White Hall, I came home and made sport with the girl and boy combing my head.
levels.paragraph: I went first to the Privy Seal, then to my Lord’s to agree with Mr. Pim on a velvet coat. Back at the Privy Seal, Sir Samuel Morland told me at length how he had served the King under the Protector and what he had sacrificed. I dined at the Tower with my father, Mr. Fairbrother, and Cooke, and received a firkin of butter from Captain Cuttance. I settled my brother’s allowance and my Master of Arts fee before going to White Hall with my wife, then came home and made sport having the servants comb my head.
levels.summary:
At the Privy Seal I attended to business, then went to my Lord’s, where the tailor Mr. Pim and I agreed that he should make me a velvet coat. Returning to the Privy Seal, I found Sir Samuel Morland with a Baronet’s grant that the King had given him to make money of.

He stayed with me a great while and told me the whole manner of his serving the King during the Protectorate: how Thurloe’s bad usage first drove him to it, how he discovered Sir R. Willis, and how he had sunk his fortune for the King.

Now the King has given him a pension of L500 a year out of the Post Office for life and the benefit of two Baronets; this makes me begin to think he is not so much a fool as I once took him to be.

I went home by water to the Tower, where my father, Mr. Fairbrother, and Cooke dined with me. After dinner young Captain Cuttance of the Speedwell came in, sent up for the gratuity given to the seamen who brought the King over, and he brought my wife a firkin of butter, which was very welcome.

My father then took his leave, after I had given him 40s. for the last half year’s allowance for my brother John at Cambridge. I also settled with Mr. Fairbrother for my Master of Arts degree, which cost me about L9 16s.

In the afternoon I went to White Hall with my wife by water, and busied myself at the Privy Seal and elsewhere. At night we came home by water, and I made good sport in the kitchen by having the girl and the boy comb my head before I went to bed.

periods.label: September 1661

levels.sentence: I saw my mother and Pall off to Brampton, dined merrily at my uncle Fenner's, was troubled by my wife's secret appointment with a French footman, and then heard that my aunt Kite is dying and wants me to take charge.
levels.paragraph: I went to the Privy Seal on business, then met my mother, wife, and Pall and put them into the waggon for Brampton, Pall crying bitterly. Afterwards I drank with my wife, Aunt Bell, and Charles Pepys, and dined at Uncle Fenner's, though my mind was troubled when a French footman privately spoke to my wife and she promised to go somewhere tomorrow. After dinner came news that Aunt Kite, the butcher's widow, is near death and has sent for my uncle and me to take charge of her affairs and her daughter.
levels.summary:
This morning I went to the Privy Seal on business, and on the way took leave of my mother, who is setting out for Brampton today. , and advised her how to behave toward my father and mother. Because it was late, I took them all to Beard's, put them into the waggon, and saw them depart; Pall cried exceedingly.

Then I went in with my wife, Aunt Bell, and Charles Pepys, whom we met there, and after drinking we went to my uncle Fenner's for dinner.

On the way, a French footman with feathers came looking for my wife and spoke to her privately; I could not learn what they said, only that my wife promised to go to some place tomorrow morning, which troubles my mind, for I do not know where it is.

At my uncle's, both his sons and daughters were present, and we were merry and dined.

After dinner, news came that my aunt Kite, the butcher's widow in London, is sick and ready to die. She has sent for my uncle and me to come take charge of things and be entrusted with the care of her daughter.

periods.label: May 1662

levels.sentence: After making up my journal and settling some business, I dined with my father, had Sarah clean my hair and wash my feet, cut off my beard in a sudden fit, and reflected on the month's news—the Queen's arrival, peace with Argier, and the discontent over the Act for Uniformity.
levels.paragraph: I started the day catching up on my journal and ended it with a cleaner head and a shaved chin, after a round of errands, a debt dunned by Anthony Joyce, and dinner with my father. Between White Hall and the office I heard the latest court news—the Queen is at Hampton Court and has pleased the King, which I fear will vex Madam Castlemaine. I cut off my beard in a sudden fit, had Sarah comb my head and wash my feet, and took stock of my estate, which I find worth about £530 clear. The month closes with fair weather, peace with Argier, and much public discontent over the Act for Uniformity.
levels.summary:
This morning I lay long in bed, then rose to bring my journal up to date for the past few days. Anthony Joyce came and dunned me for the tallow I had ordered from him lately; it vexes me to owe him, but I promised to pay him next. Afterwards I went to White Hall, hearing that Sir G.

Carteret was in town, but I could not find him, and so returned to Tom's, from whence I took my father to my house. He dined with me, and we discoursed about our businesses with uncle Thomas and T. Trice.

After he departed, I went to the office, where we met; then walked to my Brother's, the Wardrobe, and other places on business, and so home.

At home I had Sarah comb my head clean; it was so foul with powdering and other troubles that I am resolved to try keeping my head dry without powder.

In a sudden fit I also cut off all my beard, which I had been raising for a great while, so that I may use my pumice-stone on my whole face, as I already do my chin, saving time in a genteel way. Sarah then washed my feet in a bath of herbs, and I went to bed.

The month ends with very fair weather; my health is pretty well, though wind still torments me extremely from time to time.

As for news: the Queen was brought a few days since to Hampton Court, and everyone says she is a fine, handsome, discreet lady, and the King is pleased enough with her, which I fear will put Madam Castlemaine's nose out of joint. The Court is wholly at Hampton now.

Peace with Argier has lately been made, which is good news. My father is lately come to town to see us, and though it has cost and will cost more money, I am pleased with the alterations on my house at Brampton. My Lord Sandwich has lately come with the Queen from sea, very well and in good repute.

Upon auditing my estate I find myself worth about £530 clear.

The Act for Uniformity is lately printed, which it is thought will make mad work among the Presbyterian ministers; people of all sides are very discontented, some thinking themselves used contrary to promise too hardly, and others that they are not rewarded as much as they expected by the King. God keep us all.

I have by a late oath obliged myself from wine and plays, of which I find good effect.

periods.label: December 1662

levels.phrase: A year of mirth and content
levels.sentence: On the last day of 1662 I danced at the King's ball, reviewed my year with gratitude for my health, purse, and growing esteem, and resolved to renew my oaths of orderliness despite small household troubles and the heavy unsettled business with my uncle Thomas.
levels.paragraph: This last day of 1662 I spent in mirth — a merry dinner, a Tangier business errand, and a glorious ball at White Hall where I saw the King and Queen dance. I returned weary but content, and reviewed my year with gratitude: my purse near £650, my home convenient, my health good, and my industry at the office winning me notice. Yet small cares lingered: a proud maid to part with, a boy I must turn away, and my uncle Thomas's business hanging over me.
levels.summary:
I lay pretty long in bed, then went to Westminster Hall and the Swan, where Mr. W. Bowyer told me about his fair cousin Butler and Colonel Dillon being quite broke off, because he had opened letters from Ireland complaining of his knavery and forging others to the contrary.

After a barber's, I took my wife to dinner at Mrs. Pierce's by invitation. Dr. Clerke, his wife and sister, and Mr. Knight, the King's chief surgeon, with his wife, were there. We were pretty merry, the two men being excellent company, though I confess I was wedded from my opinion of Mrs.

Pierce's beauty when I saw her naked neck, she being undrest when we came in, and of Mrs. Clerke's genius, which I so much admired, finding her so conceited and fantastical in her dress and carriage this day, though the truth is, witty enough.

After dinner with much ado the doctor and I got away to follow our business for a while, he to his patients and I to the Tangier Committee, where the Duke of York was, and we stayed at it a good while. Then in order to despatch the boats and provisions for Tangier away, Mr. Povy, in his coach, carried Mr.

Gauden and me into London to Mr. Bland's, the merchant, where we stayed discoursing upon the reason of the delay of the going away of these things a great while. Then we ate a dish of anchovies and drank wine and cider, very merry; but above all things I was pleased to hear Mrs.

Bland talk like a merchant in her husband's business very well, and it seems she understands it and performs a great deal.

Thence merry back, Mr. Povy and I to White Hall, he carrying me thither on purpose to bring me into the ball this night before the King. All the way he talked very ingeniously, and I find him a fine gentleman, one that loves to live nobly and neatly, as I perceive by his discourse of his house, pictures, and horses.

He brought me first to the Duke's chamber, where I saw the Duke and Duchess at supper, and thence into the room where the ball was to be, crammed with fine ladies, the greatest of the Court.

By and by came the King and Queen, the Duke and Duchess, and all the great ones: and after seating themselves, the King took out the Duchess of York; the Duke, the Duchess of Buckingham; the Duke of Monmouth, my Lady Castlemaine; and so other lords other ladies: and they danced the Bransle.

After that, the King led a lady a single Coranto, and then the rest of the lords, one after another, other ladies; very noble it was, and great pleasure to see. Then to country dances, the King leading the first, which he called for, which was, says he, "Cuckolds all awry," the old dance of England.

Of the ladies that danced, the Duke of Monmouth's mistress, my Lady Castlemaine, and a daughter of Sir Harry de Vicke's were the best. The manner was, when the King dances, all the ladies in the room, and the Queen herself, stand up: and indeed he dances rarely, and much better than the Duke of York.

Having stayed here as long as I thought fit, to my infinite content, I went out, leaving them dancing, and to Mrs.

Pierce's, where I found the company had stayed very long for my coming, but all gone but my wife, and so I took her home by coach and so to my Lord's again, where after some supper to bed, very weary and in a little pain from riding a little uneasily to-night in the coach.

Thus ends this year with great mirth to me and my wife. Our condition is thus: we are at present spending a night or two at my Lord's lodgings at White Hall. Our home at the Navy-office is finished and made very convenient.

My purse is worth about £650, besides my goods of all sorts, which yet might have been more but for my late layings out upon my house and public assessment, and yet would not have been so much if I had not lived a very orderly life all this year by virtue of the oaths that God put into my heart to take against wine, plays, and other expenses, which I am now going to renew, I under God owing my present content thereunto.

My family is myself and wife; William, my clerk; Jane, my wife's upper maid, but growing proud and negligent upon it, we must part, which troubles me; Susan, our cook-maid, a pretty willing wench but no good cook; and Wayneman, my boy, who I am now turning away for his naughty tricks.

We have had from the beginning our healths to this day very well, blessed be God! Our late maid Sarah going from us, though put away by us, to live with Sir W. Pen does trouble me, though I love the wench, so that we do make ourselves a little strange to him and his family for it, and resolve to do so.

The same we are for other reasons to my Lady Batten and hers. I have lately had it in my thoughts, and can hardly bring myself off of it, since Mrs.

Gosnell cannot be with us, to find out another woman for my wife that can sing or dance, and yet finding it hard to save anything at the year's end as I now live, I think I shall not be such a fool till I am more warm in my purse, besides my oath of entering into no such expenses till I am worth £1000.

By my last year's diligence in my office, blessed be God, I am come to a good degree of knowledge therein, and am acknowledged so by all the world, even the Duke himself, to whom I have a good access, and by that, and my being Commissioner with him for Tangier, he takes much notice of me; and I doubt not but, by the continuance of the same endeavours, I shall in a little time come to be a man much taken notice of in the world, specially being come to so great an esteem with Mr.

Coventry.

The only weight that lies heavy upon my mind is the ending the business with my uncle Thomas about my dead uncle's estate, which is very ill on our side, and I fear when all is done I must be forced to maintain my father myself, or spare a good deal towards it out of my own purse, which will be a very great pull back to me in my fortune.

But I must be contented and bring it to an issue one way or other.

Public matters stand thus: the King is bringing, as is said, his family, and Navy, and all other his charges, to a less expense; in the mean time himself following his pleasures more than with good advice he would do, at least to be seen to all the world to do so.

His dalliance with my Lady Castlemaine being public, every day, to his great reproach; and his favouring of none at Court so much as those that are the confidants of his pleasure, as Sir H.

Bennet and Sir Charles Barkeley; which, good God, put it into his heart to mend before he makes himself too much contemned by his people for it!

The Duke of Monmouth is in so great splendour at Court, and so dandled by the King, that some doubt, if the King should have no child by the Queen, which there is yet no appearance of, whether he would not be acknowledged for a lawful son; and that there will be a difference follow upon it between the Duke of York and him; which God prevent!

My Lord Chancellor is threatened by people to be questioned the next sitting of the Parliament by some spirits that do not love to see him so great; but certainly he is a good servant to the King. The Queen-Mother is said to keep too great a Court now; and her being married to my Lord St.

Albans is commonly talked of; and that they had a daughter between them in France, how true, God knows.

The Bishops are high, and go on without any diffidence in pressing uniformity; and the Presbyters seem silent in it, and either conform or lay down, though without doubt they expect a turn, and would be glad these endeavours of the other Fanatiques would take effect; there having been a plot lately found, for which four have been publicly tried at the Old Bailey and hanged.

My Lord Sandwich is still in good esteem, and now keeping his Christmas in the country; and I in good esteem, I think, as any man can be, with him. Mr. Moore is very sickly, and I doubt will hardly get over his late fit of sickness that still hangs on him.

In fine, for the good condition of myself, wife, family, and estate, in the great degree that it is, and for the public state of the nation so quiet as it is, the Lord God be praised!

periods.phrase: A year of mirth and content
periods.sentence: On the last day of 1662 I danced at the King's ball, reviewed my year with gratitude for my health, purse, and growing esteem, and resolved to renew my oaths of orderliness despite small household troubles and the heavy unsettled business with my uncle Thomas.
periods.paragraph: This last day of 1662 I spent in mirth — a merry dinner, a Tangier business errand, and a glorious ball at White Hall where I saw the King and Queen dance. I returned weary but content, and reviewed my year with gratitude: my purse near £650, my home convenient, my health good, and my industry at the office winning me notice. Yet small cares lingered: a proud maid to part with, a boy I must turn away, and my uncle Thomas's business hanging over me.

periods.label: July 1663

levels.sentence: I spent a week in wanton dalliance with Mrs. Lane and a day of fine music and a royal spectacle at Parliament, ever mindful of my health and pleasures.
levels.paragraph: In mid-July I busied myself with small errands, bespoke a timber ruler, and indulged in familiar liberties with Mrs. Lane, which left me ashamed and fearful of cold. The next week I rode to the Wells seeking my dog, found instead excellent music sung by citizens under a tree, and hurried back to witness the King give his royal assent to Parliament's bills, a splendid sight in robes and crown.
levels.summary:
This week I was much taken with business and pleasure. After a little work with Sir J. Minnes, I ran errands, ordered a pocket ruler for measuring timber, and met Mrs. Lane at Westminster Hall. While her bands were being finished, I flirted with the pretty daughter at Mrs.

Howlett's shop, buying gloves just to talk with her. Then Mrs. Lane and I went to the Crown, where I towzed her freely but did more than I am proud of, resolving never to do so again. She spoke only of marriage, and I told her what she wanted to hear about her fortune.

The following week I rode to the Wells looking for my dog but found instead a company of citizens singing in four or five parts under a tree—a delight greater than any I have known. After a breakfast at Yowell and shoeing Creed's horse, I rode hard home, passing Mr. Gauden's fine house.

I arrived at Westminster just as the Commons went to the Lords, crowded in behind the Speaker, and saw the King in crown and robes give his royal assent—a fine sight indeed.

periods.label: September 1663

levels.sentence: I savored the wonders of Bartholomew Fayre and the grandeur of Mr. Povy's house, yet after yielding to temptation with Mrs. Lane and coming home to find my wife hard at work, I resolved to sin no more.
levels.paragraph: This September I found myself torn between pleasure and duty. I visited the fair, admired Povy's exquisite cellars, and once again sought out Mrs. Lane, though I stopped short of the worst sin. But seeing my poor wife laboring at home filled me with shame. I prayed for God's grace to keep me from such folly henceforth.
levels.summary:
I began the month by reading L'Estrange's new newsbooks and helping my wife find a maid. I dined at Mr. Povy's, whose lavish house and handsome old wife impressed me, though his vanity grated. Later I took my wife to Bartholomew Fayre, where we saw strange beasts and a wonderful mechanical sea scene.

In the last week I met with Sir Philip Warwick about the Navy debt, then slipped off to Westminster Hall and carried Mrs. Lane to Lambeth, where I did everything but the main thing—she refused, thank God. That night at home I found my wife hard at work, and my heart ached for wronging so good a woman.

I vowed never to do the like again.

periods.label: November 1663

levels.sentence: I opposed Sir W. Pen at the office, chased Howlett's daughter in Westminster Hall, flirted with a lodger at Unthank's, consulted Dr. Turner about freight, and caught a cold, while Captain Taylor gave me a plate for his ship's demorage.
levels.paragraph: This morning at the office I crossed Sir W. Pen over a mulct on the purser of the James, which made him storm out like an asse. In the afternoon I ran errands by coach, tried to overtake Howlett's daughter in Westminster Hall, and chatted with a pretty lodger at Unthank's. I then consulted Dr. Turner at Doctors' Commons about freight from East India ships. That night I came home with a scurvy cold, having earlier received a piece of plate from Captain Taylor for the demorage of his ship William.
levels.summary:
I rose and went to the office, where we sat all morning. There Sir W. Pen and I had words: I opposed him when he would have excused a mulct imposed on the purser of the James for being absent from duty, which he claimed was by his business and order.

He was mighty angry and went out of the office like an asse discontented. I was not sorry at all, for I would not have him think that I dare not oppose him where I see reason and cause.

After dinner I took a coach abroad on several businesses, among them to Westminster Hall, where I saw Howlett's daughter going out at the other end. I followed her, intending to offer talk and dally a little, but I could not overtake her. Then I called at Unthank's for something of my wife's not done.

A pretty little gentlewoman, a lodger there, came out to tell me it was not yet done; though this vexed me, I took the opportunity to take her by the hand with the boot, and so found matter to talk a little longer to her.

I was ready to laugh at myself to see how my anger would not operate, my disappointment coming to me by such a messenger.

Thence I went to Doctors' Commons and consulted Dr. Turner about differences we have with the officers of the East India ships concerning goods brought by them without paying freight, which we demand of them.

So home to my office, where I wrote letters late, then to supper and to bed, having got a scurvy cold by lying cold in my head the last night.

This day Captain Taylor brought me a piece of plate, a little small state dish, expecting that I should get him some allowance for demorage of his ship William, kept long at Tangier, which I shall and may justly do.

periods.label: December 1663

levels.sentence: I kept our Christmas all alone with my wife, witnessed Warren's open defiance of Batten at the office, and looked forward to the end of my vows on the morrow.
levels.paragraph: At the office, Sir W. Warren openly defied Sir W. Batten over a contract, and I could see Pen secretly relished it. My head ached from the press of business, but I dined at home with my wife on turkey and mince pie, keeping Christmas in a quiet, solitary state. Tomorrow my vows against plays and wine expire, and I already resolve to make new ones, finding so much good in them.
levels.summary:
This morning I went to the office and sat through the entire session. Among other matters, Sir W. Warren came about a contract and took the opportunity, with Sir W. Batten absent, to openly defy him, complaining that Batten opposed everything he offered. Sir W.

Pen rebuked Warren for it, but I knew Pen was secretly pleased to hear such talk. After that, we returned to business without further incident.

At noon, I went to the Exchange for a while, then came home to dinner. My head ached terribly from being overloaded with business. My wife and I dined alone on a fine turkey and a mince pie, in a kind of state, though we are poor wretches.

We have kept this Christmas almost entirely by ourselves, not straying out once. Tomorrow my vows against plays and wine come to an end, but I hope to make new ones soon, for I find so much good and God's blessing in keeping them.

periods.label: May 1664

levels.sentence: After two hours of roaring stone-like agony, I was delivered by chance when tumbling onto my knees, and the pain ebbed enough for me to sleep.
levels.paragraph: I rose full of pain from yesterday's cold, went to the office, and came home to dinner in extraordinary misery. After dinner the pain forced me to bed, swelling into a fit as great as ever I had with the stone, in belly and back. A glyster brought little relief, and for two hours I lay crying and roaring in anguish. At last, by chance, I got upon my knees amid my tumblings, and the pain began to lessen; within an hour I was in little pain and slept well all night.
levels.summary:
Up this morning full of pain, which I believe came from the cold I got yesterday. I went to the office and sat through the session, then came home to dinner in extraordinary discomfort. After dinner the pain worsened until I was forced to take to my bed.

For an hour or two it rose to as great a torment as ever I remember in any fit of the stone, striking both the lower part of my belly and my back.

At first I could break no wind. I took a glyster, but it brought away only a little and my height of pain followed it. For two hours I lay in the most extraordinary anguish, crying and roaring, not knowing what to do.

Then by chance, among my tumbling and turning, I got upon my knees in bed, and my pain began to lessen little by little. Within an hour I was in very little pain, though still I could not break wind nor make water.

Even so, I continued in that state and slept well all night. It is strange how the pain came and went so suddenly, and I must note that getting on my knees seemed to be the turning point.

periods.label: October 1664

levels.sentence: I spent the morning at the office, dined with Uncle Thomas, caressed Bagwell's wife in return for promises to help her husband, heard troubling news about Tangier from Mr. Cholmely, bought two silver tumblers, and finished late at the office.
levels.paragraph: Up early and to the office, where I worked all morning. At noon, Uncle Thomas came to dine and received money from me. Later, in my office, I caressed Bagwell's wife, finding her increasingly receptive to my good words and promises to get her husband a place, which I intend to do. I then visited Lord Sandwich and walked with Mr. Cholmely, who told me that Tangier is in a bad condition under Fitzgerald, a man of no honour or honesty, who offends everyone and does nothing well. On my way home, I bought two silver tumblers, returned to work late at the office, then went home to supper and bed.
levels.summary:
I began the day at the office, attending to business all morning. At noon, my uncle Thomas came to dine with me, and I gave him some money, as was our custom. After that, I returned to my office and called in Bagwell's wife, where I caressed her.

She grows more amenable each day, and I made her good words and promises to get her husband a place—a promise I fully intend to keep, as I have my own designs.

Later, I went to Lord Sandwich's lodgings, and then walked with Mr. Cholmely to Fleet Street. On the way, he told me that Tangier is likely in a bad condition under this same Fitzgerald, a man of no honour, presence, or little honesty.

Fitzgerald seeks to raise the Irish and suppress the English interest there, offends everybody, and does nothing well, which I am sorry to hear. I returned home by way of buying two silver tumblers, then spent the rest of the evening busy at my office, and finally went home to supper and to bed.

periods.label: December 1664

levels.sentence: I walked to Deptford, dined with the poor Bagwells, and then forced my attentions on Bagwell's wife, though I found little contentment in my conquest before returning home to friends and a long evening at the office.
levels.paragraph: This morning I walked to Deptford, and after some business at the yard, I went unseen to Bagwell's house, where the poor folk kindly gave me dinner. Once I sent Bagwell abroad, I pressed myself on his wife, and though I had my way against her resistance, it was not to my full contentment. I returned home and dined with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, then spent the rest of the day and much of the night at the office.
levels.summary:
This morning I walked to Deptford, and after doing something at the yard, I walked without being observed to Bagwell's house. There I was very kindly treated, and the poor people got a dinner for me in their fashion, of which I ate very well.

After dinner I found occasion to send Bagwell abroad, and then I was alone with his wife; I attempted what I wanted, and against her force I did it, yet not to my contentment. By and by he came back, and I took leave and walked home.

Back home I dined with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, who had come to see me. After dinner I left them and went to the office, where we sat all the afternoon, and I stayed late. Then I went to supper and came back to the office again very late, after which I finally went home to bed.

periods.label: January 1665

levels.sentence: A fortnight of January brought me secret meetings with Jane and Mrs. Martin, a grand French dinner, Hooke's microscope, a lost Doll, and a hare's foot that cured my colic.
levels.paragraph: In these two January weeks, I pursued my usual pleasures and business without restraint. I arranged to meet Jane again, sported with a young kinswoman, and lay freely with Mrs. Martin, though her impudence soon sickened me. Among gentlemen at Lord Brunker's, I delighted them with a ballad and enjoyed a noble French feast. I ordered Hooke's remarkable book on the microscope, and later found my colic cured by a hare's foot that Mr. Batten showed me.
levels.summary:
The first week saw me walking to White Hall with Sir W. Pen, attending to the Duke, and then paying out money. I stole a private word with my Jane at the barber's and arranged to meet her Sunday, charmed by her modest way. Later I sported with Herbert's young kinswoman at the Swan, and then went to Mrs.

Martin's new lodgings, where I had my will of her for two shillings in wine and cake, though I left sick of her impudence. That evening I made mirth at Lord Brunker's with a ballad, feasted nobly, and ordered Hooke's book on the microscope from my bookseller.

The second week brought trouble over Jane, for her mistress confessed she had thrown herself away on a fiddler and vowed to have no other. They planned to marry her to Hayes, and I seemed to persuade her, but I secured a private conference and again enjoyed her company, hoping for more on Sunday.

I dined at the Swan, kissed the girl of the house, and took home my precious Hooke's book. With my wife at the New Exchange, we discovered our pretty Doll had gone away, which I suspect worse than claimed.

On my way home I bought a hare, having learned from Mr. Batten that the foot of a hare, carried about one, prevents colic. No sooner did I handle his foot than my belly loosened and I became quite well, strange how fancy works. That evening I supped, read, played cards, and went to bed.

I ordered Hooke's remarkable book on the microscope, and later found my colic cured by a hare's foot that Mr. Batten showed me.

periods.label: February 1665

levels.sentence: Despite a painful finger from last night's struggle, I attended to business, dined with friends, discussed ticket abuses with Mr. Wayth, and spent the evening with Lady Sandwich talking of daughters, husbands, and the state of the times.

Batten and his Lady, who are now very fond of me. Later, Lord Brunkerd took me to Lincolne's Inne Fields, where I talked with my Lady Sandwich about good housewifery, husbands for her daughters, and the luxury and looseness of the times, until past ten, and she told me of Lord Castlemayne's coming from France and of the mad freaks of the Maids of Honour. Meanwhile, my wife, having been long indoors in the dirt, went with her woman to a hot-house to bathe herself, and now pretends to a resolution of being hereafter very clean—though I know how long that will hold.

I dined with Sir W. Batten and my Lady, who are nowadays very fond of me. Then I went to the 'Change, and from there with Mr. Wayth to a cook's shop, where we dined again for discourse about Hamaccos and the abuse now practised in tickets, which grows daily. We also spoke of the great profit Mr.

Fen makes of his place, he demanding but 5 per cent of all he pays, yet very little pleased with any man that gives him no more.

She told me how my Lord Castlemayne is coming over from France, and is believed will be made friends with his Lady again, and also of the mad freaks the Mayds of Honour at Court have, including something about Mrs. that I did not note fully.

Then I came home by coach, spent a little time at my office, and so to supper and to bed.

periods.label: August 1665

levels.sentence: I resolved to mend my ways with my little girle, declined to involve myself in my cousin's troubles, learned that a frightening story about Alderman Bence was false, and set to making my will as the plague raged around me.
levels.paragraph: I resisted my improper feelings for my little girle and threw myself into my work, even making a trip to Woolwich in the rain. The next week brought my cousin Porter begging for help I could not give, and grim news of the plague's toll. A tale of Alderman Bence stumbling over a corpse proved false, yet his own wife's illness troubled me. Seeing how quickly death could strike, I resolved to complete my will without delay.
levels.summary:
In the first week of August, I struggled with my own conscience, having been too familiar with my little girle. I knew I must stop such behavior, so I spent my days settling papers and went to Woolwich in the evening, though the rain came down hard.

The following week brought distress from every side. My she-cozen Porter came asking for help for her husband, who had been sent to the Tower, but I dared not involve myself. The weekly Bill of Mortality was dreadful: over four thousand dead, three thousand from the plague.

I heard a strange tale of Alderman Bence stumbling over a dead body, which frightened his pregnant wife so much that she fell sick and died—but at dinner he told us it was all false. Yet his wife was indeed ill, and that haunted me.

With the town so unhealthy, I went home to draw over my will, bound by oath to finish it by the next night.

  - B. Afternoon and evening
    - 1. Settled papers after two days of neglect

periods.label: October 1665

levels.sentence: During a plague-stricken October, I mixed public business with private pleasure and uncovered corruption in the prize goods, all while renewing my broken vows.
levels.paragraph: I sailed to Chatham and there shamed Commissioner Pett by proving that four horses were wasted hauling a timber one man could carry, then watched Sir W. Pen feign kindness I knew to be false. In Rochester I dallied with three pretty maids among the castle ruins, though the precipices frightened me more than I cared to admit. Later I visited Evelyn's glorious gardens, spent time with Sarah and my Valentine despite the plague, and learned the Bill had lessened by 740. Then I was called to Bruncker's ship, where I discovered how my Lord Sandwich's order had been abused, with goods broken and Sir W. Berkeley saying his back was broad enough to bear it.
levels.summary:
This week began with a stop at Chatham, where I viewed the Yard with Commissioner Pett and made a small show of his wastefulness by having the horses removed from a timber that one man could carry. Then Pett, Cocke, and I went to Sir W.

Pen, who gave me a forced kindness and only consented to have his silk moved before payment because I was there — a false rogue I will never trust.

In Rochester I toured the old castle ruins and amused myself with three maids among the precipices, which frightened me enough to spoil my pleasure, and later met the Mayor in his gown.

Back in London, I found my wife willing to give my sister Pall £400 and marry her, though the plague still made it unsafe. I went to the Duke of Albemarle, read Evelyn's book on libraries, and did some business that might bring me a jobb of work.

I also stopped at the Swan with Sarah and then went to Deptford to see my Valentine, not valuing the plague on every side. I ended the week at Evelyn's, admiring his evergreens and holly hedge, and wrote a late letter to Sir W.

Coventry; the plague Bill was down by 740, and I renewed my vows after neglecting them too long.

Then, before day, I went to Lord Bruncker's ship and found the King's order to examine the prize-goods strictly, with no regard for my Lord Sandwich. I discovered the worst misuse of his order: goods tossed, tumbled, and broken, mostly by Sir W. Berkeley, who said my Lord's back was broad enough to bear it.

I saw the whole shameful business laid open, and my mind turned to how my Lord might be protected from the consequences.

periods.label: January 1666

levels.sentence: Returning to a London stirring back to life, I found myself caught up in court business, dinners, and office disputes, while worrying over my Lord Sandwich's need for a pardon and taking late pleasure in Mrs Tooker's company.
levels.paragraph: Returning to London in early January, I found the town shaking off its emptiness—Covent Garden full of people and shops opening again—and I went gladly about business at White Hall and the Exchange. Mr Povy told me that Lord Bellases blames us for want of money, but I value it not, knowing I do all that can be done. More troubling was Mr Moore's news that my Lord Sandwich's case is very bad unless he gets a pardon before Spain; I am bound for him in L1000 and urged Moore to press him to pay my cousin Pepys. At the office my paper on pursers was well approved except by Sir W. Pen, who objects to everything and mends nothing, and I ended one evening in the easier company of Mrs Tooker.
levels.summary:
On the first week of January I rode to London with my Lord Bruncker and Mrs Williams, and was delighted to see Covent Garden full of people again, shops beginning to open, though Westminster and Covent Garden still stood empty of court and gentry. After a brief visit to Sir G.

Carteret at White Hall, I dined nobly with Mr Povy, who told me that Lord Bellases complains for want of money and blames us; I value it not, knowing I do all that can be done.

Later I read a discourse on the River Thames that gave me great satisfaction, explaining how encroachments and causeways at every wood-wharf have choked the river with shelves. That evening little Mrs Tooker came to supper, and I kept her very late, talking and making her comb my head, and did what I would with her.

The next week I went to the Duke of Albemarle's and was troubled at heart to see how things are ordered there without consideration or understanding. After calling on my shoemaker and finding a tailor, I met Mr Moore and took him home to dinner.

He and I concluded that my Lord Sandwich's case is very bad and may be worse if he does not get a pardon for his doings about the prizes, at Bergen, and other actions at sea before he goes for Spain.

I used all the art I could to persuade Moore to urge my Lord to pay my cousin Pepys, since I am bound for him in L1000, and I directed Moore to go express to get the pardon perfected.

At an extraordinary office meeting on pursers, my paper was received by Sir J. Minnes, Sir W. Batten, Sir W. Pen, and my Lord Bruncker with great approbation, except that Sir W. Pen must except against everything and remedy nothing.

He made objections I could not understand, though he did detect a failure or two where I had magnified, and at last declared it the best thing he ever heard of its kind. When Sir W. Batten proposed that those who know the Victualling should meet to mend all, Pen declined, saying he must be out of town.

He never attempts to mend anything, but lets all go on though never so bad; that is the character I have always known of him.

periods.label: February 1666

levels.sentence: On a cold morning I walked to White Hall, shared ominous talk with Warwicke, transacted Navy business, dallied with several women, dined with Knipp, visited Carteret who fears a general catastrophe, lent money to Lane, and ended the month resolved to apply myself better to business.
levels.paragraph: I walked to White Hall on a dry cold morning, met Sir Ph. Warwicke in the Park, and we spoke gloomily of the nation's divisive state and the new Act that hampers raising money. After business with the Duke of York, I idled at Westminster Hall, talked with Michell and Howlett, and later had my way with Mrs. Martin. At home I dined with the delightful Mrs. Knipp, then visited Norwood and Carteret, who fears a general catastrophe. I lent Mrs. Lane money and lay with her, though she grows dangerous, and I went to bed early, resolved to reform my neglected business.
levels.summary:
After rising and doing a little business at my office, I walked through the curiously dry and cold morning to White Hall. Entering the Park, I met Sir Ph. Warwicke and took a turn with him in the Pell Mall, where we talked of the melancholy posture of affairs.

Everywhere people are snarling at one another, and the new Act has taken away our power of raising money. Warwicke fears the situation as I do, but he is fearful of enlarging on the ill condition of the State. We appointed another time to meet seriously about Navy business, and so parted.

At White Hall I did business with the Duke of Yorke, then walked to Westminster Hall, where I talked at length with Mrs. Michell and Howlett and her daughter, who has become a mighty pretty woman. As I was going out, Mrs.

Thence I went to the Palace Yard and the Swan, staying until dark.

periods.paragraph: I walked to White Hall on a dry cold morning, met Sir Ph. Warwicke in the Park, and we spoke gloomily of the nation's divisive state and the new Act that hampers raising money. After business with the Duke of York, I idled at Westminster Hall, talked with Michell and Howlett, and later had my way with Mrs. Martin. periods.label: March 1666

levels.sentence: After church and dinner I wandered about Westminster in fair dry weather, visited Mrs Martin and enjoyed her while her husband fetched wine, heard of my former sweetheart Betty Howlet's marriage, and came home to accounts, with Sir Christopher Mings returning from Hambro empty-handed but for pipe-staves.
levels.paragraph: I rose with my cold better, went to church and dined at home, then walked out toward St James's in fine dry weather, hoping to see fair Mrs Butler, but she was not there. I went on to Westminster, drank at Herbert's, then visited Mrs Martin and had my will with her while her husband fetched wine, promising to try to get him a purser's place. She told me Betty Howlet, my old sweetheart called my second wife, has married a younger son of Mr Michell's, which pleased me; then I came home by coach, did accounts, and went to bed, while Sir Christopher Mings returned from Hambro with little but pipe-staves.
levels.summary:
I got up with my cold better, went to church, and then home to dinner. Afterwards I walked out to St James's Church hoping to see the fair Mrs Butler, but she was not there, and I believe she no longer lives in that area. The weather was very fine and dry, though everyone cries out for lack of rain.

I went to Herbert's and drank, then to Mrs Martin's, where I did what I would with her while her husband went to fetch us some wine. The poor man would take pains, I think, if I can get him a purser's place, which I intend to endeavour.

She told me as a secret that Betty Howlet of the Hall, my little sweetheart whom I used to call my second wife, is married to a younger son of Mr Michell's; his elder brother, who should have had her, died in the plague, and I am glad. They are to live nearer me in Thames Streete, by the Old Swan.

Then I came home by coach and to my chamber about some accounts, and so to bed. Sir Christopher Mings has come home from Hambro without anything done, except bringing home some pipe-staves for us.

periods.label: April 1666

levels.sentence: A rainy day of trouble getting to Whitehall, where the Duke judged a captain's complaint, while news of Tom Cheffin's sudden death and the spreading plague darkened the Court.
levels.paragraph: Raining and coachless, I walked to the Old Swan and took a scull to Whitehall, where the Duke of Yorke heard Sir Thomas Allen's complaint against Mr. Wayth and settled it with rare judgement. The Court buzzed with news of Tom Cheffin's sudden death, and the plague is feared to be increasing again. I saw the Archbishop of Yorke preach, carried Mrs. Hunt home to dinner, and heard old Protectoral stories. The evening ended quietly with Mercer combing my head, a psalm, and bed.
levels.summary:
I rose in great trouble, for it rained and no coach could be had to carry me to White Hall; so I walked to the Old Swan and got a scull instead. At the Duke of Yorke's, we all met to hear the debate between Sir Thomas Allen and Mr.

Wayth — Allen complaining of Wayth's ill usage of him at the late pay of his ship, though he had but a sorry poor occasion for it.

The Duke determined the matter with great judgement, chiding both, yet encouraging Wayth to continue as a check to all captains in anything touching the King's right; indeed, I never saw the Duke do anything more orderly or with more judgement.

The Court was full this morning of the news of Tom Cheffin's death, the King's closet-keeper. He had been well last night, playing at tables in the house, and not very ill at six o'clock this morning, yet dead before seven; they think an imposthume in his breast.

It looks fearfully among people nowadays, the plague, as we hear, increasing everywhere again. I went to the Chappell but could not get in to hear well; yet I had the pleasure once in my life to see an Archbishop — this was of Yorke — in a pulpit.

Being at a loss how to get home to dinner, having promised to carry Mrs. Hunt thither, I at last got my Lord Hinchingbroke's coach, he staying at Court, and took her up in Axe-yard, and home we dined.

We had good discourse of the old matters of the Protector and his family, she having a relation to them; the Protector lives in France and spends about L500 per annum.

I carried her home again, then went to Court and walked over to St James's Chappell, thinking to hear a Jesuit preach, but came too late; so I got a hackney and went home to business. At night I had Mercer comb my head, and so to supper, sang a psalm, and to bed.

periods.label: May 1666

levels.sentence: After church and a noble dinner, I sent my wife off to a christening, enjoyed Mrs. Martin's favours, discussed preferment and bribes with Blagrave and Yeabsly, inspected the navy's ships, read Bacon on fortune, and retired satisfied to bed.
levels.paragraph: I began the day with my wife at church, and we dined nobly at home alone. Afterward, my wife went to Greenwich for a christening while I visited Mrs. Martin for pleasure, though her loose company displeased me. I then spoke with Mr. Blagrave and later with Mr. Yeabsly, who had bribed Lord Ashby, and after inspecting ships and reading Bacon, I returned home to find my wife pleased with her role as godmother.
levels.summary:
In the morning I went with my wife to church, and at noon we dined mighty nobly, just the two of us alone. After dinner, my wife and Mercer took a coach to Greenwich, where she was to be gossip to Mrs. Daniel's new child. I went out to Westminster, and straight to Mrs.

Martin's house, where she had stayed at home all day for me, and I did what I would with her. Yet I was not well pleased with her over-free and loose company, so I left, heading to Westminster Abbey.

At the Abbey I fell into discourse with Mr. Blagrave, whom I find a sober, politique man who gets money and increase of places. Then I went by coach home, and met Mr. Yeabsly, whom I took up in my coach.

He told me he had presented my Lord Ashly with £100 to bespeak his friendship in his accounts now before us; my Lord received it, so I believe he is as bad as to bribes as what the world says.

I then called on all the Victualling ships to know what they had of their complements, and so to Deptford to enquire after a little business.

All the way coming and going by water, I read my Lord Bacon's "Faber Fortunae," which I can never read too often. Back home, I found my wife come home, much pleased with the reception she had there; she was godmother, held the child at the font, and it is called John.

After setting my papers in order and supping, I went to bed, desirous to rise betimes in the morning.

periods.label: June 1666

levels.sentence: Expecting a triumph, I instead learned we were beaten at sea, and amid the sad news, court factions, and my own private dealings, I felt the weight of a changed world.
levels.paragraph: I rose expecting to celebrate a victory, but news came that we had been badly beaten, losing many ships and commanders, with the Prince burned and Sir G. Ascue taken prisoner. The town's mood turned grave, and though I dined and entertained myself with little Mrs. Tooker, the evening brought letters from the fleet and a damped Duke of York. In the days after, I observed growing tensions between the Duke of Yorke and Albemarle over commanders, while I also tended to private matters—giving money to my father and profiting from Colonel Fitzgerald. Writing to Lady Sandwich, I found it as great an alteration to send a sad letter as ever I experienced in my life.
levels.summary:
The week of June 6 began with my certainty of a naval victory, but I was soon astonished to learn we had been beaten, losing many ships and good commanders, including the Prince run ashore and burned by the Dutch, and Sir G. Ascue taken prisoner.

At the Exchange, the talk and countenances of the people were much changed, and Captain Page's own account—he who lost an arm—confirmed that the Dutch had pursued us for two hours. The Duke of York was much damped, and I spent the evening abstracting letters from Coventry and Pen for setting out the fleet again.

I found great reason to think we were beaten in every respect, with ships missing, captains slain, and the Duke of Albemarle complaining he never fought with worse officers.

In the following weeks, I observed growing jars between the Duke of Yorke and the Duke of Albemarle over commanders, with Captain Du Tell at the center, and saw Sir W. Coventry reflecting on Albemarle's choices.

I also dealt with personal matters: my father prepared to leave and I gave him money for a horse and for my mother and sister; I met Colonel Fitzgerald and gained £25 for myself; and I struggled with colic from wearing a thin waistcoat.

Amid all this, I wrote a sad letter to my Lady Sandwich instead of a triumphant one, and the court's ill blood and discontent were as notable as the defeat itself.

I also dealt with personal matters: my father prepared to leave and I gave him money for a horse and for my mother and sister; I met Colonel Fitzgerald and gained £25 for myself; and I struggled with colic from wearing a thin waistcoat.

Amid all this, I wrote a sad letter to my Lady Sandwich instead of a triumphant one, and the court's ill blood and discontent were as notable as the defeat itself.

periods.sentence: Expecting a triumph, I instead learned we were beaten at sea, and amid the sad news, court factions, and my own private dealings, I felt the weight of a changed world.
periods.paragraph: I rose expecting to celebrate a victory, but news came that we had been badly beaten, losing many ships and commanders, with the Prince burned and Sir G. Ascue taken prisoner. The town's mood turned grave, and though I dined and entertained myself with little Mrs. Tooker, the evening brought letters from the fleet and a damped Duke of York. In the days after, I observed growing tensions between the Duke of Yorke and Albemarle over commanders, while I also tended to private matters—giving money to my father and profiting from Colonel Fitzgerald. Writing to Lady Sandwich, I found it as great an alteration to send a sad letter as ever I experienced in my life.

periods.label: August 1666

levels.sentence: After settling my accounts to a record £5,700 and being delayed by Sir W. Pen so that the Duke's business stood still, I walked with Sir W. Coventry to hear his discontent with the late fight, then spent the fast-day afternoon in mirth at Mrs Martin's with a dissembling widow and her companions, and came home pleased with my wife's drawing.
levels.paragraph: I rose betimes to settle last month's accounts and found myself worth £5,700, the most my book ever made out. Delayed by Sir W. Pen's return from Sheerness, I came late to St James's and found everything stood still for want of me; walking with Sir W. Coventry, I heard his discontent with the late fight and the news that the Dutch had lost 5,000 men to our 400 or 500. On this common fast-day I went fearfully to church, dined at the Swan on rabbit, and spent the afternoon at Mrs. Martin's with Mrs Burroughs, a merry widow named Mrs Eastwood, and Mrs Fenton, toying with them and carrying them home.
