levels.summary:
Up betimes this morning I settled my last month's accounts, and I bless God I find them very clear, for I am worth £5,700, the most that ever my book did yet make out. As I was going to attend the Duke of York as usual, Sir W.

Pen came home from Sheerness and held me in discourse about public business till I came by coach too late to St James's, where I found that everything stood still and nothing was done for want of me.

Walking over the Park with Sir W. Coventry, I clearly saw he is not thoroughly pleased with the late management of the fight, nor with anything that the Generals do. He was only glad to hear that De Ruyter is out of favour and that this fight hath cost the Dutch 5,000 men, as they themselves report.

He observed how strangely the slaughter runs on one hand, there being 5,000 killed on theirs and not above 400 or 500 killed and wounded on ours, with as many flag-officers lost on theirs as ordinary captains on ours: Everson and the Admiral and Vice-Admiral of Freezeland on theirs, and Seamour, Martin, and another on ours.

Leaving him going to chapel, it being the common fast-day and the Duke of York at chapel, I went to Mrs Martin's, but she was abroad; so I sauntered to the Abbey and then to the parish church, fearful of being seen doing so, and after the parish church ended I dined at the Swan upon a rabbit.

After dinner I returned to Mrs Martin's and found Mrs Burroughs; by and by came a pretty widow, one Mrs Eastwood, and one Mrs Fenton, a maid. There was merry kissing and looking on their breasts, and all the innocent pleasure in the world. But, Lord!

to see the dissembling of this widow — when Doll, Mrs Martin's sister, sang a certain jigg that her husband, who died this last sickness, had loved, she seemed to be sick and fainted and God knows what.

Yet I soon made her as merry as possible, and towzed and tumbled her as I pleased, then carried her and her sober pretty kinswoman Mrs Fenton home to their lodgings in the new market of my Lord Treasurer's, and left them there.

I was mightily pleased with this afternoon's mirth, but in great pain to ride in a coach with them for fear of being seen. So I came home, and there much pleased with my wife's drawing today in her pictures; then to supper and to bed very pleasant.

periods.label: September 1666

levels.sentence: After the Great Fire, I devoted myself to naval accounts and Parliament lists, yet a stolen evening with Bagwell's wife left me loathing my own desire.
levels.paragraph: In mid-September I handled business with the Duke of York and promised to counsel young Howlett, then dined with Balty and shipped goods from Deptford. That night I stole to Bagwell's house, gratified my lust, and was immediately disgusted with myself, slipping away when her husband returned. A fortnight later, I completed the ship and man lists for Parliament, conferred with Sir W. Coventry, and felt real satisfaction. I ended the week in good humour, bringing home my wife's new flowered tabby gown and writing over the lists in a fresh method.
levels.summary:
On the 12th, I went with Sir W. Batten and Sir W. Pen to St. James's to see the Duke of York, then walked to Westminster, where Michell and Howlett told me their children were going to Shadwell's. Howlett mentioned that the young man's unkindness to his wife had blown over, and I promised to act as counsellor.

Later, after a dinner with Balty and his wife, I took Balty to Deptford and loaded half my goods aboard the Bezan. That same evening, in the dark, I went to Bagwell's house and had my will of her — but once done, I hated her and the deed and left as soon as her husband returned, retiring late to Sir W. Pen's.

On the 26th, I met Batten, Pen, and Warren at the office to discuss our Scotch motion, but Warren was hesitant and offered only a prior proposal, so we parted with nothing resolved. I finished the lists of ships, men, and time served for the Parliament Committee, then took them to St. James's, where Sir W.

Coventry waited. He and I were mightily satisfied, and he said that once we were over this rub we must find a better Comptroller. I fetched my wife from Unthanke's, where she had finished her new flowered tabby gown, and we went home.

After writing over the lists in a new method, I went to bed in good humour, glad to have brought that matter to an end.

periods.label: October 1666

levels.sentence: Through three weeks of October 1666, I faced parliamentary cuts, attended to Tangier accounts, indulged in private pleasures, and heard Captain Guy's grim assessment of the Navy.
levels.paragraph: I took leave of my father, who had come to see the burned city, and then went to Westminster, where Parliament cut L150,000 from our wear and tear. I spent days in the Hall, visited Mrs. Martin and her sister Doll, and took on a new singing girl for my wife. I attended a Cabinet meeting about Tangier money, moved my iron chests from the damp cellar, and heard that Harry Killigrew was banished and courtiers defeated at elections. Captain Guy dined with me and despaired of the fleet's discipline, saying we had been beaten in the June fight. Amidst all this, I did my accounts and felt the weight of my own reckoning.
levels.summary:
The week of October 10th brought public and private accounts together. I saw my father off to Brampton, then went to Westminster, where Sir W. Coventry told me the House had cut L150,000 from our wear and tear. The Hall was full of people eager to attack the Vice-Chamberlain.

Later, I took a ticket for little Michell, dined alone at the Swan, played with Sarah, and then went to Mrs. Martin's, where I did what I would with her; she is very big and wants me to be godfather. I returned home to find my wife's new girl, poor and ordinary, costing us seven or eight pounds in clothes.

I spent the evening making up my accounts, which were clear but difficult.

In the week of October 17th, after church and a merry dinner with Lady Pen, I attended a Cabinet meeting about Tangier money; the King sat like an image and only my Lord Chancellor questioned whether it was in nature to help us.

I read Stillingfleet on Purgatory, then brought two iron chests out of the damp cellar into my closet, satisfied to see my money safe. Sir H. ' That afternoon I sat with Mrs. Martin and her sister Doll, with whom I did what I would.

The week of October 24th was shadowed by Captain Guy's dinner. He cried out against the discipline of the fleet, confessed we were beaten home in the June fight, and feared our ruin. He said the Dutch fight in very good order, and we in none at all.

After he went, I tumbled widow Burroughs and Doll all the afternoon, then supped with uncle and aunt Wight, where we abused my aunt with Dr. Venner.

There were further marks of the King's method: the Revenge had her forecastle blown up, and the Diamond was overset at Sheerness, with the Foresight also coming to disaster.

periods.label: November 1666

levels.sentence: In November 1666, I chased private pleasures—cake, claret, and women—while the King's service faltered and I brooded on national ruin.
levels.paragraph: November 1666 found me torn between duty and desire. At the office I answered endless pleas for money and listened to Sir W. Coventry's fears that all would be undone, while at home and abroad I indulged in sack, tumbling Doll Lane, and liberties with Mrs. Bagwell and Mrs. Burroughs. My wife and I quarrelled over fashion but found comfort again; I dined with cousins and friends, learned of the fire's aftermath, and watched Parliament press its accusations. The month closed with rumors of rebellion and a Duke of York raising an army, yet I still found time for cake houses and cards.
levels.summary:
Through November 1666 my days were torn between the King's failing service and my own unruly appetites. At the office I faced endless petitioners asking for money I could not give, and Sir W.

Coventry confessed to me that all discipline was lost in the fleet and that Parliament would have another bout with us over our accounts. We agreed to keep laying everything plainly before the Duke of York, though Coventry expected all to be undone.

Yet the same week brought small joys: Hollar's new print of the burnt City, and the news that the northern rebels were dispersed.

My private life was no less hectic. I took Mrs. Bagwell into my office and did what I would with her; I tumbled Doll Lane over burnt claret at the Swan; and I met Mrs. Burroughs several times, even stopping at a cake house with her in a coach.

periods.label: December 1666

levels.phrase: A year of wonder and mischief
levels.sentence: I closed 1666 with a mix of pleasure and anxiety, settling my accounts to find myself worth over £6,200 despite my excesses, while the nation around me languishes.
levels.paragraph: This December I have revelled in fine company and secret pleasures, yet I have also been confronted with death and debt. The drowning of Batters frightened me more than ever, and my annual accounts revealed prodigality: my spendings exceeded last year by L644, though my worth still rose to L6,200. The publick suffers, but I am thankful for my plate and family's health.
levels.summary:
During this month I entertained Lord Hinchingbroke with a magnificent dinner, saw Henry Howard admitted at Gresham College, and took my pleasure with Pegg and later Mrs. Burroughs. I also visited Mrs. Turner, who lost everything in the plague and chided me for not writing, and I promised to mend my ways.

My wife lay ill, and Kate Joyce came distressed.

The latter part of the month brought sorrow with the drowning of poor Batters, which struck me with fear. I continued my dalliances, with Mrs. Martin and with Mrs. Clerk's daughter, while also attending to business.

The climax was settling my year's accounts: I found my gettings had fallen to L2,986 and my spendings risen to L1,154, yet my worth grew to over L6,200. I pray God to make me thankful and careful. The nation's condition is sad, but my family and I are well, though my eyes are sore.

periods.label: January 1667

levels.sentence: In the frosty month of January 1667, I found myself torn between public alarms of a French invasion, the Crown's empty coffers, and my own private appetites—delighting in plays, wine, and stolen kisses while trying to keep my accounts and my conscience in order.
levels.paragraph: This January was a bitter one, both in the cold weather and in the nation's mood. The Court trembled at talk of a French landing in Ireland, yet we could not man our ships without money, and the seamen grew mutinous. Amid these alarms, I took comfort in small pleasures: a glass of wine with Doll Lane, a kiss from Mrs. Burroughs, and the incomparable singing of Knipp. I also resolved to keep my integrity, refusing a £100 bribe, and to note my good fortune in saving a little from my salary.
levels.summary:
Public affairs troubled me greatly this January. The Court was convinced the French had shipped men at Brest, likely for Ireland, but we lacked money and men to send ships to the Downes, and mutinies broke out among the seamen. At Westminster I heard a conference on the Wine Patent, and Mr.

George Montagu told me how ill things stood: the King was angering the Commons by altering their Bill for Accounts, and my Lord Sandwich's troubles seemed almost over while the Vice-Chamberlain now bore the brunt.

I was glad to attend, for the Commons' speakers outdid the Lords, and I believed no invasion plot, as the Houblons did.

My private life was full of small consolations and temptations. I walked with my wife and friends in the frosty fields, visited the Michells, and carried neats' tongues and wine to their pretty house.

I saw several plays, including "The Custome of the Country," which I thought the worst play I ever beheld, though Knipp sang admirably. I stole kisses from Mrs. Burroughs and took liberties with Betty Michell, which pleased me greatly even as I acknowledged my fault to my wife.

I also refused a bribe of £100 from the flagmakers, resolving to keep my hands clean.

Throughout the month I labored at my office, examining the loss of The Prince Royall and The Bredagh, and met with the Trinity House. I found a small gain in my monthly accounts and thanked God I could save from my salary.

The fast-day for the King's death reminded me of duties, and I stopped singing in the garden accordingly.

By the end of January, the Prince was better, Lord Sandwich had perfected peace with Spain, and I had enjoyed merry meetings with Mercer, Knipp, and Harris—yet the season left me mindful of the fragility of both public and private fortunes.

periods.label: February 1667

levels.sentence: I balanced my accounts, refused a bribe, pursued Betty Michell, and wrangled at the Duke's over unpaid tickets, all while noting the peace and Prince Rupert's recovery.
levels.paragraph: This month I kept careful watch over my money and my pleasures, from a small saving out of my salary to stolen kisses and wandering hands. I refused a hundred-pound bribe to keep my integrity, yet I could not keep my hands off Betty Michell. At the office I fought for the fleet's pay against slothful brethren, and at the playhouse I was more entertained by a witty masked lady than by the play itself.
levels.summary:
I found myself a small gainer from my month's accounts, thanking God I could save from my salary, and enjoyed walks and songs with my wife and Mercer.

Yet I also stole kisses from Mercer before bed and later, despite a bruise, made my wife shift sides so I could sit with Betty Michell, doing whatever I wished with her hand.

I refused a bribe of £100 in gold from the flagmakers, keeping my hands clean, and heard good news of Prince Rupert's recovery, Lord Sandwich's peace with Spain, and the King's speech hinting at peace.

But I also faced base brethren at the Duke's who would not speak for the money needed for the fleet, and I pressed the Duke to take notice.

I was pleased to see my Navy account papers sewn together, eased my mind about my law business, and at the playhouse I was vexed by talking ladies yet delighted by a witty masked lady's sport with Sir Charles Sedley.

periods.label: March 1667

levels.sentence: Amid the King's business and growing fears of war, I found my days filled with petty accidents, merry tales, public alarms, and small private comforts.
levels.paragraph: This March I went downriver with Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten, where Batten narrowly sprained his foot stepping into a tar hole, and we found little value in the Woolwich wharf. Later, I attended the Duke of York with worries about Lord Bruncker's revenge, but instead heard Carteret quarrel and Gawden's news that the Council doubted they could set out a fleet for want of victuals. I resolved to draw up the Victualler's stores, yet I still found time to dine with the Carterets, kiss Betty at Michell's, and receive advice to bring my father to town. The days were full of public alarms and private comforts, with merchants uncertain about war with the Dutch and France.
levels.summary:
In early March I went by barge with Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten to Deptford and Woolwich on King's business. At the storehouse, Batten nearly hurt himself stepping into a tar hole, but only sprained his foot.

We looked at cordage and the ballast wharf, which I thought not worth hiring unless we could buy the fee-simple, so we gave it up. We dined merrily at the White Hart with Captain Cocke, and Sir J. Minnes told many tales.

Later that month I attended the Duke of York with W. Batten, fearing Lord Bruncker's revenge, but heard Sir G. Carteret quarrel with him instead. Mr. Gawden told me the Council had doubts about setting out a fleet for want of victuals, which alarmed me, so I resolved to draw up the Victualler's stores.

I dined with the Carterets, kissed Betty at Michell's, and received Mr. Holliard's advice to bring my father to town for his health. At the Exchange I learned that letters suggested war with the Dutch and France, leaving merchants uncertain. I walked with Dr.

Fuller, who thinks matters will be bad, and tried unsuccessfully to see Doll Lane at Westminster Hall. Little Mis. Tooker came and I kissed her, and I resolved to speak well of Sir John Winter to the Duke.

periods.label: April 1667

levels.sentence: Amid office intrigues, a city crying for peace, and the safe delivery of Betty Michell's child, I wrestle with false friends, my own wandering affections, and the nagging trouble of my eyes.
levels.paragraph: I have been vexed by Carcasse's manners and Sir W. Pen's falseness, and even the placement of new churches serves the great, not the city. Yet there have been pleasures: a quiet dinner with my wife, some singing, and the joyful news that Betty Michell was delivered of a pretty girl. I long to see my father well, but I cannot resist the charms of Mrs Lowther or the memory of Betty's beauty. My eyes continue to trouble me, and I am ever mindful of the schemes around me, as when I prevented Pett from pressing Carcasse's business.
levels.summary:
In the first week, I was troubled by Mr. Carcasse's ill manners and discovered Sir W. Pen's falseness. I ran errands, settled accounts at Sir Robert Viner's, and heard from Mr. James Houblon that there is no hope of peace. The town cries for peace, and tenants are throwing up their land.

Even new churches are placed for the advantage of the great. I saw a mediocre play, failed to meet Knipp, kissed a little miss at the Swan, and was haunted by Betty Michell's beauty. Sir W. Batten told me how his lady's jewels were found under a china cup, and I read a well-regarded book on Turkish policy.

The next week, I sat at the office and prevented Commissioner Pett from bringing on Carcasse's business, knowing he sought to advance himself with Lord Bruncker. I enjoyed singing alone with my wife, but my eyes trouble me after candle-light. I wrote to my father, glad he is at ease and longing to have him in town.

This afternoon Mrs Lowther came to me at the office, and I took liberties with her breasts and mouth, which she willingly allowed.

The third week saw a feast at White Hall for the Swede's ambassadors. Word came that Betty Michell was in labour, and my wife went to her. I waited at the office full of expectation, and was mighty glad to hear she had delivered a pretty girl. My wife and I visited the child, which I liked mightily. Sir W.

Warren now applies to Lord Bruncker, and I oppose him in discourse. I also visited Mrs Martin, and then went home to bed.

periods.label: May 1667

levels.sentence: In a hot May week I pursue music, building schemes, and women while rumors of the Treasury and peace churn, until my father's painful fit reminds me how fragile all this vigour is.
levels.paragraph: I spent the week practising the flagelette, doing business at Westminster, and looking at ground and coach-houses for my building. I also indulged in women — tumbling a girl at the Swan and lying with Mrs. Martin — and took pleasure in spying pretty Betty Michell with her child. Rumours flew about the King's Treasury commissioners and about peace with Holland, but the deepest impression was my father's sudden fit, his bowel falling down, and his patience under it, which saddened my heart.
levels.summary:
Pleasure and business filled the week. I practised my flagelette and played with my wife in the evening. At Westminster Hall I heard contradictory reports of the King's Treasury commissioners — some said the Lord Chancellor, the two Secretaries, and Lord Ashly; others Sir W.

Coventry and Sir John Duncomb; all concluded the Duke of Albemarle. With Mr. Commander and Mr. Hide I viewed coach-houses and ground for my planned building. In the Minorys I found the young mercer with his pretty little wife, and at the Old Swan I saw Betty Michell, mighty pretty with her child.

Lust and shame mixed. I tumbled a little girl at the Swan whose uncle caught her neckcloth off; I let it pass with a laugh. Later I went to Mrs. Martin and did what I wished with her. On Sunday I was trapped in church by Mr. Howlett, so I diverted myself with a perspective glass on the fine women, then went to Mrs.

Martin again. Meanwhile doubts about peace grew: a captain reported Dutch seamen called us English dogs and cried against peace.

My father's health cast a shadow. I came home to find him recovered from an unexpected fit after his bowel fell down and W. Hewer put it back. He had shown me the place that morning. His patience and good humour under such pain saddened my heart, though I hope a steel truss will relieve him.

I also read Evelyn against Solitude and Boyle's Colours, but my father's condition stayed with me.

periods.label: June 1667

levels.sentence: Amid the stirs of the nation and my own desire to keep in favour, I visited Sir W. Coventry, delivered maps to Lord Barkeley, grew troubled over the want of money, and still found time for dalliance with Nell and Mrs. Markham.
levels.paragraph: At the beginning of June I went to White Hall and St James's, rejoicing to hear that the Duke of Cambridge was like to recover, and I made sure to visit Sir W. Coventry so the world might see my interest. When Lord Barkeley came in with the Duke of Monmouth and a crew of young Hectors, I offered him a set of pocket maps and later delivered them through Captain Aldrige. The next week was more anxious: Roger Pepys came with his silly son, we discoursed sadly on the evils of the time and the want of money, and I wrote a bold letter to Sir W. Coventry that I was at first afraid of, then satisfied with. Yet even then I dallied with my maid Nell and afterwards with Mrs. Markham before ending my evenings in reading and writing.
levels.summary:
This June I found myself much taken up with public business and my own standing in the world. I was glad to hear that the Duke of Cambridge, whom the doctors had given over, was likely to recover, and I paid a long visit to Sir W. Coventry because it kept me in his acquaintance and let the world reckon my interest.

Lord Barkeley came in with the Duke of Monmouth and a pack of young Hectors on their way to Harwich, and I made sure to offer my Lord a set of pocket maps, which I later sent by Captain Aldrige.

With Creed I wandered from a dull preacher at White Hall Chapel to a crowded church in Southwark, and at last home to dinner with my father and wife; afterward I saw Betty Michell at Westminster Church.

The following week brought Roger Pepys and his son Talbot, whom he meant to settle at the Temple but would carry back again because of the present stirs.

We had much good discourse on our misery and maladministration: he told me Lord Arlington had taken up £12,000 in gold, and promised to show me a Chancery decree with twenty-six housekeepers of our name in Cottenham.

I stayed busy at the office while Roger went to church, and allowed myself some dalliance with my maid Nell, speaking to her of her sweetheart. In the evening, troubled by the evils of our time, I wrote a plain, bold letter to Sir W.

Coventry about the lack of money; I was afeard it might give offence, but upon reading it over I was satisfied it was good, though I wished Sir W. Batten had not signed it with me.

After Roger was gone I dallied a while all alone with Mrs. Markham in the garden, then went to my chamber to read and write, and so to supper and to bed. Through all the stirs and cares, I kept my pleasures and my place as best I could.

periods.label: July 1667

levels.sentence: The sudden news of peace fills me with joy, yet I am still entangled in the Navy's want of money, my own little sins, and the strange falseness I observe in others, until the jaunt to Epsom brings me a day of content and a sprained foot.
levels.paragraph: With the news of peace I found my heart light, though our office remained at a standstill for money. I savored the report that I alone was spoken well of, and I continued my usual pleasures, from dalliance with Nell to visits at the Swan and Mrs. Martin's. At Epsom I drank the waters, heard James Houblon call me the only happy man of the Navy, and ended the day by spraining my foot in a wood. The fortnight closed with my Lady Jemimah's good news and my own uneasy wonder at the falseness I had seen.
levels.summary:
The news of peace with the Dutch arrives just as the Navy is at a standstill for money, and though the office is blamed, I alone am spoken well of. I take my pleasure where I can—with my maid, with Mrs.

Martin, and in the joyful stir of the town—yet I am struck by the falseness of Doll's anger and by ominous signs like Rolt's bleeding nose.

At last my wife and I go to Epsom, where I drink the waters, hear flattering words from James Houblon, and rest in the heat. We visit my cousin Pepys's house and wander in the wood, where I sprain my foot—a small price for a day of contentment.

My Lady Jemimah's son is also good news, and I end the fortnight lighter, though still mindful of the work that lies ahead.

periods.label: August 1667

levels.sentence: After church and a pleasant dinner with Pelling, I went by water to Westminster, where my hope of seeing Betty Michell was dashed when the turned head revealed her mother, but I found consolation in Putney church and the infinite delight of Boyle's Hydrostaticks before a quiet supper with W. Hewer.
levels.paragraph: I began the day at church and then dined at home with Pelling, whose pleasant discourse cheered me. Afterward I traveled by water, landing Pelling at White Hall and going on to Westminster, where I kissed Frank but missed Betty Michell, mistaking her mother for her and feeling vexed. My boat's oar had broken but was mended, and I went up to Putney, where I admired the fine people and young ladies in church. Then I walked to Barne-Elmes, reading Boyle's Hydrostaticks with great delight, and returned home leisurely, supping with W. Hewer and talking of the Office before bed.
levels.summary:
I rose and went to church, then home, where Pelling came by invitation to dine with me, and we had much pleasant discourse. After dinner I took water to White Hall, landed Pelling (who was going to his wife in the country at Parson's Greene), and went myself to Westminster.

At the Swan I kissed Frank, and then went to the parish church hoping to see Betty Michell; I stayed an hour in the crowd, thinking from the end of a nose I saw that it was her, but when the head turned toward me it was her mother, which vexed me.

Returning to my boat, I found one of her oars had broken in rowing but had been fastened again.

I then went up to Putney, stepped into the church to look at the fine store of people and young ladies there, and walked to Barne-Elmes, sending Russel on while I read Boyle's Hydrostaticks, which gave me infinite delight. I walked in the Elms a good while before taking my boat leisurely home with great pleasure.

There I supped with W. Hewer, with whom I had a great deal of good talk touching the Office, and so to bed.

periods.brief: After church and a pleasant dinner with Pelling, I went by water to Westminster, where my hope of seeing Betty Michell was dashed when the turned head revealed her mother, but I found consolation in Putney church and the infinite delight of Boyle's Hydrostaticks before a quiet supper with W. Hewer.
periods.full:
I rose and went to church, then home, where Pelling came by invitation to dine with me, and we had much pleasant discourse. After dinner I took water to White Hall, landed Pelling (who was going to his wife in the country at Parson's Greene), and went myself to Westminster.

At the Swan I kissed Frank, and then went to the parish church hoping to see Betty Michell; I stayed an hour in the crowd, thinking from the end of a nose I saw that it was her, but when the head turned toward me it was her mother, which vexed me.

Returning to my boat, I found one of her oars had broken in rowing but had been fastened again.

I then went up to Putney, stepped into the church to look at the fine store of people and young ladies there, and walked to Barne-Elmes, sending Russel on while I read Boyle's Hydrostaticks, which gave me infinite delight. I walked in the Elms a good while before taking my boat leisurely home with great pleasure.

There I supped with W. Hewer, with whom I had a great deal of good talk touching the Office, and so to bed.

periods.label: September 1667

levels.sentence: My September was a whirl of errands, dalliances, a fair, and council debates, all capped by the arrival of our grave new girl Willet.
levels.paragraph: In the first week, I attended to business at the Exchequer and bought heraldry for my wife, then stopped at the Swan where Doll Lane came to me. After following my wife to Walthamstow, I returned via Bartholomew Fair, where I pitied a crippled dancer and marvelled at a clockwork show, and my wife narrowly avoided being taken up by Sam Hartlib. The last week brought official duties: a Tangier committee and a Council debate on seamen's arrears, in which my speech pleased the King. At home, our new servant Willet arrived—very pretty and grave—and I began planning my journey to Brampton.
levels.summary:
The month began with a mix of errands and indulgences. I bought Guillim's Heraldry for my wife, and at the Swan I met Doll Lane and touched her. After learning my wife had gone to Walthamstow, I followed, picking up Mrs. Turner, and we gossiped about Sir W. Pen's family. At Sir W.

Batten's house we had an indifferent but clean dinner, and I admired the furnishings, though I grew tired of the company.

On returning, we stopped at Bartholomew Fair, where despite the dirt I saw a poor fellow dance on his hands with his legs tied—I pitied him and gave money—and a clockwork display of man's ages. Later, my wife was almost taken up by Sam Hartlib, but he departed when he saw me. That night we went home quietly.

The last week was filled with official business. I attended a Tangier committee that did little, then spoke before the Duke of York's Council about seamen's tickets, pleasing the King.

A debate on arrears saw Lord Anglesey oppose Lord Ashly's scheme to borrow credit from the East India Company, and I agreed it was mean for the King to do so. Domestically, I visited Mrs. Martin, promised my goddaughter a coat, and finally met our new girl Willet—very pretty and grave, almost too good for our family.

I also heard of the Turners' plan to send their son to the East Indies, which I liked, and I began thinking of my trip to Brampton.

periods.label: October 1667

levels.sentence: From the Council's long hearing on Pett's neglect, through a cheap dinner, Yeabsly's abatement, a stolen touch at Mrs Martin's, and Lord Crew's anxious talk of Sandwich's unanswerable expenses, I came home only to hear that Sir W. Batten was not expected to live till tomorrow.
levels.paragraph: I went up to Whitehall for the Council's hearing on Commissioner Pett, where the Chatham Masters gave him the lie and I thought him a weak, silly man; the matter was put off to Monday. After a scanty dinner and settling Yeabsly's claim with Lord Ashly, I slipped to Mrs Martin's and then to Lord Crew's, who talked of Lord Sandwich's monstrous spending and the difficulty of getting him money or home. Returning, I found Sir W. Batten asleep and soon heard he was not expected to live till tomorrow, which troubled my wife and me both for kindness and for the money he owes me.
levels.summary:
Up, and to White Hall to attend the Council about Commissioner Pett's business, along with my Lord Bruncker and Sir W. Pen. In the Robe-chamber the Duke of York came to us, the officers of the Navy, and we met about Navy business, Sir W. Coventry being with us.

Among other things, he nobly recommended to his Royal Highness, now the prizes were disposing, to remember Sir John Harman to the King for some bounty, and also for my Lady Minnes.

Then we all attended the Council, where there was a long hearing of Commissioner Pett; the two Masters Attendant of Chatham were called in and denied having any order from Pett about bringing up the great ships, which gave the lie to what he says.

In general, I find him but a weak, silly man, guilty of horrid neglect in this business all along. The Council broke off without coming to an issue, ordering another hearing on Monday next.

After the Council rose, I stayed walking up and down the galleries till the King went to dinner, and then I went to my Lord Crew's; but he having dined, I took a very short leave, confessing I had not dined, and so went to an ordinary hard by the Temple-gate, where I have heretofore been, and dined, costing me 10d.

Then I went to my Lord Ashly's, where after dinner Sir H. Cholmly, Creed and I, with his Lordship, handled Mr. Yeabsly's business, coming to agreement with him abating him L1000 of what he demands for ships lost. I then went to Westminster, to Mrs.

Martin's lodging, whither I sent for her, and there heard that her husband is come from sea, which is sooner than I expected; and here I stayed and drank, and so did toucher elle and away.

By coach I went to my tailor's, and thence to my Lord Crew's, where I stayed with him an hour till almost night, discoursing about the ill state of my Lord Sandwich—that he can neither be got to be called home, nor money got to maintain him there, which will ruin his family.

And the truth is, he does almost deserve it, for by all relation he hath, in a little more than a year and a half, spent L20,000 of the King's money, and the best part of L10,000 of his own; a most prodigious expense, more than ever Ambassador spent there, and more than these Commissioners of the Treasury will or do allow.

They demand an account before they will give him any more money, which puts all his friends to a loss what to answer. But more money we must get him, or call him home. I offered to speak to Sir W. Coventry about it, but my Lord would not advise to it without the consent of Sir G. Carteret.

So home, and I went to see Sir W. Batten, who fell sick yesterday morning. He was asleep, so I could not see him, but in an hour after, word was brought me that he is so ill it is believed he cannot live till tomorrow.

This troubles me and my wife mightily, partly out of kindness, he being a good neighbour, and partly because of the money he owes me upon our bargain of the late prize. So home, and to supper and to bed.

periods.label: November 1667

levels.sentence: I negotiated a remittance with Alderman Backewell and then learned from Cooling the intricate political maneuvering over the Lord Chancellor's fate.
levels.paragraph: This week I dealt with Alderman Backewell over the Tangier remittance and heard his boastful account of surviving the Sheerness business. Later, I met Cooling and learned that the Lords' stiffness toward the Chancellor stems from their own fears, not kindness, and that a trial before the Lords is better for him than the King's arbitrary court. I also spent time with Creed, visiting the Excise Office and the Temple, where I noted the plainness of Selden's tomb.
levels.summary:
I began the week by visiting Alderman Backewell to arrange a £6,000 remittance to Tangier, and he promised to send it by the next post.

He then boasted about how the Sheerness business had nearly undone him, yet he still managed to pay £7,000 for the Swedes' ambassadors and promised bankers even more, showing his shrewdness when Serjeant Maynard came demanding money.

Later in the week, I met with Cooling, who revealed the truth behind the Lords' stiffness toward the Lord Chancellor — it was not kindness but fear for their own consequences.

Cooling argued it was better for the Chancellor to face trial before the Lords than to be committed by the King and judged by a court made for that purpose, and even the Chancellor's own son had moved for the treason charges to be specified.

I then had to endure Creed's company at the Excise Office and the Temple, where I observed Selden's plain tomb beside his executor's finer one, before finally going home to dinner.

periods.label: December 1667

levels.sentence: I spent the last day of 1667 in the long suspense of White Hall and the Tangier committee, came home to a mournful dinner with my uncle and uneasy talk of the Act for Accounts, and ended the year at Westminster, going to Mrs. —.
levels.paragraph: I rose in a silent mood, said scarcely a word to my wife, and spent the morning at White Hall waiting while the Duke of York was with the King in the Cabal, hearing all the talk of the great lords being turned out of power over the Chancellor's business. Then came a dull meeting of the Tangier committee, where Lord Middleton seemed a heavy, needy man. Back home, Uncle Thomas dined with us in mourning for his daughter, and the Act for Accounts hung over the table like a threat I dared not examine. Afterwards I took my wife to Unthanke's and went on to Westminster, to Mrs. —.
levels.summary:
I rose this last day of the year and said little to my wife—not from anger, but from my own silenced mood—then made for White Hall. There I waited for a long time while the Duke of York was closeted with the King in the Cabal, and Creed and I talked in the Vane-Room.

I could feel everyone's expectation turning on the great business of thrusting those powerful lords out of the council; the quarrel, as I perceived it, was only that they stood against the King's will in the Chancellor's affair.

When the Duke at last came out, we went into the Tangier committee, where my Lord Middleton made his first appearance. He struck me as a dull, heavy man, though a stout and needy soldier—and I feared that his neediness would keep that poor garrison from ever yielding any real value to the King.

After a short meeting we broke up, and I went home to the office, found them sitting, and joined them until our business was done.

At dinner with my people, my uncle Thomas was there, wearing a mourning hat-band for his daughter Mary.

We fell to discoursing on the Act for the Accounts, which, by report of those who had read it—I have not read it, and have no mind to, for fear of meeting something in it to trouble me—gives a greater power to those commissioners than was ever given to any subjects; indeed, too much.

After dinner I walked with my wife and the girl to Unthanke's, left her there, and then went on to Westminster, and from there to Mrs. —, where the day's record breaks off.

  - Waited while the Duke of York was with the King
    - Creed and I talked in the Vane-Room
    - Public expectation about turning the great lords out of council and power
    - Quarrel: the lords stood against the King's will in the Chancellor's business
  - Duke of York came out; Tangier committee met briefly
    - Lord Middleton seemed dull and heavy, but a stout soldier and needy lord
    - I feared his neediness would keep the garrison from ever being worth anything to the King

  - Returned to the office, joined the sitting, ended business
  - Dined at home with my people
    - Uncle Thomas was there in a mourning hat-band for his daughter Mary

      - It reportedly gives the greatest power ever given to subjects, and too much

periods.sentence: I spent the last day of 1667 in the long suspense of White Hall and the Tangier committee, came home to a mournful dinner with my uncle and uneasy talk of the Act for Accounts, and ended the year at Westminster, going to Mrs. —.
periods.paragraph: I rose in a silent mood, said scarcely a word to my wife, and spent the morning at White Hall waiting while the Duke of York was with the King in the Cabal, hearing all the talk of the great lords being turned out of power over the Chancellor's business. Then came a dull meeting of the Tangier committee, where Lord Middleton seemed a heavy, needy man. Back home, Uncle Thomas dined with us in mourning for his daughter, and the Act for Accounts hung over the table like a threat I dared not examine. Afterwards I took my wife to Unthanke's and went on to Westminster, to Mrs. —.

periods.label: January 1668

levels.sentence: After a day of court business and a mistaken dinner invitation, I enjoyed an extraordinary evening of music, dancing, and good company that lasted until two in the morning, and a week later I devoted myself to the serious work of settling my accounts.
levels.paragraph: Rising early on the first of January, I went to White Hall and discovered my wife's error in inviting Mr. Pierce to dinner instead of supper; yet the mistake brought Mr. Harris, a man of excellent conversation, to my table. After a play, we gathered at my house for an evening of extraordinary music and dancing, with a fine supper and a costly cake, until two in the morning. Later, on January 26th, I turned from merriment to duty, spending the day at church and then settling my Tangier and East India accounts with Mr. Poynter, before a quiet evening at home.
levels.summary:
On the first of January I rose early and went to White Hall, where I learned from Mr. Pierce that my wife had mistaken a dinner invitation for a supper. Returning home, I found Mr. Harris there by the same error, but we quickly made a pretty dinner, and I was mightily pleased with his excellent conversation.

Later we went to a play, though I slipped away hoping to meet Mrs. Bagwell, who had just returned from Harwich; she was gone, so I rejoined my wife and watched The Tempest.

That evening we gathered at my house with many friends, including the two Mercers, Betty Turner, Pendleton, and W. Batelier. The Duke of Buckingham's musicians played for us, and we danced and sang until two in the morning, with a good supper and an excellent cake of our Jane's making.

After the company left, I gave wine and sweetmeats to Mrs. Turner and Mrs. Hollworthy, but found the latter a mean and conceited woman.

Later that month, on January 26th, I rose and went to church with my wife, then spent the day in serious business, settling my Tangier and East India accounts with Mr. Poynter transcribing. In the evening W. Hewer supped with us, and the girl combed my head until I slept.

periods.label: March 1668

levels.sentence: Amidst parliamentary defence and personal pleasures, I find my mind torn between public duty and private troubles, yet I manage to steal moments of joy and connection.
levels.paragraph: This month has been a whirl of anxiety over Parliament's scrutiny of my office, balanced by small pleasures like a talking starling and a successful feast. I have worked hard on our defences, felt the weight of new accusations, and found comfort in family and friends. Though my eyes trouble me and my wife's health worries me, I end the month with my reputation somewhat intact and a sense of cautious relief.
levels.summary:
The month of March was dominated by fears of parliamentary inquiry into our conduct of naval affairs. I spent many hours with Sir W. Coventry preparing our defence against accusations concerning tickets, victuals, and the manning of the fleet.

Though we hoped to answer effectively, I felt the constant weight of possible ruin, especially when Carcasse confessed to a prior complaint against Batten, Pen, and myself. I lost sleep over this, but made progress in clearing my name.

Despite the anxiety, I found time for personal diversions. I visited Mrs. Martin and Doll Lane for sexual encounters, bought Montaigne's Essays, and marvelled at a lifelike painting. I also planned and hosted a great dinner, impressing guests with fine pewter and good food.

My wife and I had a few quarrels, but I discovered that staying silent resolved them better than arguing. I took care of family matters, paid my uncle, and saw my cousin Roger, who pressed for a new Parliament.

The month ended with me giving a satisfactory account to a parliamentary committee, though I remained wary of their jealousy.

periods.label: April 1668

levels.sentence: Amid house alterations and political turmoil, I pursued pleasures with women and playhouses while following the impeachment of Sir W. Pen and the intrigues of Lady Castlemayne.
levels.paragraph: This April I busied myself with house alterations and office matters, but my mind was often on pleasure and gossip. I kissed Deb and later Knipp, heard that Lady Castlemayne had fallen for Hart the actor, and watched the political storm around Sir W. Pen's impeachment. I spent days at Westminster Hall, spoke with friends about saving Lord Sandwich, and tried in vain to see Betty Michell. Evenings found me at the playhouse or supping with Sir W. Pen, while my eyes troubled me and I sought diversion.
levels.summary:
I began April with house alterations and a pleasant talk with my wife, then welcomed guests including Deb, whom I kissed after giving her ten shillings. Later, though I had a great mind to kiss her again, I refrained. My days were filled with office business, dining with Mr.

Pierce, and fitting forth a little fleet, hindered by want of money and distrust.

I found mirth at the King's playhouse watching "The English Monsieur," and afterward sat with Knipp while she undressed. She told me that Lady Castlemayne is in love with Hart, giving him presents, and that Becke Marshall is the go-between—so Castlemayne is even with the King for Mrs. Davis.

I kissed Knipp in the Park but not more because of her paint.

Political troubles occupied me: Sir W. Pen is to be impeached, and the Coventrys are trying to save him by laying blame on Lord Sandwich. I stayed silent, believing that was the only way. At Westminster Hall I heard the Lords would not commit Pen until finding a precedent, and the Duke of York spoke kindly of him.

I also met with Lord Crew and G. Carteret, who saw our matters improving.

I bought Greeting's book and began learning the recorder, and later tried to see a pretty woman at a bookseller's but lost my nerve. At Michell's, Betty seemed shy and her husband unwilling, so I got little satisfaction.

I saw part of "Beggar's Bush" at the playhouse, and having nowhere else to go and my eyes too bad to read, I supped at Sir W. Pen's and sat talking late.

periods.label: May 1668

levels.sentence: In May 1668 I drifted between office duties, plays, and loose company, mistook my cousin's purchase for mine, saw a strange fire in the sky, and felt Lord Sandwich's reproach prick my conscience.
levels.paragraph: May was a whirl of business and pleasure. I attended the Office and White Hall, chased plays and music, and dined with old acquaintances, yet found many entertainments poor. I was startled to be congratulated on a purchase that was my cousin Tom's, and even more startled by the strange light that flew over the City. Through it all, I kept up my private amours while Lord Sandwich's letter reminded me how rarely I wrote to him.
levels.summary:
The month opened with old acquaintances and reflections on age: meeting Mrs. Washington after eight or nine years, I saw plainly that she had grown old, and it made me think how time alters me too. Business at the Office and White Hall mixed with poor dinners, plays, and music—Knepp and Mrs.

Pierce were often in my company, though the dinner at Pierce's was sluttish and the play at White Hall proved poor.

Public talk turned on the City Bill, the death of Sir Thomas Teddiman of a thrush, and a strange meteor that flew over the City on Saturday night; I myself saw a sudden light vanish toward Cheapside, and the world feared another fire and Papist plots.

I was also disquieted to be congratulated for a great purchase that turned out to be my cousin Tom's, not mine. Pleasures continued with Mercer and Gayet—singing at Fox Hall, walks at Neat-houses, and merry suppers—and I fell in with loose town rogues whose bawdy talk made my heart ache.

Yet Lord Sandwich's reproach for my rare letters followed me all month, and my private amours with Mrs. Martin and Bagwell's wife only added to the tangle of guilt and delight.

periods.label: June 1668

levels.sentence: In June 1668, I kept at Tangier business by day while by night I gave myself to singing, loose company, and private amours, all under the reproach of Lord Sandwich's letter pricking my conscience.
levels.paragraph: All through June I was torn between duty and pleasure. By day I wrestled with Tangier accounts, coals, and the Duke of York's commands, and I felt the sting of Lord Sandwich's letter for my neglected correspondence. By night I walked with Mercer, sang at Fox Hall, fell in with rakes who talked bawdy, and pursued my amours with Mrs. Martin, Bagwell's wife, and the rest. The merry evenings and the guilty thread of his reproach made the whole month a tangle.
levels.summary:
All through the first week I was at my Tangier accounts and the office, and the Duke of York sent me to cast up the summer fleet's charge. Sir W. Coventry argued we should obey Parliament and set out fifty sail even though it would spend money to little purpose. The King's birthday brought a dinner at Sir G.

Carteret's, but Lord Sandwich's letter troubled me: he had noticed how rarely I wrote while he was abroad, and I had no good excuse.

My chief pleasures were with Mercer and Gayet—walking at the Neat-houses, singing at Fox Hall with gallants gathering about us, and merry evenings with Mr. Pelham and the swaggering Mr. Monteith.

I also fell in with Harris, Rolt, and town rogues like Harry Killigrew and young Newport, whose bawdy talk made my heart ache; with them I first learned of the "Ballets" company and their naked dancing. My private amours continued with Mrs.

Martin, and I touched her landlady's thigh, went up to Bagwell's wife's chamber at Deptford, and enjoyed a pleasant supper at Mr. Mills's with Mrs. Hallworthy, Mrs. Andrews, and Mrs. Turner until one in the morning.

The next week was taken up with Creed and Colonel Atkins about sending coals to Tangier and settling money with Alderman Backewell; on the holyday I went by water to Westminster, calling at Michell's but not kissing, then looked in at Martin's. I saw "The Impertinents" at the Duke of York's playhouse with W.

Hewer, then went to Spring Garden to supper; coming home not very merry, Mercer and I sang together in the garden, and so went to bed. Through all this, the thread of Lord Sandwich's reproach kept pricking my conscience.

periods.label: July 1668

levels.sentence: After a busy morning at the office, I dined and then went out to my bookseller's, where I followed a pretty woman from Duck Lane to Newgate Market; I visited Lord Crew, saw my wife's almost-finished picture at Cooper's, and took my wife, Deb., and Mercer to Spring Garden, where I was troubled by gallants forcing themselves on women, before returning home with pleasure to receive my four costly little plates.
levels.paragraph: This morning I was busy at my office, and after dining at noon I went out to Duck Lane to see my bookseller, but his wife was not at home. There I spied a pretty woman with a wanton look and followed her round the streets until she turned back and I lost her. I then visited my Lord Crew, whose face is sore but hopeful, and afterwards saw my wife's picture at Cooper's, almost done and mighty fine. I took my wife, Deb., and Mercer to Spring Garden, where we ate and walked, though I was troubled by the rude gallants who almost forced women in the arbours. We returned by water with much pleasure, and my plate-maker brought me four little plates costing £5, which both troubled and pleased me.
levels.summary:
This morning I was busy at my office until noon, when I dined. Afterward I went out to my bookseller's in Duck Lane, but his wife was not at home.

While I was there, I noticed a pretty woman passing by with a wanton look, and I followed her around the streets from Duck Lane to Newgate Market, until she turned back and I lost her. From there I called on my Lord Crew, whom I found up; his face was sore, but he was hopeful of doing well again.

Next I went to Cooper's, where my wife's picture is almost done and looks mighty fine indeed. , and Mercer to Spring Garden. We ate and walked there, but I was troubled to see how rude some of the young gallants of the town have become—they go into people's arbours where there are no men, and almost force the women.

This confidence of the age's vice upset me. Yet we returned by water with much pleasure. Also this day my plate-maker came with my four little plates of the four Yards, which cost me £5; that troubles me, but it pleases me too.

periods.label: August 1668

levels.sentence: A busy August of official duties, art, and stolen pleasures, from Sir W. Coventry's absence to the painting of my wife's picture and Deb's delightful attentions.
levels.paragraph: This August I balanced pressing public business with private delights, from the splendor of Goring House to the satisfaction of my wife's finished portrait. I took my pleasures where I found them—with Deb, with a pretty girl at the fair, and even with a moment at the Swan. Yet I also felt the pangs of disappointment when women I sought were unavailable or when the portrait's resemblance fell short. Still, the month closed with new comforts, including a spaniel for my wife and my first night in Deb's freshly hung chamber.
levels.summary:
I began the month seeking Sir W. Coventry, only to find he had left town, so I visited Lord Arlington at Goring House, where he received me with great respect. There Lord Orrery surprised me with a complimentary discourse on shipping, which greatly swelled my pride.

Later, I saw my book vendor's wife but had no chance to enjoy her, and I spent the afternoon at Cooper's watching him finish my wife's picture, paying him £30 plus £8 3s. for the case.

That night Deb combed my head and I touched her with great pleasure. Toward month's end, I stole kisses at the Swan, dined alone, and saw Hamlet with Betterton at the Duke of York's playhouse, accompanied by my wife, Deb, Mary Mercer, Batelier, and W. Hewer.

I also visited the fair, saw Polichinelle, and first slept in Deb's newly hung chamber. On September 1, I was at the office nearly all day while my wife went to Hales's for her picture, and though I called on Betty Michell, her husband was at home.

At the fair a mare told money and earned me a kiss from a pretty girl; later a wicked wench accosted me, but I gave her a shilling and left.

periods.label: September 1668

levels.sentence: Amidst business and flirtations, I found myself drawn by duty to lend money for my Lord's return, even as I savored theater and kisses.
levels.paragraph: At the end of August I gave myself to pleasure—kissing a girl at the Swan, dining at Hercules Pillars, and watching Betterton's Hamlet with my wife and companions, then finishing the night at the fair. Come September, I spent the day at the office and pursued flirtations, yet found no satisfaction with Betty Michell or the weeping bookseller's wife. Later that month, duty took hold: the Duke of York desired a proposal from me, and at Lord Burlington's house I encountered Sidney Montagu, who brought urgent news of my Lord Sandwich and a need for L500, which I supplied despite my shame at having written so seldom.
levels.summary:
Early in September, I indulged my appetites while still tending to business.

I kissed a girl at the Swan, dined alone at Hercules Pillars, and had my shoe mended, then went to the Duke of York's playhouse to see Betterton in Hamlet—whom I rate the best actor ever—in company with my wife, Deb, Mary Mercer, Batelier, and W. Hewer.

Afterward we visited the fair and saw Polichinelle, and that night I first slept in Deb's newly hung chamber. Mrs. Batelier gave my wife a pretty spaniel bitch, though I cannot yet love it as a newcomer.

The next day I was at the office, but still found time for small adventures: I called on Betty Michell, but her husband was home, so I had no pleasure there. At the fair, a mare that told money cost me twelvepence but granted me a kiss from a very pretty girl.

I found the bookseller's wife weeping, and later a wicked wench accosted me near Shoe Lane, whom I gave a shilling to be rid of.

Later that month, duty called. Knepp's maid Betty came to tell me it was women's day at the playhouse, so I went to support their profit and gave her half-a-crown and kisses.

I then took water to St James's to speak with the Duke of York, who again asked me to prepare something for better managing our Office, and I promised to do it. From there I visited Lord Burlington's house, built by Sir John Denham, to see Lord Hinchingbroke and his lady, and found Mr.

Sidney Montagu just arrived from Mount's Bay. He brought word that my Lord Sandwich was well, but that money was urgently needed; I felt it my duty to my Lord to do something extraordinary, and so supplied L500, though I was ashamed of having been so remiss in writing to him during the voyage. Sir W.

Godolphin then came to see Sidney, and I reflected on the heavy cost of this unexpected visit.

periods.label: October 1668

levels.sentence: Despite the troubling news of James Southern's petition, I secured support from Lord Brouncker and the Duke of Albemarle, and wrote to the Duke of York, to make sure T. Hater and Mr. Turner got the places our clerks deserved.
levels.paragraph: This morning I got Lord Brouncker's assent for T. Hater to have Mr. Turner's place and also Sir J. Minnes's, but at the Board Mr. Wren told me that James Southern was petitioning the Duke of York for the Storekeeper's place at Deptford, which troubled me and the Board. After Wren left, we agreed to press hard for our clerks and for preferment by seniority and merit. That night, with Mr. Turner, I visited the Duke of Albemarle and asked him to befriend Turner before Wren; he took it kindly. I came away well pleased, stopped at Lord Brouncker's to get his signature on my letter to the Duke of York for T. Hater, and felt hopeful.
levels.summary:
This morning, before the Board sat, I spoke with Lord Brouncker and secured his ready assent for T. Hater to have Mr. Turner's place, as well as Sir J. Minnes's place. But once we were at the Board, Mr.

Wren came to town and told me that James Southern was petitioning the Duke of York for the Storekeeper's place of Deptford. This troubled me and the whole Board.

After Wren left, we reasoned together and resolved to move hard on behalf of our clerks, insisting that places of preferment should go according to seniority and merit.

After the Board rose, I went home with my people to dinner, then returned to the office and did some business. In the evening I went with Mr. Turner to the Duke of Albemarle's house, where I spoke to the Duke about appearing to Mr. Wren as a friend to Mr. Turner; he took my request kindly.

We came away well pleased with what we had done, and on the way home I stopped at Lord Brouncker's to get his hand to a letter I had written to the Duke of York for T. Hater. I felt hopeful that our efforts would keep the places in the hands of our own clerks.

periods.label: November 1668

levels.sentence: After pursuing my mistress Deb against my wife's suspicions, I was caught, confessed everything, and was forced to swear never to see the girl again, leaving me in shame and my wife in grief.
levels.paragraph: I spent a day of deceit, slipping away to find Deb while my wife suspected, and though I comforted myself with a stolen kiss, the very next morning my wife confronted me with the truth. I confessed everything, and she raged with threats to disfigure the girl and leave me, until my servant Hewer helped calm her. In the end I signed a promise never to see Deb again, and I lied about my intentions, but my heart was full of shame and my home was never the same.
levels.summary:
On November 18th, I rose late with my wife, who voiced her jealousy over Deb. I denied it, but as soon as I was out, I went searching for Deb, who had been sent away from our house.

I tracked her through porters and eventually found her at a coach near my tailor's, where I kissed her, gave her counsel and twenty shillings, and arranged a way to reach her through my bookseller.

I returned home and told my wife a fair tale, but she had been busy preparing our best chamber, and I felt a secret relief that all seemed safe.

The next morning, my joy turned to horror: my wife confronted me, knowing I had been with Deb. I denied it at first, but then confessed all, and she spent the afternoon cursing me, threatening to slit the girl's nose and to leave me, demanding money to keep quiet.

My servant Hewer, whom I was forced to trust, wept and persuaded her to stay on condition that I sign a promise never to see or speak to Deb again. I signed it, and even promised for Deb, though I lied to myself about keeping it.

The day ended in the most perfect confusion of face and heart, sorrow and shame, and I knew my peace was broken.

periods.label: March 1669

levels.sentence: I took a cold, windy day-trip to Maidstone, pleased by the countryside and old sights, then spent a late, flirtatious evening at Captain Allen's with the willing Mrs. Jowles before walking home through snow.
levels.paragraph: I set out with Gibson and Coney for Maidstone, stopping on the way to spy Mrs. Jowles through a window at Captain Allen's without letting on. I delighted in the Medway valley, Sir John Bankes's abbey-house, and the pretty town of Maidstone, where I watched flax-beating and bought fish for dinner. On the way back I viewed an ancient Saxon monument, then returned to Captain Allen's, where Mrs. Jowles allowed me great liberties. We stayed near midnight, and I walked through snow and darkness back to Chatham with Coney.
levels.summary:
Waking, I walked in the garden and found that Mrs Tooker had not brought any of her daughters as I had expected. I went to the yard, leaving Middleton at the pay, and after walking up and down I gave orders at the Hill-House for the coach to be made ready.

I took Mr Gibson with me, and Mr Coney the surgeon, and set out for Maidstone, which I had a mighty mind to see.

On the way, at St Margett's, I pretended to call on Captain Allen to see whether his daughter Mrs Jowles was there. His wife came to the door—he was in London—and I spied Jowles through a window but took no notice, excusing myself until night and promising to come again.

It was a mighty cold and windy but clear day, and I had the pleasure of seeing the Medway winding through a very fine country.

I went a little out of my way to visit Sir John Bankes, but he was in London; still I had a sight of his house, an old abbey just like Hinchingbroke and as good, finely placed by the river with handsome grounds and walls.

At Maidstone I walked all about the town and up to the top of the steeple for a noble view. I saw an old man beating flax, stepped into the barn to give him money, and found that piece of husbandry very pretty.

I bought a dish of fresh fish and sent it to our inn, the Bell, and after a good dinner a barber came and trimmed me so I should be clean to visit Mrs Allen at night.

Staying until about four, I set out alone in the coach, and on the way back stopped to see a Saxon monument near Aylesford—three upright stones with a great round one lying across them, a thing of great antiquity.

I stopped again at Captain Allen's, sent the coach and Gibson home, and stayed with Coney. Mrs Jowles came in, a very fine, proper, well-dressed lady, and there was also Major Manly and his wife, and later a pretty cozen of hers, daughter-in-law to Manly, who had such a cold she could not speak.

I set Coney and the Major to play while Mrs Jowles and I talked over all our old stories; I had the liberty to salute her often and pull off her glove, and found her mighty free and kind.

I do not doubt I might have had what I desired had there been time to carry her to Cobham, for she was very willing; she is certainly a whore, but a brave and comely one.

I got her to the street door and there kissed and touched her breasts without any force, and believe I might have had all else had it been time and place.

We stayed till almost twelve, and then with a lantern I walked with Coney over the fields,—dark as pitch, mighty cold and snowy,—to Chatham. Everyone was already in bed when I got home, and I presently went to bed.

periods.label: April 1669

levels.sentence: I stole meetings with Bagwell’s wife and Deb today, and though each encounter gave me pleasure, guilt followed me even into the evening’s company.
levels.paragraph: I went out on business in the morning, but my true errands were secret ones: first to enquire after Deb’s aunt in Jewen Street, and then to keep a noon appointment with Bagwell’s wife in Moorfields, where the holiday crowd let us do no more than talk. Later I saw Deb on Holborne Hill, followed her into a blind alehouse, and took liberties with her, though she stayed coy and modest; I gave her twenty shillings and agreed to meet her again at Westminster. My coach had gone when I returned, and at Povy’s, among friends, I tried to be merry but could not shake my fear of what I had done. At last I carried my wife home by Islington, and we supped quietly.
levels.summary:
Being up early, I went to the office, and before the session sat with W. Hewer at the Excise Office, though business carried me another way to the Temple. By Deb’s direction I knew where in Jewen Street to send my hackney coachman while I waited in the coach in Aldgate Street, so I sent him to enquire whether Mrs.

Hunt, her aunt, was in town; the answer was that she was not. This was all I could do at that moment, and I went away troubled because I could do no more.

Coming to the office, I found Bagwell’s wife, who slipped a note into my hand inviting me to meet her in Moorfields at noon.

My wife had already gone to dine with my cozen Turner, so after the office was up I went to the place, and after walking up and down by the windmills I found her and talked with her; but being a holiday and the place full of people, we parted, leaving further discourse and doing to another time.

Then I drove through Jewen Street, my mind, God knows, running that way, but I did not stop; going down Holborne Hill by the Conduit I saw Deb on foot going up the hill. She saw me but would not stop or speak, so I alighted and followed, overtaking her at the end of Hosier Lane in Smithfield.

I led her into a little blind alehouse within the walls, and there we talked alone, and I kissed her and touched her breasts; but she was mighty coy and, I hope, modest. I gave her 20s. in a paper, and we agreed to meet again in the Hall at Westminster on Monday.

She gave me great hopes by her carriage that she continues modest and honest, and so we parted.

When I came back to where I had left my coach, it was gone, for I had stayed too long, and I was troubled to have abused the poor fellow; so I took another coach and directed him to find out the fellow and send him to me. At my cozen Turner’s I found they were all gone to dinner to Povy’s, and thither I went.

They were all there—W. Batelier and his sister—and had already dined, but good things were brought me. I was mightily pleased with the fine rooms, though in truth there are so many bad pictures that they lessen the pleasure of the good ones. The.

and Betty Turner were in new flowered tabby gowns, and we were pretty merry, only my fear of what I had newly done kept my content from being full.

About five or six o’clock I took my wife and the two Bateliers homeward; W. Batelier alighted, and I carried the women round by Islington and so down Bishopsgate Street home. We talked and supped, and then to bed.

periods.label: May 1669

levels.sentence: In May 1669 I juggled worries about my wife's May-dew outing, the Duke's fury over Mr Child, my sister's pregnancy, my failing eyes, and my disordered accounts, all while readying myself to go abroad.
levels.paragraph: In May 1669 I was kept busy with small troubles and public quarrels. My wife slipped out before dawn to gather May-dew, and I feared for her, but she came home safe. At Whitehall the Duke of York fell out with Sir T. Littleton over Mr Child, and I kept silent, dreading the heartburnings that must follow. I dined with Lord Crew, much broken, who spoke of how country families decay as they draw nearer to London; and later my brother told me my sister was with child, which left me of two minds. Through it all I wrestled with my accounts and my ailing eyes, trying to put things in order before I went abroad.
levels.summary:
In May 1669 I was fretted by my wife's predawn trip to gather May-dew, though she returned safe and slept it off. At Whitehall the Duke of York fumed against the Council of Trade and Mr Child; Captain Cox and Sir T. Littleton clashed, and I kept quiet, fearing that the quarrel would breed lasting heartburnings.

The Duke afterwards chid the Treasurers, and I thought it foul that they sided against the Navy. I dined with Lord Crew, much broken since his illness; he told me how the old gentry feared to come to London, and how a family's endurance matched its distance from the capital.

Later I met Roger Pepys fresh from the country, and invited Sidney Montagu to dinner before his travels. I called on Mrs Martin, newly come from Portsmouth, who talked proudly of her husband's worth and the gentry's visits; I was glad but doubted they would keep their money.

I saw an old play, 'The Roman Virgin,' which hurt my eyes with candlelight, and I heard from my brother John that my sister is far gone with child—which left me uncertain whether to be pleased or troubled. All the while I laboured over my accounts with W.

Hewer, preparing for a voyage abroad, my eyes ailing, yet I made a good start. I ended the month with a merry outing to the Park and The World's End with my wife, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman.

periods.sentence: In May 1669 I juggled worries about my wife's May-dew outing, the Duke's fury over Mr Child, my sister's pregnancy, my failing eyes, and my disordered accounts, all while readying myself to go abroad.
periods.paragraph: In May 1669 I was kept busy with small troubles and public quarrels. My wife slipped out before dawn to gather May-dew, and I feared for her, but she came home safe. At Whitehall the Duke of York fell out with Sir T. Littleton over Mr Child, and I kept silent, dreading the heartburnings that must follow. I dined with Lord Crew, much broken, who spoke of how country families decay as they draw nearer to London; and later my brother told me my sister was with child, which left me of two minds. Through it all I wrestled with my accounts and my ailing eyes, trying to put things in order before I went abroad.

levels.sentence: In 1660 I gained a clerkship that left me suspicious of Downing's motives, and later I heard Morland's tale of rewarded royal service while managing family affairs in London.
levels.paragraph: In January I was made one of the Clerks of the Council, yet I could not thank Mr. Downing heartily, fearing he only meant to save his own salary. I spent the day on errands and dined at the French Ordinary, and learned that all the other clerks were turned out, which made me dread my own place. By August my fortunes had steadied: I arranged for a velvet coat, heard Sir Samuel Morland's story of how he served the King and was rewarded with a pension, and settled my father's allowance and my Master's degree. I ended the day at home with my wife, and made sport in the kitchen as I went to bed.
levels.summary:
In January, Mr. Downing sent for me and told me he had made me a Clerk of the Council. I was stumbled and thanked him without heartiness, suspecting he wanted to ease himself of my salary. I met Mr. Sheply, went to Whitehall, and settled lodgings with Sir Ant. Cooper.

That day I ran errands for Downing, reading the Dutch Ambassador's answer, and dined with Mr. Moore and Mrs. Jem. Later I went to the French Ordinary, where Downing feasted Sir Arthur Haselrigge and others, and gave me notes to invite members.

But I heard from the Clerks that all but the Leighs were turned out, and though my name was mentioned, nothing was done. I went home uneasy about Downing's true intent and fearful for my place.

In August, I attended to business at the Privy Seal and agreed with tailor Pim to make me a velvet coat. Sir Samuel Morland came with a Baronet's grant and told me how he had served the King during the Protectorate, driven by Thurloe's bad usage; he had discovered Sir R. Willis and sunk his fortune for the King.

Now he had a pension of L500 a year and the benefit of two baronets, which made me think him less a fool than I once did. I dined at home with my father, Mr. Fairbrother, and Cooke, and young Captain Cuttance brought my wife a firkin of butter, welcome indeed. I gave my father 40s.

for my brother John's allowance and settled my Master's degree, costing about L9 16s. In the afternoon I went to Whitehall with my wife, and at night we came home by water, and I made sport in the kitchen having the girl and boy comb my head before bed.

levels.sentence: I saw my mother and Pall off to Brampton, dined merrily at my uncle Fenner's, was troubled by my wife's secret appointment with a French footman, and then heard that my aunt Kite is dying and wants me to take charge.
levels.paragraph: I went to the Privy Seal on business, then met my mother, wife, and Pall and put them into the waggon for Brampton, Pall crying bitterly. Afterwards I drank with my wife, Aunt Bell, and Charles Pepys, and dined at Uncle Fenner's, though my mind was troubled when a French footman privately spoke to my wife and she promised to go somewhere tomorrow. After dinner came news that Aunt Kite, the butcher's widow, is near death and has sent for my uncle and me to take charge of her affairs and her daughter.
levels.summary:
This morning I went to the Privy Seal on business, and on the way took leave of my mother, who is setting out for Brampton today. , and advised her how to behave toward my father and mother. Because it was late, I took them all to Beard's, put them into the waggon, and saw them depart; Pall cried exceedingly.

Then I went in with my wife, Aunt Bell, and Charles Pepys, whom we met there, and after drinking we went to my uncle Fenner's for dinner.

On the way, a French footman with feathers came looking for my wife and spoke to her privately; I could not learn what they said, only that my wife promised to go to some place tomorrow morning, which troubles my mind, for I do not know where it is.

At my uncle's, both his sons and daughters were present, and we were merry and dined.

After dinner, news came that my aunt Kite, the butcher's widow in London, is sick and ready to die. She has sent for my uncle and me to come take charge of things and be entrusted with the care of her daughter.

levels.sentence: In 1662 I kept my accounts, renewed my oaths against wine and plays, and found content in my orderly life while the King danced, the Queen came, and the nation murmured.
levels.paragraph: In 1662 I balanced my ledgers and my pleasures, cut off my beard, swore off wine and plays, and saw the King dance at Whitehall. I took note of the Queen's coming and Lady Castlemaine's favour, and watched the Act of Uniformity stir the Presbyterians. My purse grew to about £650, my health held fairly well, and I parted with servants who no longer served. Through it all I lived orderly, owing my quiet of mind to the oaths God put into my heart.
levels.summary:
In May I brought my journal up to date, dined with my father, and paid my debts as I could, though owing Anthony Joyce for tallow still vexed me. I cut off my beard, kept my head dry without powder, and had Sarah wash my feet. The weather was fair, and though wind tormented me, my health was pretty good.

I audited my estate at £530 and took an oath against wine and plays, which I found good effect from.

News came that the Queen had arrived at Hampton Court, handsome and discreet, and that peace was made with Argier. I feared the King's pleasure would put Madam Castlemaine's nose out of joint.

In December I went to a ball at Whitehall, where the King danced the Bransle, a single Coranto, and country dances; my Lady Castlemaine and Sir Harry de Vicke's daughter were the best dancers. I was merry with Mrs. Pierce's company, though her naked neck and Mrs. Clerke's conceit changed my opinion of them.

By year's end my estate stood at £650 besides goods. My family consisted of myself, my wife, and servants; Jane grew proud, Wayneman was naughty, and I resolved to part with them, while Sarah's going to Sir W. Pen troubled me. My diligence at the office was acknowledged even by the Duke, and I had access to Mr.

Coventry. The only weight on my mind was the suit with my uncle Thomas about my dead uncle's estate, which might force me to maintain my father.

Public matters were uneasy: the King followed his pleasures openly with Lady Castlemaine, Monmouth was dandled, the bishops pressed uniformity, and a plot was found for which four were hanged. The Act for Uniformity was printed, making mad work among the Presbyterians. My Lord Sandwich kept his esteem; Mr.

Moore was sickly. For my good condition and the quiet of the nation, I thanked God.
