levels.sentence: In 1663 I balanced Navy business with Westminster flirtations, yielding to Mrs. Lane and the glove-seller's daughter, delighting in a citizen choir and the King's assent, quarreling with Sir W. Pen, and closing the year quietly with my wife as my vows ran out.
levels.paragraph: I divided my year between the Navy Office and the temptations of Westminster Hall, where Mrs. Lane and the pretty daughter at Mrs. Howlett's shop led me into follies I regretted. Yet I also rode to the Wells to hear citizens sing in parts under a tree, and crowded into the Lords to watch the King give his royal assent. In November I stood up to Sir W. Pen, chased Howlett's daughter in vain, and laughed at myself when a pretty lodger softened my vexation. As Christmas came, my wife and I dined quietly on turkey and mince pie, and I resolved to renew my vows as the old ones ended.
levels.summary:
July found me at Westminster Hall on business and pleasure. After errands for Sir J. Minnes, I ordered a pocket ruler and flirted with the pretty daughter at Mrs. Howlett's shop while buying gloves. Then Mrs.

Lane and I went to the Crown, where I towzed her freely and did more than I am proud of, promising her what she wanted to hear about marriage. I resolved never to do so again.

Later I rode to the Wells looking for my dog, found instead a company of citizens singing in four or five parts under a tree, and delighted in it beyond any pleasure I had known. I also followed the Commons to the Lords and saw the King in crown and robes give his royal assent.

September brought more temptation. I dined at Mr. Povy's lavish house, visited Bartholomew Fayre with my wife, and then carried Mrs. Lane to Lambeth, where she refused the last thing—thank God. That night my heart ached for wronging my wife, and I vowed again never to do the like. In November I quarreled with Sir W.

Pen when I opposed his excusing the purser of the James; he stormed out like an asse, and I was glad to show I dare oppose him. Later I tried to overtake Howlett's daughter, talked with a pretty lodger at Unthank's, and consulted Dr. Turner about East India ships.

Captain Taylor brought me a plate, hoping I would get him allowance for his ship's demorage.

December I sat through office sessions, where Sir W. Warren openly defied Sir W. Batten, and Sir W. Pen secretly enjoyed it. At home my wife and I dined alone on a turkey and mince pie in a kind of state, poor wretches, keeping Christmas to ourselves.

My vows against plays and wine come to an end tomorrow, but I hope to make new ones, for I find great good and God's blessing in keeping them.

levels.sentence: A year marked by sudden bodily torment, and by my persistent and questionable amorous advances, all amid the usual round of office and acquaintance.
levels.paragraph: In May I was struck down by a violent fit of the stone, whose agony came and went as suddenly as it had arrived, eased only when I stumbled onto my knees. By autumn my desires turned toward Bagwell's wife, whom I coaxed and finally took by force, though it gave me little contentment. All the while I kept to my office business, dined with friends and kin, and heard troubling news of Tangier under Fitzgerald.
levels.summary:
This year began with a dreadful fit of the stone in May, one of the worst I ever remember. The pain struck my belly and back, and for two hours I cried and roared in anguish, unable to break wind or make water.

A glyster did little good, but by chance I got upon my knees in bed, and the pain began to ease, vanishing almost as suddenly as it came. I slept well that night, though I marveled at the strange turning point.

Come October, I was pursuing Bagwell's wife with promises of a place for her husband, and I caressed her at the office. By December, I walked to Deptford and contrived to be alone with her, sending Bagwell abroad; against her force I did what I wanted, yet found no contentment.

My days were otherwise filled with office business, dining with my uncle Thomas and later with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, and hearing from Mr. Cholmely that Tangier lies in a bad condition under Fitzgerald—a man of no honour or honesty, who offends everyone.

I also bought two silver tumblers, a small pleasure in a busy, wayward year.

- May: A Sudden Fit of the Stone

periods.brief: A year marked by sudden bodily torment, and by my persistent and questionable amorous advances, all amid the usual round of office and acquaintance.
periods.full:
This year began with a dreadful fit of the stone in May, one of the worst I ever remember. The pain struck my belly and back, and for two hours I cried and roared in anguish, unable to break wind or make water.

A glyster did little good, but by chance I got upon my knees in bed, and the pain began to ease, vanishing almost as suddenly as it came. I slept well that night, though I marveled at the strange turning point.

Come October, I was pursuing Bagwell's wife with promises of a place for her husband, and I caressed her at the office. By December, I walked to Deptford and contrived to be alone with her, sending Bagwell abroad; against her force I did what I wanted, yet found no contentment.

My days were otherwise filled with office business, dining with my uncle Thomas and later with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, and hearing from Mr. Cholmely that Tangier lies in a bad condition under Fitzgerald—a man of no honour or honesty, who offends everyone.

I also bought two silver tumblers, a small pleasure in a busy, wayward year.

levels.sentence: In 1665 I chased pleasure, wrestled with conscience, watched the plague turn London deadly, and uncovered a betrayal that threatened my Lord Sandwich.
levels.paragraph: This year brought me both delight and dread. I enjoyed stolen moments with Jane and Mrs. Martin, yet my conscience pricked me over my little girle. The plague's weekly bills grew horrifying, driving me to make my will. Amid it all, I inspected prize-goods and found Sir W. Berkeley had abused my Lord Sandwich's trust, leaving me to protect my Lord from the fallout.
levels.summary:
I began 1665 in pursuit of pleasure, dallying with Jane and Mrs. Martin, while also attending to business at White Hall and buying Hooke's Micrographia. My colic was cured by carrying a hare's foot, such is the power of fancy.

In February I spoke with Lady Sandwich about husbands for her daughters and the looseness of the times, and my wife took to bathing herself, though I doubt her cleanliness will last.

By August the plague was raging, with over four thousand dead in a week. I struggled with my conscience over my little girle, resolved to stop, and drew over my will. My she-cozen Porter's husband was sent to the Tower, but I dared not interfere.

In October I inspected prize-goods at Lord Bruncker's ship and discovered Sir W. Berkeley had abused my Lord Sandwich's order, tumbling and breaking the goods, saying my Lord's back was broad enough to bear it. Though the plague bill fell by 740, I renewed my vows, weary of the world's betrayals.

levels.sentence: In 1666, amid war, plague, and the Great Fire, I balanced public duty and private pleasure, only to find myself confronted at year's end by death, debt, and my own reckoning.
levels.paragraph: In 1666 I returned to a London reviving from plague, only to face the Dutch war and the Great Fire. I went about my business at Whitehall and the Exchange, took what pleasure I could with Mrs. Martin and others, and watched the nation split and the fleet suffer defeat. Through it all I kept my accounts, growing richer despite my spendthrift ways, but the drowning of Batters and the weight of my own calculations left me fearful. By December I was thankful for my plate and family's health, yet aware how close ruin stood.
levels.summary:
I began the year hopeful, with London shaking off emptiness and my paper on pursers well received, though Sir W. Pen objected to everything. My patron Lord Sandwich was in trouble, bound for Spain without a pardon, and I was bound for him in £1000. Through winter and spring I courted Mrs.

Martin and Doll Lane, worried over the plague's return, and heard of Tom Cheffin's sudden death. By summer the Dutch beat us badly, the Prince burned and Sir G. Ascue taken, and I found it a great alteration to write a sad letter to Lady Sandwich.

In August I was worth £5,700, the most my book ever made out, though the nation fasted and feared. I stole to Bagwell's house, was disgusted with myself, and continued my petty pleasures even as Parliament cut £150,000 from our wear and tear.

The Great Fire had burned the city, my father came to see it, and by autumn I took on a singing girl and moved my iron chests.

As winter closed, Batters's drowning frightened me more than ever, and my accounts showed prodigality—spending £644 more than last year—yet my worth still rose to £6,200, and I gave thanks for my plate and family's health.

levels.sentence: I navigated a year of public panic and private pleasure, refusing bribes while chasing kisses, mourning my father's health and Sir W. Batten's end, and finding joy in music, books, and the peace with Holland.
levels.paragraph: In 1667 I found England anxious about war and invasion, yet I took comfort in wine, women, and song. I refused a hundred-pound bribe, tended to Navy business, and watched my father suffer a terrible fit. The year ended with peace rumours, a new servant named Willet, and Sir W. Batten on his deathbed. Through it all, I remained a man of appetites and ambition.
levels.summary:
This year was a whirl of public alarms and private comforts. The Court feared a French landing and Dutch war, while our fleet lay unpaid; I refused a hundred-pound bribe to keep my integrity, yet could not keep my hands off Doll Lane, Betty Michell, Mrs. Martin, or my maid Nell.

I took delight in Knipp's singing, the flagelette, Boyle's Hydrostaticks, and the news of peace.

At the Office I fought for the fleet's pay and drew up the Victualler's stores, though money was ever wanting. My father's sudden fit and suffering saddened me deeply, and I resolved to bring him to town. I watched Sir W. Batten decline and heard Lord Sandwich's monstrous spending lamented.

Even in official business, from Carcasse's vexations to Pett's shame and the Tangier committee, I schemed to preserve my interest, and I basked in being called the only happy man of the Navy.

The domestic thread ran through it all: quiet dinners with my wife, new servant Willet, Uncle Thomas in mourning, and my own building plans. My eyes troubled me, my conscience pricked me, but I ended the year still chasing pleasure, from a scanty dinner and a masked lady at the playhouse to a visit to Mrs.

— at Westminster.

levels.sentence: In 1668 I balanced naval business and parliamentary danger against pleasures and secret amours, until my wife discovered my pursuit of Deb and broke my peace.
levels.paragraph: This year I navigated public duties and private desires, from preparing naval defences against Parliament to stealing kisses and following wanton women. My amours with Mrs. Martin, Doll Lane, and others gave me delight but also guilt, and my neglect of Lord Sandwich pricked my conscience. The discovery of my pursuit of Deb, our servant, brought my wife's fury and my own shame, forcing me to sign a promise to give her up. Through it all, I found moments of mirth in plays, music, and company, yet the fear of ruin and the weight of my own failings never left me.
levels.summary:
In 1668 my life swung between the public stage of White Hall and the Office and the private shadows of secret meetings and guilty pleasures. I spent months preparing our naval defence against a jealous Parliament, giving account to committees and brooding over possible ruin. At the same time I pursued Mrs.

Martin, Doll Lane, and Bagwell's wife, visited booksellers' wives, and followed a pretty woman through the streets. I enjoyed plays, music, and dancing, bought Montaigne's Essays and a recorder, and took pride in my wife's portrait, yet Lord Sandwich's reproach for my rare letters followed me all year.

My domestic life was shaken in November when my wife discovered my dealings with Deb, our maid. Though I had kissed her and given her money, I denied it until forced to confess. My wife cursed me, threatened to leave, and demanded a signed promise never to see or speak to Deb again.

I signed it, but lied to myself about keeping it, and ended the day in the most perfect confusion of face and heart, sorrow and shame. The year closed with me still struggling to keep my place in the world, both in the King's service and in my own house, knowing my peace was broken.

I enjoyed plays, music, and dancing, bought Montaigne's Essays and a recorder, and took pride in my wife's portrait, yet Lord Sandwich's reproach for my rare letters followed me all year.

My domestic life was shaken in November when my wife discovered my dealings with Deb, our maid. Though I had kissed her and given her money, I denied it until forced to confess. My wife cursed me, threatened to leave, and demanded a signed promise never to see or speak to Deb again.

I signed it, but lied to myself about keeping it, and ended the day in the most perfect confusion of face and heart, sorrow and shame. The year closed with me still struggling to keep my place in the world, both in the King's service and in my own house, knowing my peace was broken.

periods.paragraph: This year I navigated public duties and private desires, from preparing naval defences against Parliament to stealing kisses and following wanton women. My amours with Mrs. Martin, Doll Lane, and others gave me delight but also guilt, and my neglect of Lord Sandwich pricked my conscience. The discovery of my pursuit of Deb, our servant, brought my wife's fury and my own shame, forcing me to sign a promise to give her up. levels.sentence: In the spring of 1669, I gave in to restless lusts—pursuing Mrs Jowles at Maidstone, meeting Bagwell's wife and Deb in London—while my eyes and conscience ailed, and I prepared for a voyage abroad amid business and family cares.
levels.paragraph: That spring I was driven by wandering desires, from the willing Mrs Jowles at Maidstone to the coy Deb in Smithfield, yet each pleasure was shadowed by trouble and fear. Business at the Navy Office chafed me, the Duke of York fumed, and my eyes grew worse as I labored at my accounts. Still, I found moments of country beauty, old monuments, and merry suppers with my wife and friends, though my mind was seldom at rest.
levels.summary:
In March I rode to Maidstone, pretending to call on Captain Allen’s wife so I might see her daughter Mrs Jowles, a fine, free lady. I walked the town, climbed the steeple, gave money to an old man beating flax, and admired the Medway valley.

That night I stayed at Allen’s, talked over old stories with Mrs Jowles, kissed and touched her freely, and believed I might have had all had there been time and place. I walked home through snow, and wrote that she was certainly a whore, but a brave and comely one.

In April my thoughts turned to Deb, my wife’s former maid. I sent my coachman to Jewen Street to enquire after her aunt, then met Bagwell’s wife in Moorfields, though too crowded for anything. Later I saw Deb on Holborne Hill, followed her into a blind alehouse, kissed and touched her, but she was coy and modest.

I gave her 20s. and arranged to meet again. My coach had gone, and I was troubled; at Povy’s dinner I was merry, but fear of what I had newly done spoiled my content.

In May my wife went out before dawn for May-dew, and I fretted until she returned safe. At Whitehall the Duke of York railed against the Council of Trade, and I kept quiet to avoid heartburnings.

I dined with Lord Crew, heard of the old gentry’s fear of London, and called on Mrs Martin, who bragged of her husband’s worth. My brother John told me my sister was far gone with child, and I was uncertain whether to be pleased or troubled. My eyes ailed as I worked on my accounts with W.

Hewer, preparing for a voyage abroad, and I ended the month with a merry outing to the Park and The World’s End with my wife, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman.

periods.label: 1660s

levels.sentence: In the 1660s I served the King, chased advancement and pleasure, faced plague and fire, and wrestled with my own guilt, all while trying to keep my place in the world and in my house.
levels.paragraph: In the 1660s I rose as a Clerk of the Council and worked hard at the Navy Office, yet my diary is full of temptations and falls. I chased Mrs Lane, Doll Lane, Bagwell's wife, and Deb, while vowing again and again to reform. The decade brought plague, the Great Fire, and war, and I watched public men and my own patrons struggle. Through it all I counted my growing estate and thanked God for my family's health, though my peace was often broken by my own misdeeds.
levels.summary:
I began the decade as a Clerk of the Council, anxious about Downing's intentions, and soon learned the ways of Whitehall.

My family was woven through these years: my mother set out for Brampton, my father needed support, my wife endured my neglect, and I took pleasure in small comforts like a firkin of butter and a velvet coat.

Plague and fire overshadowed the middle years, and I struggled to do my duty for the Navy while Parliament and the Court were in turmoil. I inspected prize-goods, drew up stores, and sent sad letters to Lady Sandwich after our losses.

I also indulged my appetites with many women, from Mrs Lane and Doll Lane to Bagwell's wife and eventually Deb, and each time I resolved to stop, only to fall again.

By the end of the decade my household had been shaken when my wife discovered my dealings with Deb, and I signed a promise never to see her again. I grew richer, worth over six thousand pounds, but my conscience pricked me and my eyes ailed.

I closed the decade still serving the King, still straying, and still afraid that my peace might never be fully restored.

periods.brief: In the 1660s I served the King, chased advancement and pleasure, faced plague and fire, and wrestled with my own guilt, all while trying to keep my place in the world and in my house.
periods.full:
I began the decade as a Clerk of the Council, anxious about Downing's intentions, and soon learned the ways of Whitehall.

My family was woven through these years: my mother set out for Brampton, my father needed support, my wife endured my neglect, and I took pleasure in small comforts like a firkin of butter and a velvet coat.

Plague and fire overshadowed the middle years, and I struggled to do my duty for the Navy while Parliament and the Court were in turmoil. I inspected prize-goods, drew up stores, and sent sad letters to Lady Sandwich after our losses.

I also indulged my appetites with many women, from Mrs Lane and Doll Lane to Bagwell's wife and eventually Deb, and each time I resolved to stop, only to fall again.

By the end of the decade my household had been shaken when my wife discovered my dealings with Deb, and I signed a promise never to see her again. I grew richer, worth over six thousand pounds, but my conscience pricked me and my eyes ailed.

I closed the decade still serving the King, still straying, and still afraid that my peace might never be fully restored.

periods.sentence: In the 1660s I served the King, chased advancement and pleasure, faced plague and fire, and wrestled with my own guilt, all while trying to keep my place in the world and in my house.
periods.paragraph: In the 1660s I rose as a Clerk of the Council and worked hard at the Navy Office, yet my diary is full of temptations and falls. I chased Mrs Lane, Doll Lane, Bagwell's wife, and Deb, while vowing again and again to reform. The decade brought plague, the Great Fire, and war, and I watched public men and my own patrons struggle. Through it all I counted my growing estate and thanked God for my family's health, though my peace was often broken by my own misdeeds.
